items.title: ROLE OF INSECTS IN AGRICULTURE AND ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: Abstract: Insects are among the most ancient and successful organisms on Earth, having existed for over 400 million years. They form the most diverse group of living organisms, constituting more than 75% of all known animal species. Found in almost every habitat, insects play essential roles in agriculture, natural ecosystems, climate regulation, biodiversity maintenance, and food webs. Their interactions with plants, animals, and microorganisms create intricate ecological networks that support life on Earth. In the context of agriculture, insects occupy a unique dual position: they are both indispensable allies and challenging adversaries. Beneficial insects contribute to pollination, soil formation, nutrient cycling, and natural pest regulation, thereby facilitating sustainable agricultural productivity. Conversely, insect pests cause extensive crop losses, transmit plant diseases, and damage stored food, resulting in significant economic impacts globally. In an era of rapid climate change, land-use transformation, and pesticide overuse, the conservation and management of insect populations have become crucial. Understanding their ecological functions and integrating this knowledge into agricultural practices is a key step toward achieving sustainability, food security, and environmental resilience. Keywords: Environment, ecology, balance, ecosystem
authors: Neha Negi, Jag Mohan, Bharti Gautam, Babita Bharti and Ridhima Arya

items.title: Family environment, health risk behaviors, and mental health among chinese five-year vocational education students: a cross-sectional network analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background Adolescent mental health problems, particularly depression and anxiety, pose a global public health challenge. Family environment and health risk behaviors are key influencing factors, yet their complex interrelationships with psychological symptoms remain unclear. This study employed network analysis to investigate these associations, aiming to identify core symptoms and potential gender differences. Methods A total of 1,601 students were recruited from two higher vocational colleges in Nanning, Guangxi, using a cluster random sampling method. Adolescents' family environment, health risk behaviors, and mental health status were assessed using the Family Environment Scale, the Student Health Status and Influencing Factors Questionnaire, and the Mental Health Scale for Middle School Students, respectively. The EBICglasso method was used to estimate networks and derive centrality indices, followed by the Network Comparison Test to evaluate gender differences. Results "Depression" and "Anxiety" exhibited the highest strength centrality as core symptoms. Family "Cohesion" and "Conflict" served as key bridge nodes connecting health risk behaviors to mental health. The strongest association was observed between "Sleep deprivation" and "Depression." No significant gender differences were found in network structure. Conclusion Depression and anxiety are central to adolescent mental health problems, with family cohesion and sleep deprivation representing important intervention targets. Family-based emotional communication training and sleep health promotion may hold preventive value.

items.title: Risk factors for seizures in patients with brain metastases: integrating clinical features and molecular markers.
items.abstract: Brain metastases (BM) affect nearly 30% of patients with solid tumors. Despite this prevalence, the mechanisms underlying brain tumor-related epilepsy (BTRE) in this population remain incompletely elucidated. This study aims to investigate risk factors associated with seizure occurrence in patients with BM, focusing on histology and molecular markers of the primary tumor. We conducted a retrospective cohort study on 325 patients who underwent surgical resection of BM between 2014 and 2019. Clinical, radiological, and molecular data were analyzed using univariate and multivariable regression models to assess seizure risk factors. Overall Survival (OS) was assessed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression models. Seizures occurred in 32% of patients. Frontal (P<0.001) and parietal (P=0.05) locations were significantly associated with seizure occurrence. Ovarian cancer exhibited the highest seizure prevalence (80%, P=0.001), followed by melanoma (44%), breast (35%), and colorectal cancer (34%). Regarding molecular status, we found a significant association between seizures and both BRAF mutations in melanoma (P=0.03) and HER2 positive subtype breast cancer (P=0.01). Seizure occurrence at onset correlated with improved OS (P=0.01). Our findings suggest an association between seizure risk and molecular status of the primary tumor, specifically BRAF mutations in melanoma and HER2+ breast cancer subtype. Additionally, we found an improved OS in BM patients experiencing seizures at onset of disease. These findings are exploratory and warrant confirmation in larger cohorts; this could help refine seizure-risk estimation and prognostic assessment in surgically treated patients with brain metastases.

items.title: Longitudinal evolution of O-(2-[18F]-fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET metrics in serial imaging during glioblastoma progression.
items.abstract: Most studies evaluating O-(2-[18F]-fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine (FET) PET for glioblastoma progression rely on single-scan assessments, leaving diagnostic uncertainties in cases with borderline tracer uptake. We evaluated metabolic activity evolution during the transition of glioblastoma progression using serial FET PET to determine whether longitudinal parameter changes improve diagnostic certainty. Between 2016 and 2026, 182 patients with glioblastoma undergoing 690 dynamic FET PET scans (median, 3; range, 2-12) were retrospectively evaluated. Eligible cases required documented progressive disease according to RANO 2.0 criteria and serial FET PET at least 2 time points (at suspected progression and within a 6-month prior window). Static PET parameters, ie tumor-to-brain ratios (TBRmean, TBRmax) and metabolic tumor volume (MTV), and their longitudinal changes were evaluated according to PET RANO 1.0 criteria, alongside additional dynamic PET parameters (time-to-peak). Single-scan metrics and serial changes were compared in cases with borderline uptake. Ninety patients with 102 confirmed progression events met all selection criteria (median interscan interval, 2.7 months). At progression, TBRmean, TBRmax, and MTV increased significantly (P < .001). Median percentage increases were modest for TBRmean (+4%) and TBRmax (+17%), whereas MTV exhibited a substantial expansion (+182%). In cases with borderline uptake, applying a longitudinal MTV increase criterion of ≥40% per PET RANO 1.0 substantially improved progression detection to up to 89%, yielding a 14% higher diagnostic detection rate compared to single-scan thresholds. In glioblastomas with documented RANO 2.0 progression, integrating longitudinal MTV changes markedly improves diagnostic certainty over single-scan uptake metrics, particularly in challenging cases with borderline uptake.

items.title: Defining and managing NF1-related peripheral nerve sheath tumors at risk for malignant transformation: Consensus from the Atypical Neurofibroma Symposium.
items.abstract: People with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) are at risk for developing peripheral nerve sheath tumors (PNSTs) ranging from benign neurofibromas to high-grade sarcomas. PNSTs known as atypical neurofibromas are at increased risk for malignant transformation. In 2017 the term ANNUBP (atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential) was proposed for PNSTs at increased risk for malignant transformation based on histopathologic features. Subsequently it was recognized that PNSTs not meeting ANNUBP criteria could still have concerning clinical, imaging and molecular features. A State of the Science conference addressed how to define these pre-cancerous PNSTs and reached consensus regarding clinical management and priority areas of research. Key recommendations from this symposium include: (1) using a combination of histologic, molecular and imaging features to define pre-malignant "at-risk" PNST; (2) recognizing that people with NF1 may be divided into "higher-risk" and "average-risk" for MPNST based on features such as their germline NF1 variant, internal tumor burden and history of malignancy or radiotherapy and; (3) the need to validate consensus screening and surveillance strategies based on personal and tumor-related risk factors. These recommendations will advance the ability to standardize care, and potentially fuel research that enables early diagnosis, prevention of malignant transformation and improved outcomes.

items.title: FLT3 Kinase Inhibition Reshapes the Neuronal Transcriptome to Suppress Seizures.
items.abstract: Approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy are refractory to current anti-seizure medications, highlighting the need for new, mechanism-based therapeutic approaches. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), a receptor tyrosine kinase classically studied in hematopoiesis and leukemia, is also expressed in neurons, although its function in the brain remains largely unexplored. Our prior work identified small-molecule FLT3 inhibitors (FLT3i) as unexpected enhancers of potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 (KCC2), a neuron-specific chloride transporter essential for maintaining GABAergic inhibition. Here, we applied a functional genomics framework in mouse primary neurons and human stem cell-derived neurons to define FLT3i-induced transcriptional programs, revealing conserved gene networks governing synaptic function and ion channel regulation. A complementary CRISPR/Cas9-based screen of candidate transcription factors identified FLT3-responsive neuronal gene regulatory networks linked to epigenetic remodeling and neuroinflammatory signaling. We further demonstrate that KW-2449, an orally bioavailable FLT3 inhibitor, penetrates the blood-brain barrier, elevates KCC2 expression in vivo for up to 24 hours, and significantly reduces seizure susceptibility in a kainic acid-induced mouse model of epilepsy. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for FLT3 in neuronal function and establish proof-of-principle for FLT3 inhibition as a mechanistically supported candidate strategy warranting further development as a next-generation anti-seizure therapy.

items.title: The 2026 Taiwan headache society guideline on the use of treatments targeting the CGRP pathway.
items.abstract: The introduction of CGRP-targeted therapy has markedly influenced migraine care in Taiwan, together with accumulating evidence and clinical experience. Therefore, the Treatment Guideline Subcommittee of the Taiwan Headache Society updated its 2022 consensus on preventive migraine therapy, with a specific focus on CGRP-targeted therapies. This updated guideline also provides evidence-based recommendations and practical guidance on the use of gepants following their introduction in Taiwan. After reviewing recent clinical trials, meta-analyses, and international guidelines, and integrating expert panel opinions, we developed this new guideline to update the treatment options, recommended populations, timing of initiation and discontinuation, and practical considerations for CGRP-targeted therapy, organised into ten clinical questions. According to the current consensus, preventive treatment is recommended for patients with ≥4 headache days per month, significant disability, failure of or contraindications to acute therapy, complicated migraine with severe aura (such as hemiplegic migraine or migrainous infarction), or when patient preference favours prevention after balancing potential benefits and risks. Currently, CGRP-targeted therapies for migraine prevention include anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies, namely erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and eptinezumab, as well as small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists, including rimegepant and atogepant. In this 2026 updated guideline, CGRP-targeted therapy is listed as one of the first-line treatment options for both episodic and chronic migraine prevention. A history of failure of multiple preventive medications is not required before initiating CGRP-targeted therapy, as early initiation may provide better migraine control than delayed treatment. For both episodic and chronic migraine, the Taiwan Headache Society recommends that CGRP-targeted therapy may be continued for up to 12 months. This update is crucial for improving migraine care and highlights the importance of continuous CGRP-targeted therapy, rather than premature or unnecessary treatment interruption.

items.title: Branched optimal transport for stimulus to reaction brain mapping.
items.abstract: A central problem in systems neuroscience is to determine how an external stimulation is propagated through the brain so as to produce a reaction. Current deterministic and stochastic control models quantify transition costs between brain states on a prescribed network, but do not treat the transport network itself as an unknown. Here we propose a variational framework in which the inferred object is a graph/current connecting a stimulation source measure to a reaction target measure. The model is posed as an anisotropic branched optimal transport problem, where concavity of the flux cost promotes aggregation and branching. The support of an optimal current defines a stimulus-to-reaction routing architecture, interpreted as a brain reaction map. We prove existence of minimizers in discrete and continuous formulations and introduce a hybrid stochastic extension combining ramified transport with a path-space Kullback-Leibler control cost on the induced graph dynamics. This approach provides a mathematical mechanism for inferring propagation architectures rather than controlling trajectories on fixed substrates.

items.title: Global disparities in dengue, climate, and extreme weather research: a bibliometric analysis of alignment with disease burden and climate-driven vector suitability.
items.abstract: Dengue is a climate-sensitive vector-borne disease that imposes a substantial public health burden in tropical and subtropical regions. Temperature, rainfall, and extreme weather can affect mosquito ecology, human exposure, and the environmental suitability for transmission. This study characterized the global research landscape of dengue and extreme weather and examined whether country-level research output corresponded to dengue burden and climate-driven vector suitability. The Web of Science Core Collection was searched on 22 May 2026. Publication trends, collaboration networks, journals, authors, co-cited references, citation bursts, keyword patterns, and thematic evolution were examined using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the bibliometrix R package. Country-level publication output was linked to estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 dataset, the socio-demographic index for 2021, and mean index-p values for 1990-2022. Associations between publication output and dengue burden were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation among countries classified as dengue-endemic. A total of 290 publications from 2008 to 2026 met the eligibility criteria. Annual publication output increased overall and remained comparatively high after 2020. The United States contributed the largest number of publications, followed by China, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Brazil. The literature connected tropical medicine and infectious disease epidemiology with environmental health, climate science, vector ecology, modeling, and public health. Major themes included climate change, temperature, rainfall, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, extreme weather, Aedes vectors, transmission modeling, risk prediction, and early warning. Among 80 countries classified as dengue-endemic, publication output was positively correlated with the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) in 2023 (Spearman's ρ = 0.32, P = 0.004, n = 80) and the disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) rate in 2023 (ρ = 0.36, P < 0.001, n = 80). In contrast, its association with the estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) in ASIR from 1990 to 2023 was not statistically significant (ρ = 0.20, P = 0.070, n = 80). Several dengue-endemic countries with comparatively high disease burden or long-term climate-driven vector suitability had no eligible Web of Science-indexed publications in the present dataset. Research on dengue and extreme weather has expanded, and publication output showed modest positive associations with contemporary dengue burden among dengue-endemic countries. However, research output was not significantly associated with the long-term trend in dengue incidence, and substantial geographic disparities remained. The separate assessment of burden, research output, and climate-driven vector suitability identified geographic areas that may warrant closer consideration when research capacity, surveillance support, and equitable international partnerships are developed.

items.title: Influence of sex, puberty, and childhood psychopathology on developmental trajectories of the visual P300 across adolescence.
items.abstract: Research indicates the visual P300 decreases across adolescence due to maturation of neural attention networks. However, there is limited research examining whether assigned sex at birth and puberty influence this neurodevelopment. A blunted visual P300 has also been linked with internalizing and externalizing psychopathology, but it is unclear whether childhood psychopathology predicts changes in the P300 across adolescence. The present study examined whether sex, pubertal development, and childhood internalizing and externalizing symptoms predicted trajectories of the visual P300 across adolescence. The sample included 531 New York youth (45.5% female; 89.4% White; 19.7% Hispanic) who completed a flanker task to elicit the visual P300 at ages 9, 12, 15, 18, and 21 (2010-2025). Multilevel growth modeling indicated that the visual P300 was characterized by a quadratic decrease from late childhood to early adulthood; males showed a slower rate of change than females. Females with greater age 12 pubertal development showed a faster rate of change. Males with higher age 9 externalizing symptoms and depression symptoms had blunted baseline P300s. Age 9 internalizing and externalizing symptoms did not relate to slope. Results highlight the need to better understand the developmental of neural indicators of attentional processing that have been linked to future psychopathology.

items.title: A brief intervention highlighting counter-stereotypical role models changes children's gender stereotypes about values and careers.
items.abstract: Care-oriented values and careers are vital, yet men and boys remain less engaged with them. We tested a brief, preregistered role-model intervention to reduce children's gender stereotypes about communion (caring for others) and agency (achievement and independence). We also examined whether this intervention would narrow gender differences in children's own values and career interests. 7- to 10-year-olds from the U.S. and Canada (N = 244; 121 boys, 123 girls) viewed 6 animated vignettes about fictional children who grew up to choose careers aligned with their values. In the "stereotypical" condition, girls were communal and entered communal careers, while boys were agentic and entered agentic careers. In the "counter-stereotypical" condition, these pairings were reversed. A third, "counter-stereotypical + status" condition added wealth cues to both communal and agentic careers. Compared with the stereotypical condition, both counter-stereotypical conditions weakened children's gender stereotypes about communal and agentic values and careers. They also reduced gender differences in children's own communal values and career interests, although these effects were smaller and less consistent. Wealth cues did not strengthen the intervention. These findings suggest that counter-stereotypical role models are a promising, scalable method for combating stereotypes that steer boys away from communion-though likely one component of broader efforts.

items.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation.
items.abstract: The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.

items.title: Association of Self-Reported Sleep and Circadian Variability and Moral Judgements and Decision-Making.
items.abstract: Sleep and social processes are bidirectionally interrelated. Circadian factors such as sleep duration, quality, and chronotype can influence social processing, including moral judgements and decision-making. We investigated the associations of self-reported sleep and circadian factors with measures of human moral and social judgements, including online vigilantism, aversion to causing and witnessing harm, and generosity. A total of 109 healthy adults (18-39 years) completed an observational online survey of self-report measures of sleep and circadian factors (quality, chronotype, sleep regularity, social jetlag), as well as self-report or behavioural measures related to moral concerns, such as willingness to engage in online vigilantism, aversion to causing and witnessing harm to others, and generosity (the Dictator Game). We found significant associations between increased online vigilantism and earlier chronotype, higher sleep regularity, and less social jetlag (r > 0.20, all p 0.20, all p 0.06). Hierarchical regression analyses identified moderate effect sizes for sleep regularity and (to a lesser extent) social jetlag as significant contributors to vigilantism and aversion to causing and witnessing harm (R2 > 0.21, all p < 0.05), after controlling for sociodemographic characteristics, mental health conditions, and medication intake. A small, non-significant effect size was identified for sleep quality and dictator game generosity (R2 = 0.13, p = 0.06). The findings highlight the importance of considering sleep and circadian regularity in human moral judgements and decision-making.

items.title: Day-to-day peer and family stress as proximal correlates of self-injurious thoughts during adolescence.
items.abstract: Theory and research both highlight interpersonal stressors as precipitants to self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) during adolescence. Yet, little is known about near-term risk or which types of interpersonal stressors (e.g., peer and/or family) are most likely to precipitate adolescent SITBs. This study used an intensive longitudinal design to examine whether peer- and family-related stress were associated with adolescents' same- and next-day self-injurious thoughts. Participants were 154 female adolescents aged 12-17 years (77.3% White). Youth were oversampled for risk such that 73.4% ( n = 113) were at high risk for future SITBs. Youth completed a 30-day ecological momentary assessment procedure assessing interpersonal experiences and SITBs. Multilevel models showed that peer stress predicted same-day nonsuicidal self-injury urges and suicidal ideation (SI), whereas family stress predicted same-day nonsuicidal self-injury urges only. Neither peer nor family stress predicted next-day self-injurious thoughts. Exploratory models examining bidirectional effects showed that non-suicidal self-injury urges predicted next-day peer and family stress while SI predicted next-day family, but not peer, stress. Findings suggest that daily interpersonal stress is proximally associated with self-injurious thoughts during adolescence and underscore the importance of studying these processes in real time. Results may have implications for ecological momentary interventions to interrupt interpersonal risks for SITBs.

items.title: Prevalence and Correlates of Service-Connected Disability Among U.S. Military Veterans.
items.abstract: Objective Veterans with general medical or mental health conditions that were caused or exacerbated by military service may be eligible for U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) service-connected disability compensation, which entails financial support, access to health care, and long-term benefits. Using a contemporary, nationally representative sample of U.S. military veterans, the authors compared the sociodemographic, military, and clinical characteristics of veterans with and of those without service-connected disability and identified factors associated with receipt of benefits for mental health versus general medical conditions. Methods Data were analyzed from 2,636 U.S. military veterans who participated in the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study. Participants reported service-connected disability status, disability rating, and primary service-connected conditions and completed assessments for sociodemographic characteristics, military status, trauma exposure, psychiatric disorders, and general medical conditions. Results Overall, 39% of veterans reported having a VA service-connected disability. Multivariable analyses indicated that younger age, longer military service, a greater number of deployments, lifetime psychiatric diagnosis, and greater medical burden were independently associated with increased odds of receiving service-connected disability benefits. Having a service-connected psychiatric disability was strongly associated with lifetime psychiatric diagnosis, a greater number of deployments, and military sexual trauma. Conclusions A substantial percentage of U.S. veterans receive service-connected disability benefits. Veterans receiving these benefits represent a clinically complex population with substantial cumulative service-related exposures and elevated mental and general medical health burdens. These findings may inform clinical care, resource allocation, and policies aimed at addressing the long-term health needs of veterans with service-connected disabilities.

items.title: Contemporary Revisional Bariatric Surgery Reflects Historical Primary Procedure Selection: A Fourteen-Year Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Revisional metabolic and bariatric surgery is part of long-term obesity management. Contemporary revisional workload includes operations after previous surgery at the treating institution and external referrals. We assessed changes in primary procedure selection and the temporal origin of preceding institutional surgery among observed internal revisions over 14 years. We retrospectively analyzed bariatric procedures performed during 2012-2025, grouping primary operations into 2012-2018 and 2019-2025. Internal and external revisions were distinguished by previous bariatric operations at the study institution. Indications for all 228 revisions underwent retrospective case-by-case clinical adjudication from available records. Among 2,343 bariatric procedures, 2,115 were primary and 228 revisional. Primary procedure distribution differed between eras (global P < 0.001), with fewer SG and more OAGB, RYGB and primary SADI-S in the later era. Of the 228 revisions, 71 (31.1%) were internal and 157 (68.9%) external. Indications were weight-related only in 120 (52.6%), reflux-related only in 61 (26.8%), combined in 39 (17.1%), and other complications in eight (3.5%). Among 71 internal revisions, 57 (80.3%) followed a previous institutional operation performed in Era 1; 40/54 (74.1%) internal revisions performed in Era 2 followed Era 1 institutional surgery. Contemporary revisional activity reflects preceding institutional operations and referral patterns. Unequal follow-up between eras and incomplete ascertainment of revisions elsewhere preclude conclusions about comparative revisional risk. Revision workload should therefore be interpreted alongside previous surgical history, procedure mix, referral patterns, and follow-up maturity.

items.title: The breast at perimenopause.
items.abstract: Perimenopause, defined as the transition between regular menstrual cycles and confirmed menopause, is characterized by erratic hormonal secretions and metabolic disorders which can have potential consequences for breast health. During this period, benign breast diseases may worsen, adversely affecting quality of life and possibly increasing the risk of breast cancer. These aspects have implications for the clinical management of these women. Breast cancer has different characteristics and risk factors for women in premenopause, perimenopause and postmenopause. This narrative review analyzed available data on these risk factors during perimenopause, including the impact of hormonal contraception and menopause hormone therapy. Incidence and mortality, and subtypes of breast cancer differ in women according to the stage of menopause, ethnicity, the level of income of countries and public health resources. These inequalities in risk levels, breast cancer types and prognosis may affect screening and preventive strategies - an issue clinicians should be aware of. Among breast cancer survivors, the menopausal transition raises the question of a shift from tamoxifen, usually used in perimenopausal women, to aromatase inhibitors, indicated after menopause; the treatment may complicate the diagnosis of menopause. Women in the perimenopause may experience differences in the frequency and severity of endocrine therapy side effects.

items.title: Threshold-triggered microneedle applicators: converting user-applied force into reproducible dissolving microneedle insertion for global vaccination.
items.abstract: Vaccine distribution in low- and middle-income countries is constrained by healthcare workforce shortages - averaging one health worker per 435 people - and by unreliable facility infrastructure. Dissolving microneedle patches address these bottlenecks by reducing cold-chain reliance and enabling dose-sparing immunization through skin-resident antigen-presenting cells. However, reproducible administration by minimally trained personnel remains a critical barrier to deployment. This review examines five representative applicator architectures from the peer-reviewed and patent literature, detailing how each converts variable user input into a standardized, high-velocity impact that overcomes rate-dependent skin viscoelasticity to ensure deep, reproducible stratum corneum penetration. Each is evaluated against three prerequisites for global deployment: sufficient insertion force and rate, low-cost manufacturability, and power independence. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Patents were searched from 2004 to June 2026. Validation remains weighted toward mechanical and ex vivo testing, so the field's engineering maturity runs ahead of its translational readiness. Realizing the public health potential of microneedle vaccines will require user-independent operation, scalable manufacturing, and integration of threshold-triggered mechanisms with patch design so that delivered dose and immune response are reproducible. Eliminating pre-loaded energy components is central to the cost competitiveness that mass immunization in resource-limited settings demands.

items.title: Evaluation of the Systematic Use of Multilocus Variable Number Tandem Repeat Analysis in Comparison With gp60 Genotyping to Detect Cryptosporidium parvum Clusters.
items.abstract: Many cryptosporidiosis outbreaks of various origins have been reported in recent years. In 2010, Cryptosporidium was responsible for 8.6 million cases and 3759 deaths of foodborne origin worldwide. The aim of this study was to compare a multilocus variable number tandem repeat analysis (MLVA) scheme and standard gp60 genotyping to detect clusters of Cryptosporidium parvum. We compared the performance of an MLVA scheme and that of gp60 genotyping to detect C parvum clusters in France. During a 2-year period, stool samples received at the coordinating center of the French National Reference Centre for Cryptosporidiosis, Microsporidia and Other Digestive Protozoa were systematically analyzed via the MLVA scheme and gp60 genotyping. A total of 1025 stools were analyzed, leading to 748 fully interpretable MLVA profiles on C parvum isolates. We identified 53 genotypes using gp60 and 455 MLVA profiles. Based on the investigation of >10 cases with the same MLVA profile, 5 clusters were investigated; probable foodborne origins were identified. MLVA showed higher discrimination than gp60, facilitating the investigation of clusters, but gp60 remained useful. Alerts notifying health authorities of potential outbreaks should be based on threshold values for MLVA. MLVA could facilitate the detection and investigation of C parvum clusters. Further gp60 sequencing is still required. Defining appropriate alert thresholds could improve surveillance, outbreak investigation, and prevention strategies for public health.

items.title: Self-Perceived Recovery from Substance Use Problems among Young Adults: A Pooled Cross-Sectional Analysis of National Survey Data.
items.abstract: Introduction Recovery among young adults with substance use problems is increasingly understood as a multidimensional process, but population-based evidence on self-perceived recovery, mental health recovery, treatment access, and barriers to care remains limited. Methods We conducted a pooled cross-sectional secondary analysis of 2021-2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health Public Use File data. The analytic sample included adults aged 18-29 years who reported ever having had a problem with their own alcohol or drug use and had valid information on self-perceived recovery. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined associations of past-year substance use disorder severity, self-perceived mental health recovery, depression, suicidality, sociodemographic characteristics, family income, and survey year with self-perceived recovery from an alcohol or drug problem. Results Among 6,371 respondents, 68.1% reported being in recovery from an alcohol or drug problem. Compared with no past-year substance use disorder, moderate and severe substance use disorder were associated with lower odds of self-perceived recovery, particularly severe substance use disorder (adjusted odds ratio = 0.31, 95% confidence interval: 0.23-0.41). Self-perceived recovery from a mental health problem was strongly associated with self-perceived recovery from an alcohol or drug problem (adjusted odds ratio = 3.15, 95% confidence interval: 2.52-3.94). Treatment pattern and classified treatment need were not independently associated with recovery status in the 2022-2023 subsample. Among young adults with perceived unmet treatment need, common barriers included believing one could handle substance use alone, not being ready to start treatment, not being ready to stop or reduce use, and not knowing where to obtain treatment. Conclusion Self-perceived recovery from an alcohol or drug problem was common but did not necessarily indicate absence of past-year substance use disorder. Findings support integrated, developmentally responsive recovery systems that address substance use, mental health, and access barriers while recognizing that recovery was self-perceived rather than clinician-defined.

items.title: Estimating the summer 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration needed to avoid winter vitamin D deficiency in Australia.
items.abstract: Australian guidelines recommend an end-of-summer concentration of at least 60 nmol/L to avoid winter vitamin D deficiency. To estimate (1) the risk of end-of-winter vitamin D deficiency (25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration [25(OH)D] < 50 nmol/L) according to end-of-summer 25(OH)D concentrations and (2) the required 25(OH)D concentration at the end of summer to avoid vitamin D deficiency through winter across Australian regions. Prospective population-based cohort study, nested within a randomized controlled trial (the Sun-D Trial). We recruited residents of Australia's eastern states via the Australian electoral roll, media, and email lists. Sun-D Trial control group participants who did not use vitamin D supplements (N = 251). Vitamin D deficiency at end of winter. The overall prevalence of vitamin D deficiency at the end of winter was 41%. In those whose end-of-summer 25(OH)D concentration was ≥60 nmol/L, it was 31%. In the absence of vitamin D supplementation, end-of-summer 25(OH)D concentrations of 84 to 98 nmol/L, depending on location, are required to ensure a 90% probability of maintaining vitamin D adequacy through winter. Only 8% of participants in Victoria and Tasmania and less than half in other jurisdictions met these targets. Higher end-of-summer 25(OH)D concentrations than currently recommended are required to avoid vitamin D deficiency in winter in Australia. Clinicians might consider recommending vitamin D supplementation during winter for patients who do not meet end-of-summer targets, as this is likely the most practical option for mitigating the risk of winter deficiency, particularly for people living at higher latitudes.

items.title: Gaps in implementation of controlled substance diversion prevention safeguards: A cross-sectional study of hospitals in Ontario, Canada.
items.abstract: Drug diversion, defined as the theft or loss of opioids and other controlled substances (CS), is a persistent concern in hospitals, threatening patient safety, staff well-being, and public trust. Despite rising CS losses in hospitals, the implementation of hospital safeguards remains poorly characterized. This study examined diversion prevention practices and identified gaps in hospital practice. A cross-sectional study of hospitals in Ontario, Canada, was conducted using an online self-assessment tool for diversion risks, hosted by the Institute for Safe Medication Practices Canada. Participating hospitals rated their implementation of 61 diversion safeguards on a 5-point scale, from 0 (not implemented) to 4 (used more than 90% of the time), grouped into 7 domains. Between May 2022 and October 2025, 36 hospitals completed the assessment. Substantial vulnerabilities were identified across multiple domains. The lowest mean scores were observed in the auditing domain (mean of 1.5), where a high percentage of hospitals reported rarely or never implementing key safeguards, including 83% for audits of anomalous prescribing, 78% for audits of CS waste, 75% for anonymous reporting mechanisms, and 78% for timely investigation of reports. The governance and education domain also had low scores for implementation (mean of 2.1), with similarly high percentages of hospitals reporting rarely or never implementing staff diversion prevention education (89%) and interprofessional diversion response teams (69%). Critical gaps exist in the implementation of auditing, governance, and education safeguards for CS diversion in hospitals, with key safeguards rarely or never implemented in 69% to 89% of hospitals despite regulatory and accreditation standards.

items.title: Herpes zoster in rheumatoid arthritis and in relation to biologic/targeted synthetic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs: a Swedish national study.
items.abstract: To assess and compare the incidences of herpes zoster (HZ) in rheumatoid arthritis patients (RA) receiving biologic/targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (b/tsDMARDs), in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA, and general population. We identified all patients with RA in Sweden 2014-2024, and b/tsDMARD starts among them, through register linkages. For each b/ts-DMARD treatment start, five age/sex-matched population controls were selected. A history of HZ was defined as a listing with an ICD-10 code for HZ and/or dispensation of an antiviral drug up to one year before treatment start. Incident HZ was defined as the first HZ ICD-10 code during follow-up accompanied by prescription of an antiviral within 90 days. 77694 unique RA patients contributed to the following: 69962 subjects in the b/tsDMARD-naïve cohort, and 20033 TNFi-, 9410 non-TNFi-, and 4023 JAKi-treatment episodes. Based on 95 incident HZ cases (incidence rate (IR) 2.0, 95% confidence interval 1.6-2.4 per1000 person-years) with TNFi, 55 cases (IR 2.4, 95% CI 1.8-3.1) with non-TNFi, 41 cases (IR 5.1, 95% CI 3.7-6.9) with JAKi, 561 cases (IR 1.5, 95% CI 1.4-1.6) in b/tsDMARD-naive RA and 494 cases (IR 0.6, 95% CI 0.6-0.7) in the general population, the multivariable-adjusted hazard ratio (using TNFi as reference) with JAKi was HR = 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-3.0 and HR = 0.9; 95% CI 0.6-1.3 for non-TNFi. The incidence of a first ever HZ is higher in b/tsDMARD-naïve patients compared to general population, is further and similarly increased in patients receiving TNFi or non-TNFi, and yet higher in those starting JAKi.

items.title: Operationalizing smoking cessation models of care in oncology settings: a mixed-methods systematic review.
items.abstract: Integrating smoking cessation care with cancer management is a pillar of high-quality care. However, implementation remains variable and little is known about how smoking cessation models are effectively operationalized in oncology settings. To describe the characteristics, adaptations, and operationalization of evidence-based smoking cessation models in oncology settings, and identify approaches to the definition, measurement, and evaluation of implementation outcomes. This systematic review followed JBI methodology. Five databases were searched to identify reports published between January 2010 and August 2025. Included reports described the implementation of evidence-based smoking cessation care models or process enhancements in hospitals or cancer services delivering care to people with cancer. Data sources were treated as complementary, synthesized separately, and integrated as a narrative summary. Thirty-eight reports were included, identifying 33 implementation strategies and 38 models of care. Models of care included 3As (n = 18), 5As (n = 11), and 4As (n = 1) brief interventions, and specialist care models (n = 8). Nurses were commonly delegated to initiate smoking conversations (10/38) and facilitate referrals (17/38). Implementation strategies varied, however, education and training programs, and technology enhancements were commonly reported. Adaptation was a prominent feature and identified across most implementation strategies (24/33). Reporting and measurement of implementation outcomes was limited and not always aligned to a defined framework. Brief 3A models, nurse involvement, and opt-out referral pathways are core characteristics of smoking cessation care in oncology settings. Adaptation and tailoring components appear as a common feature of implementation strategies. Further reporting and evaluation of implementation outcomes is warranted.

items.title: Statin-Ezetimibe Therapy and Incident Myocardial Infarction Across Modified Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Groups: A Nationwide Target Trial Emulation.
items.abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain. Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation. Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95). Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.

items.title: Reasons to Retain Policy Research Within the Scope of the National Institutes of Health.
items.abstract: Recent developments at the NIH raise concerns that the agency is narrowing its definition of mission-relevant research to exclude studies evaluating the effects of public policies or explicitly seeking to generate evidence for policymakers. This position piece outlines five reasons why policy research and engagement with policymakers should remain within the scope of NIH-supported mental health and substance use (i.e., behavioral health) research. First, public policies shape behavioral health outcomes at a population scale, and exclusion of policy research would therefore undermine efforts to understand and improve behavioral health outcomes. Second, policy research is integral to translational behavioral health science-including science that is focused on clinical interventions. Third, effective evidence-informed policymaking-such as that envisioned by the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018-requires policy-relevant research evidence. Fourth, communicating findings from policy research is not lobbying or advocacy per NIH definitions. Fifth, policy research represents a small share of NIH funding, accounting for approximately 2% of NIMH funding. NIH's mission is to generate knowledge that improves health. Understanding how policy shapes health-and communicating that knowledge to those responsible for policymaking-is essential to fulfilling that mission.

items.title: Lessons From the Development and Assessment of a Community Participative Mental Health and Substance Policy Agenda in the Bronx, NY.
items.abstract: In 2025, the Bronx, one of New York City (NYC)'s Boroughs, experienced the largest mental health and substance use disparity in NYC. The goal of this practice report is to describe and evaluate the 2025 community-centered policy agenda proposed by a community collaborative named the # not62 campaign. The campaign has fostered constructive partnerships over 2 decades to improve the Bronx's residents' well-being. Experts in health services, social work, and behavioral health used measures of legitimacy, feasibility, and government support to assess each policy agenda item, with the purpose of assisting in prioritizing the agenda items and supporting long-term community engagement. Policy Agenda items ranged from supporting more educational and training initiatives for Bronx Youth in the health care field to health education campaigns to reduce stigma and monetary incentives to ensure patient compliance with treatment. Results from the evaluation indicate that the initiatives with the greatest potential for success at the present time are those related to improving and expanding access to mental health services through existing NYC-funded programs and investing in higher education in academic programs related to the health service workforce. Although the Bronx is faced with health disparities in multiple mental health and substance use conditions, this community participatory process showcases the Bronx's community strength and long-term commitment to participatory processes.

items.title: Rare diseases and orphan therapies in India: burden and pharmacopeial considerations.
items.abstract: Rare diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that collectively impose a substantial health burden despite their low individual prevalence. India is estimated to have 70-80 million individuals affected by rare diseases and has implemented the National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021) to improve diagnosis and treatment access. However, information on the pharmacopeial status of therapies used in rare disease management remains limited. A structured review was conducted using official Indian government resources, rare-disease registries, established rare-disease organisations, and published literature retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Searches were conducted up to 24 June 2026. Search concepts included rare diseases, India, prevalence, epidemiology, treatment, pharmacotherapy, orphan drugs, and individual disease names combined with terms such as "India", "prevalence", "treatment", "management", "therapy", and "pharmacotherapy". The pharmacopoeial status of medicines was assessed using Indian Pharmacopoeia 2026 (IP 2026), the USP-NF Online resource, and the 12th Edition of the European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.). Approximately 450 rare diseases are currently registered in India, predominantly genetic, metabolic, and immunological disorders. Evaluation of the most prevalent rare diseases revealed that many symptomatic therapies are included in IP, USP, and Ph. Eur. However, several orphan drugs, enzyme replacement therapies, and disease-specific treatments, including agalsidase alfa, asfotase alfa, ivacaftor, carglumic acid, and alglucosidase alfa, lack monographs in one or more major pharmacopoeias. Rare diseases remain a significant public health challenge in India. Strengthening rare disease registries, expanding pharmacopeial coverage of orphan therapies, and enhancing regulatory harmonization are essential to improve access to quality-assured treatments and support long-term patient care.

items.title: Multidimensional Protein-Based Antimicrobial Materials: Construction, Mechanisms, and Applications.
items.abstract: Bacterial contamination and associated infections remain persistent threats to global public health. Proteins, as renewable biomacromolecules with diverse functional groups, programmable hierarchical structures, and favorable biocompatibility, have emerged as versatile building blocks for antimicrobial materials. Through self-assembly, amyloid-like aggregation, interfacial engineering, and chemical or physical functionalization, proteins can be constructed into zero-dimensional (0D) micro/nanoparticles, one-dimensional (1D) fibers, two-dimensional (2D) films and coatings, and three-dimensional (3D) hydrogels, aerogels, and sponge scaffolds. Dimensional architecture extends beyond morphological classification: it governs active-site exposure, interfacial contact, mass transport, mechanical properties, and antimicrobial-agent retention and release, thereby determining bactericidal activity, resistance to bacterial adhesion, and antibiofilm performance. Nevertheless, the relationships connecting dimensional construction, interfacial structure, antimicrobial mechanism, and application-specific performance remain fragmented. This review therefore adopts dimensionality as the central framework for critically examining the structural design, assembly, and functionalization of protein-based antimicrobial materials across 0D-3D architectures. Particular emphasis is placed on how dimensional features regulate the antimicrobial mechanisms involving membrane disruption, cell-wall hydrolysis, reactive oxygen species generation, physical bacterial trapping, controlled antimicrobial release, and resistance to bacterial adhesion. Recent advances in the applications of these antimicrobial materials, categorized by their dimensional architectures, are further evaluated across biomedicine, food preservation, functional textiles, and agriculture in relation to their operating environments and functional requirements. Finally, challenges concerning mechanistic validation, long-term stability, scalable manufacturing, biological safety, and application-specific evaluation are critically discussed to identify barriers to practical implementation and future directions for technological translation. Emerging opportunities in AI-assisted protein and peptide design, precise interfacial engineering, and multifunctional integration are further highlighted to guide the rational development of next-generation protein-based antimicrobial materials.

items.title: A Dual Effort Choice paradigm reveals pharmacological divergence between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation within the same task environment
items.abstract: Motivation loss is a transdiagnostic symptom, prevalent across neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Current treatments fail to effectively treat this symptom domain, giving it significant clinical importance. The fields of neuroscience and drug development have primarily focused on extrinsic motivation, whereby an animal must perform an action to receive an external food or water-based reward. However, many of our everyday activities are facilitated by intrinsic motivation, where completing an action is inherently rewarding. By utilising tasks focused only on extrinsic motivation, we may miss critical neurobiological and therapeutic differences between motivation types. Previous work has shown divergence in drug effect between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation tasks across a wide range of clinically-used drugs, indicating translationally-relevant differences across motivation domains that warrant further study. Therefore, the aim of this work was first to develop a task capable of simultaneously quantifying intrinsic and extrinsically motivated behaviour within the same task environment. Secondly, to use this task to further investigate this neurochemical divergence by examining a wide range of clinically-relevant drugs within this new task context. Here, we find that a pharmacological reduction in dopaminergic signalling reduced motivation across both extrinsic and intrinsic options within the new task, though this effect was mechanism dependent. In contrast, acute serotonergic and dopaminergic signalling increase produced a more heterogenous pattern, indicating nuanced mechanistic differences even when presented in the same task environment. Therefore, this task provides a new approach for characterising drug effects on distinct forms of motivated behaviour that may go unnoticed using conventional assays.

items.title: Mathematical Relationships Between Brains and Consciousness
items.abstract: A chief aim of the neuroscience of consciousness is to derive how states of conscious experience (i.e., qualia) are related to supporting brain states (e.g., patterns of neural activation within patterns of neural connectivity). This aim goes beyond identifying neuronal correlates of consciousness (NCC) on the one side, and beyond structural descriptions of conscious experience (e.g., qualia structure) on the other side. The ultimate goal is to link these two sides by mapping specific neuronal states or mechanisms to specific conscious experiences. Relating two or more phenomena in science often takes the form of mathematical mappings, such as equations (e.g., E = mc^2). This raises the possibility that there also are mathematical mappings that relate conscious states to brain states. Here we review empirical work on mapping neuronal spiking activity to conscious contents. We specifically contrast pioneering paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge loci”, in the form of NCC, with paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge laws”, such as relating psychometric to neurometric functions. We then examine how these paradigms are augmented by mapping structural descriptions of conscious experience to structural descriptions of neuronal activity.

items.title: Central Chronotropic Incompetence After Rhombencephalitis.
items.abstract: Background Rhombencephalitis is a rare inflammatory brainstem condition. Central cardiovascular dysfunction, specifically chronotropic incompetence (CI), remains an underrecognized chronic sequela. Case summary A 50-year-old man was evaluated for progressive exertional dyspnea. Cardiopulmonary and structural cardiac assessments were unremarkable. One year earlier, he survived idiopathic biopsy-proven necrotizing rhombencephalitis, successfully managed with immunomodulatory therapy. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing unmasked profound CI. At the 2-year follow-up, peak oxygen uptake and workload normalized, but functional limitation persisted because of a rigidly blunted maximal heart rate. Discussion This unique case demonstrates a persistent decoupling of the heart-brain axis. The isolated CI may reflect focal structural destruction of medullary sympathetic premotor neurons, despite preserved intrinsic cardiac function. Take-home messages In otherwise unexplained exercise intolerance following brainstem injury, central autonomic dysfunction may be considered as a potential contributor. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing may help identify a disproportionate chronotropic limitation when routine cardiac investigations are unremarkable.

items.title: Tongue ultrasonography as a quantitative biomarker for oropharyngeal dysphagia in neuromuscular disorders: a systematic review.
items.abstract: Oropharyngeal Dysphagia (OD) is a prevalent and potentially life-threatening complication of Neuromuscular Disorders (NMDs). Tongue ultrasonography is an inexpensive, non-ionising, point-of-care technique that permits quantitative assessment of lingual muscle structure, but its value as a biomarker of OD across NMDs has not been systematically appraised. This systematic review aims to synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, reliability and clinical utility of quantitative tongue ultrasonography as a biomarker of OD in adults with NMDs. We systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for studies correlating quantitative tongue-ultrasound parameters, Tongue Thickness (TT) or Echo Intensity (EI), with instrumental swallowing assessment in adults with NMDs, following the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Study selection, data extraction and risk-of-bias appraisal were performed independently by two reviewers. Six studies (n = 10-38 per cohort) met the inclusion criteria. Reduced TT was a consistent marker of lingual atrophy in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and correlated with oral-phase swallowing impairment, whereas functional measures of tongue strength were stronger predictors of aspiration risk. In Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), increased TT reflected "pseudohypertrophy" from fatty and connective-tissue infiltration rather than preserved function and EI provided a complementary index of tissue quality in myopathic NMDs. Tongue ultrasonography is a promising, disease-sensitive biomarker for monitoring bulbar dysfunction in NMDs, but morphological indices should be integrated with functional swallowing data to predict aspiration risk. Standardized acquisition protocols and larger, longitudinal, multicentre studies are required before clinical implementation.

items.title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
items.abstract: Background In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. Purpose To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. Study type Cross-sectional cohort study. Population Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female). Field strength/sequence 3T; Magnetization prepared rapid acquisition with gradient echoes (MPRAGE) sequence (anatomical imaging) and a diffusion echo-planar imaging sequence with modified diffusion gradients for spherical tensor encoding (μFA measurement). Assessment MPRAGE images underwent cortical and subcortical segmentation to obtain regions of interest. MD and μFA maps were derived from diffusion MRI data. μFA, MD, and volumes were compared between FTD variant carriers (n = 5 symptomatic, and n = 7 asymptomatic) and familial non-carriers. Statistical tests Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent confidence intervals were computed to analyze between-group differences in outcomes while controlling for age (alpha = 0.05). Results FTD variant carriers exhibited significantly lower insula μFA than non-carriers (η 2 p = 0.22). Post hoc contrasts showed significantly reduced insula μFA in symptomatic carriers compared to non-carriers (d = 1.57). Mean μFA in asymptomatic carriers (mean ± standard error (SE): 0.454 ± 0.010) was not significantly different to that in non-carriers (mean ± SE: 0.471 ± 0.009, p = 0.465), nor in symptomatic carriers (mean ± SE: 0.430 ± 0.012, p = 0.290). Data conclusion μFA is reduced in the insula, a region vulnerable to early atrophy in FTD, reflecting microstructural changes in genetic FTD with greater effect sizes than MD and volume. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy Stage 2.

items.title: miR-665 Ameliorates Neuroinflammation After Intracerebral Hemorrhage by Modulating Myeloid Cell Polarization via Targeting STAT3.
items.abstract: Background Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation contributes to secondary injury after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the role of miR-665 remains unclear. Methods An ICH rat model was established. A combination of techniques, including Neurological scoring, brain water content measurement, histology and molecular assays were employed to assess miR-665, the STAT3/NF-κB pathway, myeloid polarization and inflammation. Stereotaxic miR-665 agomir/antagomir delivery verified its function. The targeting relationship between miR-665 and STAT3 was confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In vitro experiments were performed in Hemin-stimulated BV2 cells with miR-665 mimics/inhibitor, followed by flow cytometry detection of cell polarization and inflammatory factor analysis. Rescue experiments with STAT3 overexpression were conducted both in vivo and in vitro . Results After ICH, miR-665 was downregulated andinduced excessive activation of the STAT3/NF-κB signaling axis in peri-hematomal tissue, accompanied by M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Upregulation of miR-665 ameliorated neurological function, reduced brain edema, promoted M2-like/repair-associated polarization, and suppressed inflammation, whereas miR-665 downregulation aggravated injury. Dual-luciferase assay confirmed that miR-665 directly targets STAT3. In vitro , miR-665 overexpression inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation and further suppressed the downstream NF-κB signaling, reversing the Hemin-induced M1-like/pro-inflammatory polarization. STAT3 overexpression counteracted the protective effects of miR-665. Conclusion Downregulated miR-665 after ICH exacerbates neuroinflammation by promoting M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization via disinhibition of STAT3 and subsequent activation of NF-κB signaling. Upregulating miR-665 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation and facilitating M2-like/repair-associated myeloid cell polarization, highlighting the miR-665/STAT3 regulatory cascade as a promising therapeutic target for post-ICH neuroinflammation.

items.title: Vorasidenib in IDH1/2-mutant low-grade gliomas: a prospective study on volumetric MRI and seizure outcome.
items.abstract: Background The IDH1/2 inhibitor vorasidenib demonstrated efficacy in residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant gliomas after surgery. However, there is lack of knowledge regarding factors predicting the probability of response. Patients and methods We conducted a prospective single-centre study on 54 grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant astrocytomas and IDH1/2-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas treated with vorasidenib. MRI response (2D and 3D) and seizure outcome were longitudinally assessed. Factors associated with response were explored using regression models. Results With a median follow-up of 17.5 months, vorasidenib induced progressive tumour shrinkage on MRI, with median volume reductions of - 12.2% at cycle 6, -27.8% at cycle 12, and -55.5% at cycle 18. Best volumetric response was CR in 1 patient, PR in 5, MR in 9, SD in 31 and PD in 7. The ORR (CR + PR + MR) was 28%. Eighteen patients who had focal grade 3 areas showed similar volumetric response and ORR. 9/12 (75%) patients with baseline seizures achieved ≥50% reduction or seizure freedom. MRI response correlated with early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction. Vorasidenib was generally well tolerated, with liver enzyme elevation being the main adverse event. Conclusions Vorasidenib induced sustained tumour shrinkage and seizure control. Early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction were associated with MRI response.

items.title: Cognitive trajectories before and after the Global Financial Crisis: a 20-year cohort study of older adults in Australia.
items.abstract: Objectives Macroeconomic shocks may influence cognitive function in later life. We examined cognitive trajectories around the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis (GFC) among older Australians and whether resilience factors modified these trajectories. Methods We used longitudinal data from 1,872 community-dwelling adults in the 60-66-year cohort of the PATH Through Life Study. Participants were followed from 2001-2002 to 2020-2021 across six waves (∼4-year intervals). Perceived financial impact of the GFC and co-occurring distress/anxiety were assessed at wave 3 (2009-2010) and categorised as no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety. A global cognitive composite was calculated and standardised as z-scores. Linear mixed-effects models estimated pre-GFC change, change during the GFC, and post-GFC change. Effect modification by 13 resilience factors was examined. Results Most reported no financial impact (66.2%); 23.8% reported impact without distress/anxiety, and 10.0% with distress/anxiety. Pre-GFC cognitive decline was similar across groups. During the GFC, all groups experienced a decline (-0.057 to -0.091 SD). During the post-GFC period, cognition declined further at similar rates in the no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety groups: -0.073 SD/year (95% CI: -0.080, -0.066), -0.070 (-0.079, -0.060), and -0.069 (-0.083, -0.056), respectively. Higher physical health-related quality of life attenuated the decline during the GFC, while greater life satisfaction and positive social support were associated with slower post-GFC decline. Discussion Cognitive decline increased around the GFC period and continued thereafter, with no evidence that these changes differed by perceived financial impact or distress/anxiety. Causal attribution to the GFC is limited by the absence of an unexposed comparison group.

items.title: Olfactory network variability is associated with odor identification and cognitive performance in mild cognitive impairment.
items.abstract: BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early marker of Alzheimer's disease pathology and predicts dementia conversion in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the pathophysiological role of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) variability within olfactory networks remains unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize seed-based dFC variability across olfactory pathways in MCI with odor identification impairment (MCI-OII) and examine its associations with olfactory and cognitive performance.MethodsNinety-seven patients with MCI were recruited and subdivided into MCI-OII and those without odor identification impairment (MCI-NOII), along with 97 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent neuropsychological assessment, olfactory testing, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Seed-based dFC variability was computed using a sliding window approach. Correlation and exploratory mediation analyses examined associations among abnormal dFC, odor identification, and cognition.ResultsCompared to MCI-NOII and HC, MCI-OII exhibited increased dFC variability between the left piriform cortex/right insula and right caudate nucleus, and between the left insula and left middle frontal gyrus. For the connection between the left insula and left cerebellar lobule VI, dFC variability showed a graded pattern from MCI-OII to HC to MCI-NOII. Increased caudate-centered dFC variability was associated with poorer odor identification, memory, and executive performance. Furthermore, exploratory mediation analyses suggested indirect associations involving odor identification, caudate-centered dFC variability, and memory or executive function.ConclusionsMCI-OII is characterized by increased olfactory-network dFC variability, particularly in caudate-centered pathways. These findings suggest that dFC variability may serve as a candidate network-level marker of concurrent olfactory impairment and cognitive dysfunction in MCI.

items.title: Reading the gene in the eye: Clinical discrimination and confidence-accuracy calibration in genetic frontotemporal dementia.
items.abstract: BackgroundClinical evaluation in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) occurs under diagnostic uncertainty, particularly in stages when symptoms are subtle, heterogeneous, and may resemble primary psychiatric disorders. Less attention has been devoted to clinicians' evaluation of judgment reliability.ObjectiveTo characterize clinicians' decision-making and confidence calibration when evaluating individuals at risk for genetic FTD within the Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia Initiative (GENFI) cohort.MethodsTwo analyses were conducted. First, determinants of diagnostic confidence were examined in asymptomatic participants (N = 837) using univariate analysis and logistic regression including demographic, neuropsychological, and clinical factors. Second, clinicians' ability to predict disease, based on mutation status, was evaluated in a subset of asymptomatic individuals (N = 133) using signal detection theory. Discriminability (d'), response bias (c), and metacognitive performance (meta-d' and M-ratio) were estimated from confidence ratings.ResultsLower diagnostic confidence clustered around boundary neuropsychiatric presentations characterized by subtle symptoms, lower cognitive scores, older age, and features including psychiatric history and current depression or anxiety. Clinicians predicted mutation status above chance level (accuracy ≈ 0.71), with better identification of non-carriers than carriers. Metacognitive modelling revealed imperfect calibration between confidence and accuracy (d' ≈ 1.06; meta-d' ≈ 0.85; M-ratio ≈ 0.80), indicating that confidence carried information about reliability but did not fully reflect available evidence.ConclusionsClinical decision-making in genetic FTD shows moderate accuracy, with lower confidence at the interface between neurodegenerative and psychiatric symptoms. Improving clinical decisions requires not only diagnostic accuracy, but also awareness of when judgments are correct. Biomarkers and structured assessments may help identify cases requiring evaluation.

items.title: The Effects of Methylphenidate on the EEG of Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
items.abstract: AimsAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (AD/HD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder, with the symptom profile consisting of hyperactivity, impulsivity and inattention. Currently methylphenidate is the most widely used treatment for AD/HD. Studies on mixed stimulant use have found that stimulants result in normalisation of electroencephalogram (EEG) activity during an eyes-closed resting condition. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of Methylphenidate alone on the EEG of children with AD/HD and to extend the investigation into the gamma band.MethodFifty children with AD/HD and 50 typically developing children, between the ages of 8 and 12 years, participated in this study. Clinical participants were assessed for AD/HD at an initial session at which an EEG was performed. They returned within 1 week for a medication assessment, and a second EEG was recorded 1.5 h after ingestion of 10 mg of methylphenidate. EEG was recorded during an eyes-closed resting condition, and Fourier transformed to provide absolute and relative power estimates in delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma bands.ResultsUnmedicated, the AD/HD group had elevated global absolute and relative delta, elevated posterior absolute theta, elevated posterior relative theta, reduced global relative alpha, and reduced global absolute and relative gamma activity compared to the control group. Methylphenidate ingestion was associated with a global increase in absolute and relative beta, and in relative gamma activity.ConclusionsSignificant increases in fast wave activity were observed with methylphenidate use. However, unlike past research, it is not clear that this should be considered as normalisation of the EEG.

items.title: Physical Functioning, Crime, and Cognitive Decline in Mexican Americans: A Multi-Level Analysis of Protective Interactions.
items.abstract: ObjectiveHispanic individuals are understudied in cognitive aging research and are disproportionately exposed to crime, yet the cognitive consequences of this exposure remain unclear. We examined whether county-level crime moderates the association between physical functioning (PF) and cognitive change among Mexican Americans aged 75 years and older without cognitive impairment at baseline.MethodsParticipants included 1,189 older adults from the Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly (HEPESE). Cognitive functioning was measured using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), PF was assessed using performance-based measures, and total crime was measured at the county level. Multilevel models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and cardiovascular factors.ResultsBetter PF was associated with higher MMSE scores. A significant interaction among PF, crime, and time indicated that the protective association between PF and cognitive functioning weakened as county-level crime increased. Higher PF predicted less cognitive decline in low- and moderate-crime areas, although this association was attenuated in moderate-crime contexts and largely absent in high-crime areas.DiscussionCounty-level crime may undermine the cognitive benefits of better PF in late life. These findings underscore the role of contextual factors in cognitive aging among older Mexican Americans and highlight potential targets for community-level prevention efforts.

items.title: The evolution of understanding of the lymphatic and glandular system: from topographical anatomy to 3D models.
items.abstract: During the 17 th century, European anatomy underwent a profound epistemological transformation, leading to the gradual abandonment of Galenic doctrines and the adoption of the experimental method. In this context, the discovery of the lymphatic system and the functional redefinition represented a major innovation in modern medicine. Through systematic dissections, vivisections, vascular injection techniques and microscopic observations, anatomists such as Gaspare Aselli (1581-1626), Jean Pecquet (1622-1674), Thomas Bartholin (1616-1680), Thomas Wharton (1614-1673), Niels Stensen (Stenon) (1638-1686) and Marcello Malpighi (1628-1694) helped to redefine the mechanisms of nutrition, absorption and circulation of bodily fluids. This paper analyzes the key stages of these discoveries, their theoretical significance and the epistemological impact on the transition from classical topographical description to modern three-dimensional simulation models and predictive diagnosis.
