items.title: Editorial: Harnessing optimal control for eco-epidemic stability: a vision for future ecosystems
items.abstract: The study conducted by Ghosh and Singh [6] analyzes an eco-epidemic model involving black alder, beetles, parasitoids, and predators under seasonal and annual variability. The authors show that phenological variability can significantly influence ecological coexistence and stability. This contribution highlights the need to account for temporal variation when assessing ecological interactions and considering management strategies, rather than relying solely on fixed or average environmental conditions.In terms of environmental transmission, Ramraj and Poornima [5] investigate the spread of primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) using an SEIDW model in which water reservoirs contribute to disease transmission. Their analysis considers the role of environmental transmission in infection persistence and examines how human and environmental factors affect disease dynamics. In addition, the paper links the threshold and stability analysis with optimal environmental control and demonstrates how environmental control interventions could be analyzed using a mathematical model.Optimal control theory is also applied beyond epidemiological and ecological systems to sustainable production. Ahammed et al. [4] examine biodiesel synthesis using mechanical agitation and ultrasound-assisted transesterification. Their comparative study considers how ultrasound can improve mass transfer and production efficiency, while optimization can support cost-conscious use of resources. This work illustrates the potential of mathematical optimization for technological processes in which efficiency and resource use must be considered together.A further contribution by Agboka et al. [1] develops a quantile-normalisation approach for interpreting and spatially prioritising areas of persistence-related mechanistic suitability for the tomato red spider mite (Tetranychus evansi ) in Africa under uncertainty. By focusing on spatial prioritisation and uncertainty, the study adds a pest-management perspective to the Special Issue. Its relevance lies in showing how modelling outputs can be made more interpretable for identifying areas that may warrant attention, while acknowledging uncertainty in suitability estimates.The HIV study by AlShamrani [3] considers a diffusion-based model incorporating inflammatory cytokines and adaptive immune impairment. The work examines how spatial diffusion, inflammatory processes, and immune impairment interact in HIV dynamics. By incorporating these mechanisms into a spatial model, the study broadens the analysis beyond homogeneouspopulation assumptions and provides a framework for investigating how spatial structure and immune processes influence infection dynamics.Several cross-cutting themes emerge from these contributions. First, threshold quantities help identify conditions associated with disease persistence, ecological coexistence, or transitions in system behaviour. Second, stability and resilience analysis provides information about how systems respond to perturbations and changing conditions. Third, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis is important because model parameters and environmental conditions are rarely known with complete precision. Finally, optimal control links mathematical analysis with the evaluation of feasible management strategies.The papers approach these themes from different perspectives: phenological variability shapes ecological interactions; environmental transmission affects epidemic dynamics; spatial structure and immune mechanisms influence HIV dynamics; uncertainty-aware spatial prioritisation supports pest-risk assessment; and optimization informs sustainable production. Taken together, these contributions demonstrate the breadth of mathematical approaches available for studying biological and environmental systems, while also showing that the methods and objectives must be tailored to the particular system under consideration.Future research could extend deterministic models to better represent changing environments and uncertainty. Stochastic modelling and robust optimization may help assess outcomes when parameters or external conditions are uncertain. Spatial, network, delayed, and multiscale models may provide more detailed representations of interactions across ecological and epidemiological scales. Data-driven methods, adaptive control, and model predictive control may also support interventions that can be updated as new information becomes available.Another important direction is the development of multi-objective control strategies that balance disease reduction, biodiversity conservation, production efficiency, cost, resource availability, and long-term sustainability. Such approaches are particularly relevant when improving one component of a system may produce unintended effects elsewhere. Their practical value will depend on transparent assumptions, appropriate validation, and careful treatment of uncertainty.This Special Issue shows how mathematical modeling can be used to bridge the gap between theoretical investigations and the issues that arise in ecology, epidemiology, environmental management, and sustainable production. Instead of describing the concept of stability as something new that needs to be addressed in management, the papers elaborate on well-known concepts using mathematical tools. Such future studies would enhance these links through the inclusion of analyses related to stability and resilience, along with assessments of uncertainty and spatial modeling in order to design interventions based on data. What matters most is not simply knowing if a modeled system is stable, but rather how its persistence, resilience, and management could be affected by uncertainties.

items.title: An ecological framework linking intratumoral microbiota to antitumor immunity in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
items.abstract: Intratumoral bacteria have been linked to antitumor immunity, but the relevance of these findings to laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma remains uncertain. We propose a framework that integrates absolute bacterial load, spatial and cellular localization, and the surrounding immune state. The framework distinguishes an association that may support risk stratification from a causal mechanism requiring temporal and experimental evidence. We specify candidate decision rules for detection above background, quantitative load categories, cellular association, and neutrophil enrichment with CD8 T cell exclusion. These rules require prospective calibration and must be locked before independent validation. A ranked sampling strategy prioritizes tumor tissue, safely obtainable adjacent mucosa, and blood while allowing restricted analyses when compartments are missing. Paired sampling around planned checkpoint blockade can characterize immune changes over time but cannot establish microbial causality by itself. Selective bacterial depletion, matched add-back, and immune perturbation in appropriate laryngeal models are needed to test the proposed mechanism. This approach retains taxonomic information while making the load and localization hypothesis measurable, clinically feasible, and open to refutation. It does not support empirical antibiotic treatment or current treatment selection from unvalidated microbial states.

items.title: Soil reclamation induced salinity decline is associated with shifts in bacterial, fungal and protistan communities and higher wheat yield in saline-alkali fields
items.abstract: Soil reclamation is widely practiced in saline–alkali land areas. However, limited research has focused on how reclamation duration regulates soil microbial communities and crop yield via modifying soil environmental conditions. In this study, high-throughput sequencing, ecological network analysis, and soil physicochemical characterization were integrated to investigate variations in soil properties, microbial community composition, and crop yield across saline–alkali fields with different reclamation durations (1, 5, and 10 years). The results showed that prolonged reclamation significantly reduced soil salinity and increased soil nutrient contents as well as wheat yield. The richness of fungi and protists increased with the extension of reclamation durations, whereas bacterial richness exhibited an opposite trend. Network-associated key taxa of bacteria, fungi and protists were significantly correlated with wheat yield, soil salinity, soil organic matter (SOM), total nitrogen (TN), as well as the activities of leucine aminopeptidase (LAP) and β-glucosidase (Glu). Structural equation modeling (SEM) further revealed that soil salinity was associated with soil physicochemical traits, network-associated key taxa and enzyme activities, altered the soil microecological environment, and ultimately affected wheat yield. In conclusion, reclamation durations mitigated soil salinity, which drove the screening of microbial taxa by soil microhabitats and reconstructed the overall microbial community structure, thereby influencing wheat productivity. These findings provide theoretical and technical support for the sustainable reclamation of saline–alkali land, health management of farmland soil, and stable improvement of grain productivity.

items.title: High-resolution mapping reveals trade-offs among tea production, food security and biodiversity conservation
items.abstract: Tea plantations are an important source of income across Asia and Africa, yet their land requirements may create trade-offs with food security and biodiversity conservation. Using satellite observations and cloud computing, we developed GlobalTea10m and assessed a composite score integrating yield and quality to represent potential economic benefits (SEconomic), food security, and ecological security across nine tea-producing countries. Here we show that five countries achieved relatively high performance in at least two dimensions. China showed the strongest overall balance, whereas India combined favorable food- and ecological-security profiles with weaker SEconomic. Sri Lanka had the highest SEconomic but lower food- and ecological-security scores. Rwanda and Tanzania showed contrasting imbalances, and Kenya underperformed in all three dimensions. Spatial overlaps with productive cropland and conservation-priority areas indicate potential land-use trade-offs but do not by themselves demonstrate reduced food production or ecological degradation. These results support spatial planning, improved plantation management, and value-chain development tailored to national conditions. Tea production shows uneven trade-offs among economic returns, food security, and biodiversity across major producing countries, with China achieving the strongest balance and Kenya underperforming in all three, based on 10-m satellite mapping and cross-country sustainability assessments.

items.title: Microbial Stewardship in Bioethics and Environmental Governance: A Minireview.
items.abstract: Background: Microbial communities constitutes essential components of health and ecosystem processes across people, animals, plants, and environments. However, the main focus of public policy is on pathogens and antimicrobial resistance while beneficial functions and microbial habitats are minimally considered. Objectives: This minireview offers a stewardship of how microorganisms can link bioethics, environmental governance, One Health, conservation, and emerging-biotechnology initiatives. Methods: A targeted narrative investigation of PubMed and Crossref through 4 November 2026, supported by publicly available policy documents was conducted. Intentional selection of peer-reviewed research and policy sources in English language was based on thematic relevance; no new data was collected. Results: Five ethical principles were identified as being interlinked within the synthesis. These included stewardship, intergenerational responsibility, justice, epistemic humility and respect for microbial communities. The study also explored the implications of the Nagoya Protocol, Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, digital sequence information, the 2024 United Nations declaration on antimicrobial resistance and the Quadripartite One Health framework. Practical considerations to incorporate into research include microbial biomarkers, sustained monitoring, interdisciplinary evaluation and meaningful engagement. Conclusion: Microbes, when treated as context-dependent ecological partners and potential risks, instead of as threats or globally beneficial agents, would optimally provide more adaptive, transparent, and fair governance, with attention to ecology, unreliability, and the risks and benefits distribution.

items.title: Dwarf Galaxy Halo Masses from Spectroscopic and Photometric Lensing in DESI and DES
items.abstract: Abstract We present the most precise and lowest-mass weak lensing measurements of dwarf galaxies to date, enabled by spectroscopic lenses from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and photometric lenses from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) calibrated with DESI redshifts. Using DESI spectroscopy from the first data release, we construct clean samples of galaxies with median stellar masses log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) =8.310.1 and measure their weak lensing signals with sources from DES, KiDS, and SDSS, achieving detections with signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) up to 12 for dwarf galaxies ( log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) < 9.25)—opening up a new regime for lensing measurements of low-mass systems. Leveraging DES photometry calibrated with DESI, we extend to a photometric dwarf sample of over 700,000 galaxies, enabling robust lensing detections of dwarf galaxies with combined S/N = 30 and a significant measurement down to log 10 ( M * / M ⊙ ) =8.0. The photometric sample is characterized using a self-organizing map calibrated with DESI spectroscopy, a methodology designed to scale to future surveys like Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST where spectroscopic coverage will be relatively limited. We show that the one-halo regime (scales ≲0.15 h −1 Mpc) is insensitive to various systematic and sample selection effects, providing robust halo mass estimates, while the signal in the two-halo regime depends on galaxy color and environment. These results demonstrate that DESI already enables precise dwarf lensing measurements, and that calibrated photometric samples extend this capability. Together, they pave the way for novel constraints on dwarf galaxy formation and dark matter physics with upcoming surveys like LSST.

items.title: The Multiphase Circumgalactic Medium of DESI Emission-line Galaxies at z ∼ 1.5
items.abstract: Abstract We study the multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM) of emission-line galaxies (ELGs) at z ∼ 1.5, traced by Mg II λ 2796, λ 2803 and C IV λ 1548, λ 1550 absorption lines, using approximately 8000 ELG-quasar pairs from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. Our results show that both the mean rest equivalent width ( W 0 ) profiles and covering fractions of Mg II and C IV increase with ELG stellar mass at similar impact parameters, but show similar distributions when normalized by the virial radius. Moreover, warm C IV gas has a more extended distribution than cool Mg II gas. The dispersion of Mg II and C IV gas velocity offsets relative to the galaxy redshifts rises from ∼100 km s −1 within halos to ∼200 km s −1 beyond. We explore the relationships between Mg II and C IV W 0 and show that the two are not tightly coupled: at a fixed absorption strength of one species, the other varies by several-fold, indicating distinct kinematics between the gas phases traced by each. We measure the line ratios, Fe II /Mg II and C IV /Mg II , of strong Mg II absorbers and find that at <0.2 virial radius, the Fe II /Mg II ratio is elevated, while the C IV /Mg II ratio is suppressed compared with the measurements on larger scales, both with ∼4 σ significance. We argue that multiphase gas that is not cospatial is required to explain the observational results. Finally, by combining with the measurements in the literature, we show the redshift evolution of CGM properties and estimate the neutral hydrogen, metal, and dust masses in the CGM of DESI ELGs—found to be comparable to those in the interstellar medium.

items.title: Mitigating effects of nonlinearities in homodyne quadrature interferometers
items.abstract: Homodyne Quadrature interferometers (HoQI) are an interferometric displacement sensing scheme proven to have excellent noise performance, making them a strong candidate for sensing and control schemes in gravitational wave detector seismic isolation. Like many interferometric schemes, HoQIs are prone to nonlinear effects when measuring displacements. These nonlinearities, if left unsuppressed, would substantially limit the use cases of HoQIs. This paper first shows a means of measuring and quantifying nonlinearities using a working HoQI and a mechanical resonator. We then demonstrate a method for real-time correction of these nonlinearities and several approaches for accurately calibrating the correction technique. By correcting in real time, we remove one of the biggest obstacles to including HoQIs in upgrades to future gravitational wave detectors. Finally, we discuss how to post correct data from HoQIs, suppressing even further the nonlinearity-induced errors, broadening the appeal of such sensors to other applications where measurement data can be reconstructed after the fact. We demonstrate all of this on a working HoQI system and show the measured suppression of nonlinear effects from each of these methods. Our work makes HoQIs a more broadly applicable tool for displacement sensing.

items.title: FEADME: Fast Elliptical Accretion Disk Modeling Engine
items.abstract: Abstract We present FEADME (Fast Elliptical Accretion Disk Modeling Engine), a GPU-accelerated Python framework for modeling broad Balmer-line emission with a relativistic elliptical accretion-disk formalism. Using JAX and NumPyro for differentiable forward modeling and Bayesian inference, FEADME enables reproducible analyses of large samples of disk-dominated emission-line profiles. We apply the framework to 237 double-peaked emitters (DPEs) and five tidal disruption events (TDEs) with disk-like H α emission, fitting three model families per spectrum and selecting the preferred model using the widely applicable information criterion (WAIC). After posterior-quality filtering, the disk-bearing active galactic nuclei (AGNs) sample contains 165 sources, and the TDE sample contains 27 usable epochs. Within the common elliptical-disk model, AGNs occupy a broad, continuous distribution of disk geometries and kinematics summarized by five phenomenological Gaussian-mixture morphology bins, while TDE and AGN parameters overlap in radial scale, local broadening, and emissivity slope. The TDE epochs tend toward lower fitted eccentricities and broader nondisk Gaussian components. Comparison with published circular-disk plus spiral-arm fits to the same AGN spectra produces substantially different distributions of inclination, radii, emissivity slope, and local broadening, demonstrating that these inferred parameters depend strongly on the treatment of profile asymmetry. Most AGNs and TDEs favor models containing a disk and an additional broad-line component, suggesting that disk emission commonly coexists with more isotropic or wind-driven gas. These results demonstrate FEADME ’s utility for population studies and the importance of a consistent asymmetry prescription when comparing disk structures across accretion environments.

items.title: Unveiling Multimessenger Emission from Hidden Cores of Microquasars
items.abstract: Abstract Microquasars are radio-emitting X-ray binaries with relativistic jets and are established sources of ∼100 TeV gamma rays, making them promising candidates for cosmic-ray acceleration. Motivated by recent detections of ∼100 TeV photons from Cygnus X-1 and multi-PeV photons from Cygnus X-3, we employ the Astrophysical Multimessenger Emission Simulator (AMES) to model their multimessenger emission from radio to ultrahigh-energy gamma rays. Our modeling suggests that particle acceleration is extremely efficient in the jet region. The observed ≳0.1 PeV gamma rays can originate from either pγ or pp interactions, depending on the location and physical conditions of the emission region, while also reproducing the lower-energy spectra. These configurations yield observationally testable predictions. In the poorly constrained 0.1–10 TeV band, the models predict either a deep valley, a mild suppression, or a power-law spectrum. Additionally, models involving compact emission regions comparable to the orbital separation predict strong variability, while those invoking more extended and static external zones show more stable behavior. We also provide a possible qualitative explanation for the energy-dependent modulation patterns, relying primarily on changes in the Doppler factor and external γγ absorption. In particular, explaining the PeV emission from Cygnus X-3 favors a compact emission region, for which a magnetic field strength of order 10 2 G is required. Finally, after accounting for pion and muon cooling, the predicted neutrino flux is suppressed, implying that detection is more challenging than previously thought.

items.title: The Environmental Switch in Black Hole Feeding: Bar-driven versus Merger-driven Growth in IllustrisTNG50
items.abstract: Abstract The relative roles of secular disk processes and galaxy interactions in driving the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain unclear. We present a time-resolved, per-galaxy analysis of SMBH mass assembly that explicitly tracks bar formation, merger events, and the environment along the main progenitor branches using the high-resolution IllustrisTNG50 cosmological simulation. We analyze barred and unbarred disk galaxies in isolated and nonisolated environments using physically motivated boundary definitions. We found that SMBH fueling pathways are regulated by the environment through the timing of bar formation relative to mergers. In isolated barred galaxies, stellar bars form early in dynamically cold disks and establish sustained, coherent accretion phases that regulate late-time SMBH growth. In contrast, in nonisolated galaxies, SMBH growth is dominated by early merger-driven accretion episodes, whereas bars form later and contribute weakly to the primary growth phase. Unbarred control samples show that mergers can trigger rapid SMBH growth without bars, but such growth remains episodic, whereas isolated disks without bars lack sustained accretion. These results suggest that SMBH-fueling pathways depend sensitively on environment through the relative timing of bar formation and merger activity. This study provides a unified time-domain framework linking galaxy environment, disk dynamics, and SMBH growth by resolving the temporal ordering of bars, mergers, and accretion.

items.title: Analytic solutions for spinning particles on near equatorial, plunging orbits in Kerr spacetime
items.abstract: This work presents, the first time, analytic solutions for the nearly equatorial, plunging motion of a spinning test-particle in Kerr spacetime. The equations of motion are solved at first-order in the small-body spin for all classes of plunging orbits with energy $E < 1$. The solutions incorporate the small precession of the orbital plane caused by the precession of the particle's spin. Additionally, we present the correction to the radius of the innermost bound circular orbit in closed form, and introduce a novel, Keplerian-like parametrization for generic plunging orbits. Our solutions will be useful in the modelling of inspiral-merger-ringdown waveforms with self-force methods and black hole perturbation theory.

items.title: Far-infrared Polarization Properties of Nearby Star-forming Regions: A New Compendium of SOFIA/HAWC+ Observations
items.abstract: Abstract We present a comprehensive polarimetric study of 26 nearby molecular clouds in four far-infrared bands (53–214 μ m) using 52 archival SOFIA/HAWC+ datasets, over half of which are unpublished. Far-infrared dust polarization observations probe the plane-of-sky magnetic field. To investigate scale-dependent trends, we group the molecular clouds by distance and analyze the data at common angular (25″) and common physical (0.052 pc and 0.32 pc) resolutions. The two shorter wavelengths are more impacted by smoothing, exhibiting a larger decrease in percent polarization. We analyze the polarization spectrum—the polarization fraction as a function of wavelength—and find that it depends more strongly on column density than dust temperature. We find a “falling” spectrum at the 0.052 pc resolution, but find a “flat” spectrum at the 0.32 pc resolution, suggesting that resolution plays an important role in the observed polarization spectra. We propose that warm dust grain emission in small-scale structures (≲ 0.1 pc) traces different magnetic field geometries only resolved in our near regime data. There is no preferred magnetic field orientation across our data, which suggests that the magnetic field in our ∼parsec-scale regions is decoupled from the large-scale field that is primarily parallel to the Galactic plane. The relationship between percent polarization and column density varies between clouds, but the correlation between percent polarization and polarization angle dispersion is consistent across regions. This compendium highlights the value of observing at multiple far-infrared wavelengths and enables additional population-level studies of magnetic fields and dust across star-forming environments.

items.title: HESS J1832-085: Evidence of a new gamma-ray binary candidate
items.abstract: The Galactic plane survey conducted by the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) has revealed numerous teraelectronvolt (TeV) sources, many of which remain unidentified. HESS J1832-085 is a point-like TeV source lacking a confirmed multiwavelength (MWL) counterpart. In this paper, we present evidence supporting a gamma-ray binary interpretation of HESS J1832-085 . We aim to investigate the nature of HESS J1832-085 using the available X-ray and Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data, complemented by a near-infrared (NIR) identification of a possible stellar companion and broadband radiative modeling, to assess its classification as a potential gamma-ray binary. Archival X-ray observations were examined to search for a counterpart and to characterize its spectrum and potential variability. We further analyzed ∼17.3 yrs of Fermi LAT data between 1 and 300 GeV to establish a possible gigaelectronvolt (GeV) counterpart of HESS J1832-085. We also examined archival NIR images from the UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS) and the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), together with 2MASS catalog photometry. The broadband emission was interpreted using models commonly applied to gamma-ray binaries. A potential X-ray counterpart was identified in archival X-ray data, exhibiting a hard, absorbed spectrum and moderate variability. We also identified a tentative GeV gamma-ray excess that is spatially consistent with HESS J1832-085 and the proposed X-ray counterpart. We further identified a candidate stellar counterpart in both the UKIDSS and 2MASS images, located in close spatial proximity to the X-ray counterpart. The adopted illustrative binary radiative model broadly reproduces the X-ray and TeV emission, but fails to explain the emission from the tentative GeV excess. Our results support HESS J1832-085 as a promising gamma-ray binary candidate , motivating dedicated MWL follow-up observations to confirm the source nature.

items.title: Axion magnetohydrodynamics and reconnection-driven axion bursts
items.abstract: We formulate axion magnetohydrodynamics beyond the ideal limit, retaining axion inertia and the essential physics of non-ideal plasmas from first principles. In this framework, regions where magnetic flux freezing breaks down acquire a new physical role: whenever $\mathbf{E} \cdot\ \mathbf{B} \neq 0$, magnetic dissipation acts as a localized source of axion radiation. We show that magnetic reconnection naturally excites mixed Alfvén-axion modes, enabling coherent energy exchange between magnetic fields and axions in magnetically dominated environments. In neutron stars and magnetars, this mechanism leads generically to transient axion bursts powered by reconnection--driven Alfvénic dissipation. We connect this production process to observational prospects and derive a characteristic sensitivity to the axion--photon coupling, complementary to searches based on static magnetic fields.

items.title: Suppression of star formation at the centre of barred AGN galaxies
items.abstract: Abstract We measured the Concentration (C) index of H α and CO (J = 2-1) in 17 nearby star-forming galaxies from the PHANGS survey. We have found four barred spiral galaxies with a C(H α)/C(CO) ratio of ~ 0.3-0.4, while the other 13 galaxies exhibit ratios of ~ 1 (ranging from 0.7 to 1.3). All four barred galaxies with low ratios host active galactic nuclei (AGNs), consistent with a scenario in which star formation is suppressed by mechanical and radiative feedback from the AGN. Therefore, negative feedback may be effective in these four barred galaxies even when AGN activity is relatively weak. The formation of bar structures causes molecular gas to collect in the central region, leading to starburst activity. However, after the starburst, the remaining gas becomes inefficient for star formation rapidly due to AGN feedback. This can mean the quenching process occurs more rapidly in AGN-barred galaxies. Furthermore, since gas remains in the central region, AGN activity is likely to continue. These quenching processes are a unique mechanism found in barred spiral galaxies and are essential to understanding galaxy evolution.

items.title: Mock Catalogs of Strongly Lensed Gravitational Waves via a Halo Model Approach with Spaceborne Detectors
items.abstract: Abstract Future spaceborne gravitational-wave (GW) detectors, such as LISA and DECIGO, are expected to detect a large number of GW events, a fraction of which may be strongly lensed by intervening galaxies or galaxy clusters. In this work, we develop a comprehensive framework to simulate strongly lensed GWs in the context of spaceborne detectors. Based on realistic astrophysical models for both the source population and the lens distribution, we construct mock catalogs of lensed GW events, referred to as GW–LMC–space. Our results show that, for a 4 yr LISA observation, the expected number of lensed events ranges from 0 to 131, depending on the adopted formation model of massive black hole binaries (MBHBs). The corresponding lensing probability for MBHBs can reach up to ∼0.3%. For DECIGO, we find that the number of lensed events in a 1 yr observation is expected to lie in the range of 0–44, with a lensing probability of ∼0.15% for stellar-mass binary black holes (BBHs), binary neutron stars (BNSs), and neutron star–black hole binaries (NSBHs). We further show that the overlap of lensed signals is a common feature in spaceborne detectors, which can significantly affect both the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) estimation and event identification. These results highlight the importance of accounting for signal overlap in the analysis of strongly lensed GW events in future spaceborne GW observations.

items.title: A Grid of Fast-rotating, Chemically Homogeneous, Supernova and/or Long Gamma-ray Burst Progenitors
items.abstract: Abstract The understanding of the mechanism(s) by which massive stars collapse and possibly explode is rapidly maturing. Uncertainties in the structure of the stellar core at the onset of collapse are often dominant in numerical simulations, and a limited number of progenitor grids are available. This is especially true for explosions where rotation and magnetic fields play a significant or primary role. We present a grid of 113 single-star models with initial masses M ZAMS = 30–90 M ⊙ and initial rigid rotation ω ZAMS = 0.5–0.99 ω crit computed at Z = 0.001 with the open-source stellar evolution code MESA . We adopt a 128-isotope nuclear reaction network capable of following the weak reactions deleptonizing the core during and after silicon core burning. By construction, these models experience rotationally induced chemically homogeneous evolution, and reach the onset of collapse ( v infall ≲ −300 km s −1 ) with large and structured amounts of angular momentum, possibly sufficient to form accretion disks on a protocompact object. Therefore, these progenitor structures provide a homogeneous set of models with updated input physics and improved algorithmic accuracy to understand stellar explosions of (some types of) stripped-envelope supernovae, possibly jetted and/or broad-lined, collapsars or magnetar-powered, and/or long gamma-ray bursts.

items.title: Reflection polarization of close binaries as a probe of axion dark matter birefringence
items.abstract: We propose close binary polarimetry as a probe of birefringence induced by ultralight axion dark matter. In a close binary, reflection or scattering can generate a small linear polarization whose time dependence is locked to the orbital phase. This phase-locked polarization provides a template against which an oscillatory rotation of the polarization angle induced by the axion can be searched for. We show that axion birefringence appears as sidebands around the orbital harmonics. For a single bright binary, with parameters motivated by observed systems and current high-precision optical polarimetry, we estimate the sensitivity to the axion-photon coupling under white noise assumption to be the level of $10^{-12}$ GeV$^{-1}$ at an axion mass of $10^{-20}$ eV. A future array of suitable binaries could further improve the sensitivity to $10^{-13}$ GeV$^{-1}$ in an optimistic scenario. This method could provide a complementary high-cadence optical probe of axion birefringence, compared to existing astrophysical searches.

items.title: Bright Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn: A Cloud-Scale Star Formation Model Unifying Variable SFE, IMFs, and Stochasticity
items.abstract: Abstract To investigate the origins of the high abundance of UV-bright galaxies at z > 10, we present a new semi-analytic model that bridges the gap between small-scale star formation physics and large-scale galaxy evolution by explicitly tracking discrete star-forming clouds within smoothly evolving dark matter potentials. Unlike conventional semi-analytic models, our approach naturally captures the stochasticity of star formation, allowing us to isolate how cloud properties, star formation efficiencies (SFEs), and stellar initial mass functions (IMFs) shape the star-formation burstiness of early galaxies. Clouds are drawn sequentially from a cloud mass distribution, assigned an SFE and IMF depending on cloud mass, metallicity, and redshift, and evolve under the influence of short-timescale stellar feedback. We identify three distinct star formation regimes arising from the interplay between cloud masses, densities, and feedback timescales: a stochastic, feedback-limited regime in low-mass halos with long quiescent phases; a bursty regime regulated by the cloud mass distribution; and a smooth, continuous regime in massive halos. Our fiducial model adopts a dynamic IMF, an SFE linked to cloud properties and the IMF, and massive, moderately dense clouds. Varying assumptions reveals that top-heavy IMFs and enhanced SFEs in massive clouds amplify burstiness, while altering the upper cloud mass or density normalisation is secondary. Among model ingredients, the IMF most strongly impacts the UV luminosity function (LF), while switching to a constant SFE boosts the faint end, and reducing the maximum cloud mass decreases the bright end. These results demonstrate that cloud-scale physics critically shape early galaxy UV luminosity distributions.

items.title: From S2 to LISA: Astrometric bounds on extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and bursts
items.abstract: Stellar orbits around the massive black hole at the center of our galaxy provide a unique local probe of the compact-object population in the Galactic Centre and, consequently, of the sources of millihertz gravitational waves: periapse passages lead to extreme-mass-ratio bursts (EMRBs) while successful captures lead to extreme-mass ration inspirals (EMRIs). In this paper we use recent astrometric limits from the GRAVITY observatory on perturbations of the orbit of the star S2 to place upper limits on the normalisation of a stellar-mass black-hole cusp within ${\sim} \,0.02\,\mathrm{pc}$. For a benchmark $10\,M_\odot$ Bahcall--Wolf population anchored to this data, we obtain upper limits of ${\sim} \,2.4\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{Gyr}^{-1}$ on the EMRI rate and ${\sim} \, 0.2\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ on the detectable EMRB rate in the Milky Way, which fall within the broad range of previous theoretical estimates. Assuming a self-similar scaling of the cusp normalisation with central black-hole mass, we extend this calibration to cosmological populations. The resulting EMRI background is detectable by LISA across all scenarios considered, whereas the flatter EMRB background can reach LISA sensitivity when mass segregation is efficient in low-mass galactic nuclei. Our results highlight the complementarity of precision stellar astrometry and millihertz gravitational-wave observations.

items.title: Squeezed quantum states and partner modes in the moving mirror model of black hole evaporation
items.abstract: The standard moving mirror model in (1+1)-dimensional spacetime is known to reproduce several quantum aspects of black hole evaporation. A perfectly reflecting, accelerating mirror can emit radiation whose frequency spectrum resembles that of Hawking radiation, although this correspondence holds only under certain approximations. Moreover, the standard in-out formulation does not provide a natural notion of the partner modes associated with the Hawking radiation. In this paper, we reformulate the moving mirror model in terms of Rindler/Milne modes. This formulation not only attributes the origin of the required approximations to mode squeezing effects but also naturally incorporates the notion of partner modes. Furthermore, as a consequence of these mode squeezing effects, the radiation received by an inertial observer at future null infinity exhibits additional nontrivial quantum correlations, even though its frequency spectrum approximately follows a Bose--Einstein or Fermi--Dirac distribution.

items.title: Interacting supernovae: A radio and x-ray strategy to constrain the structure of the circumstellar medium
items.abstract: The interaction of supernova (SN) ejecta with the dense circumstellar medium (CSM) converts shock kinetic energy into radiation across multiple wavebands. We investigate the dependence of the X-ray and radio emission on the CSM geometry, considering spherical, hourglass, and disk shapes for the CSM. We find that the spectral and light-curve properties, both in X-ray and radio, significantly differ for spherical and non-spherical CSM structures. For a non-spherical CSM, the radio light curve flattens out near the peak frequency, due to efficient free-free absorption by the unshocked CSM. Moreover, the early rise of the radio light curve is shallower when the CSM density along the observer line of sight is larger than that in other directions. If the CSM density is lower along the observer line of sight, the radio light curve flattens near its peak, and the reverse-shock component is negligible in X-rays. Building on these features, we provide a method to constrain the CSM structure based on the rising part the radio light curve in the proximity of its peak; we show that the decay part of the radio light curve, after its peak, carries insight on whether the CSM density profile is wind-like or not. We further adopt the X-ray signal to corroborate the information extracted from radio. We test our strategy on SN 1993j and SN 2023ixf. For both SNe, we find that an asymmetric CSM is in excellent agreement with radio and X-ray observations and provides a viable alternative to non-wind scenarios suggested in the literature. Our findings highlight the crucial insight provided by radio and X-ray signals into the mass-loss history of the SN progenitor.

items.title: The MegaWave Radio Surveyor
items.abstract: Several Decadal-level questions in astrophysics, exoplanets, astrobiology, and cosmology can be addressed only at low radio frequencies inaccessible from Earth. The MegaWave Radio Surveyor would open this largely-unexplored region of the electromagnetic spectrum with a space-based interferometer to (1)~Track the space weather of other stars; (2)~Detect magnetically-generated emission from exoplanets to probe their interiors and assess magnetic shielding of their atmospheres; (3)~Probe the Universe's evolution during the Dark Ages via the highly-redshifted HI hyperfine line; and (4)~Assess the role of cosmic rays and magnetic fields in the cosmic web. An Astrophysics Strategic Technology & Research Accelerator (ASTRA) Initiative concept, the MegaWave Radio Surveyor's science objectives respond to the Pathways to Discovery Decadal Survey and three other National Academies studies, and it would serve as a Formative Era mission in the Enduring Quests, Daring Visions roadmap. Developments in U.S. space industries enable this observatory to be realized. The MegaWave Radio Surveyor would offer a versatile, scalable, and resilient architecture capable of sensitive and simultaneous observations below 45~MHz and unprecedented angular resolution at these frequencies. The concept builds upon NASA's Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment (SunRISE), Star-Planet Activity Research CubeSat (SPARCS), and Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment (LuSEE-Night). The MegaWave Radio Surveyor could leverage multiple elements of the Artemis program, such as access to and beyond cislunar space and communications, and there are opportunities to infuse new autonomy/AI modes for mission operations. By opening one of the last windows in the electromagnetic spectrum and pioneering space interferometry at unprecedented scales, the MegaWave Radio Surveyor would establish a transformational capability.

items.abstract: We improve upon previous efforts to optimally combine overlapping galaxy samples in the DESI baryon acoustic oscillation analysis. items.title: Tale of two calibrators: Comparing Newtonian and photon calibration in advanced LIGO after the third observing run
items.abstract: Precise calibration of LIGO's strain readout plays a vital role in our ability to extract information from gravitational-wave detections. We present a comparative analysis of two independent direct-force calibration methods: the Newtonian Calibrator (NCal) and Photon Calibrator (PCal) systems. Currently, LIGO relies solely on the PCal system as its absolute calibration reference. To facilitate comparison, a series of direct-force injections were performed using the NCal and PCal systems at the LIGO Hanford observatory just after the completion of the third observing run. We compute the ratio of the measured to expected strain amplitudes for every injection. For each injection frequency across a 30 Hz band, the ratios of NCal and PCal differ by $\sim$0.5-1%, demonstrating a small systematic difference between the two systems. This offset highlights the importance of maintaining multiple independent calibration references to validate LIGO's calibration.

items.title: Temperature Measurements up to 700 km Using Metastable Helium Fluorescence LiDAR
items.abstract: Abstract Measuring temperature in the upper atmosphere is important for spacecraft operations, debris mitigation and space climate, but remains challenging above about 500 km due to limited observational techniques. Here, we report temperature profile observations of metastable helium (He*) from 500 to 700 km by a He* fluorescence LiDAR in Danzhou, China. The system employs a three‐wavelength laser near 1,083 nm with large‐aperture telescope array and superconducting nanowire single‐photon detectors, enabling high‐sensitivity detection of extremely weak fluorescence signals. The retrieved profiles showed broadly consistent altitude‐dependent variations with nearby incoherent scatter radar ion temperature observations, although the comparison is qualitative because the instruments measure different physical quantities. This technique provides a promising observational tool for investigating neutral–ionosphere coupling and offers valuable support for space weather research, orbit prediction, and atmospheric environment monitoring across diverse space applications.

items.title: Correcting stellar contamination in transmission spectroscopy with contemporaneous monitoring: Application to GJ 1214 b
items.abstract: Transmission spectroscopy has emerged as an essential tool for characterising the atmospheres of transiting exoplanets. However, stellar surface inhomogeneities contaminate transmission spectra, which poses a major challenge, particularly to high-precision observations such as those from the (JWST). James Webb Space Telescope We developed and applied a set of practical methodologies to correct for stellar contamination in transmission spectroscopy data, thereby improving the accuracy of exoplanet atmospheric characterisation. We obtained coordinated multi-band photometry and high-resolution spectroscopy around JWST observations of GJ,1214,b and applied two correction frameworks: (i) an inversion with the StarSim code, in which we infer stellar activity parameters from the monitoring data and propagate them to corrections; and (ii) , a data-driven approach in which neural networks (NNs) are trained on a large suite of simulations to learn the mapping from the monitoring data to the corrections. StarSim Both frameworks agree within the uncertainties and indicate that the JWST observations of GJ,1214 occurred at a favourable rotation phase with low stellar contamination. For , the inferred corrections can be constrained at the ∼10--30 ppm level across the JWST wavelength range, implying post-correction residuals of the same order. If the same system were observed near activity maximum, the predicted contamination would be strongly chromatic and substantially affect atmospheric retrievals, highlighting the importance of coordinated ground-based monitoring and robust activity correction techniques to accurately interpret transmission spectra. The two approaches are complementary but serve different roles. The inversion yields physically interpretable parameters and surface maps, whereas marginalises more efficiently over surface-configuration degeneracies and provides tighter predictive corrections once trained and validated within the relevant simulation domain. The NNs carry an upfront training cost, but then enable fast predictions within their training distribution. Our pipeline can potentially be generalised to other active stars: with multi-band and multi-technique monitoring around JWST visits, it can provide activity-level forecasts for scheduling and activity corrections for atmospheric analyses.

items.title: Stochastic Snowball States in Planetary Climate
items.abstract: Motivated by the recent finding of Ji and Abbot (2025) that at moderate eccentricity (0.2–0.3) the planetary Snowball bistability vanishes, we have introduced stochasticity of the orbital eccentricity into a simplified version of the energy balance model of Eisenman and Wettlaufer (2009) to study a general Earth-like planet. The stochastic eccentricity is approximated by two dominant time scales, annual and daily, and is introduced through an analysis of the Kepler equation. We find that, apart from mean eccentricities less than 0.1, the stochastic dynamics are quantitatively and qualitatively different than the deterministic dynamics. For a fixed mean eccentricity, fluctuations in eccentricity amplify the asymmetry and intermittency in radiative flux forcing, thereby increasing the time it takes to reach a stable seasonal cycle. As the mean eccentricity increases above 0.1, the stochastic transition from the Snowball to non-Snowball state occurs over a range of mean stellar flux ΔS* rather than at a particular stellar flux S* for the deterministic case. Moreover, as the mean eccentricity increases from 0.1 and the variance of the annual eccentricity fluctuations increases, ΔS* increases, and the probability of the system reaching a steady state and experiencing a Snowball to non-Snowball bifurcation decreases. This implies that there may be many high eccentricity planetary systems in a perpetually transient state.

items.title: Anisotropic Radiation in Super-Eddington Active Galactic Nuclei: The Responsivity of Broad-line Regions to Continuum Variability
items.abstract: Abstract Anisotropic ionizing radiation is a natural theoretical expectation for super-Eddington accretion in active galactic nuclei (AGNs), implying that the ionizing flux incident on the broad-line region (BLR) clouds differs from that measured along the observer’s line of sight. Reverberation mapping studies have revealed systematically shortened time lags of the broad H β emission line relative to continuum variations in super-Eddington AGNs, a phenomenon that can be naturally interpreted as a consequence of anisotropic ionizing continuum radiation. To further investigate this anisotropy, we perform a systematic analysis of the H β line responsivity, defined as the ratio of the variability amplitude of H β to that of the driving continuum, for both sub- and super-Eddington AGNs. By combining the effective responsivities measured relative to the driving continuum, after correcting for the continuum–emission-line delay, with photoionization calculations, we infer the ionizing radiation field received by their BLRs. We find that, in super-Eddington AGNs, the ionizing flux inferred from the H β responsivity differs significantly from that observed along the line of sight, whereas the two are in closer agreement in sub-Eddington AGNs. These results provide compelling evidence for strong anisotropy of the incident ionizing radiation in super-Eddington AGNs. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of this anisotropy, including its potential relevance to the “little red dots” recently discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope.

items.title: On the Orbital Evolution of Giant-planet Pair Embedded in a Gaseous Disk. III. Simultaneous Gas Accretion and the Final Mass Ratio
items.abstract: Abstract Recent exoplanet surveys reveal a systematic trend in the mass ratios of giant-planet pairs (>30 M ⊕ ). Although the M outer / M inner is broadly centered near unity, it exhibits a dependence on orbital separation. Compact pairs tend to have comparable masses, whereas widely separated pairs show outer-heavy configurations. To investigate the origin of this trend, we perform 2D hydrodynamic simulations that couple gas accretion and orbital migration of two giant planet embryos with initial masses of 15−30 M ⊕ . We explore the effects of disk viscosity, surface density slope, and initial mass ratio on the coupled evolution of planetary growth and migration. We find that convergent migration drives the planets to open a common gap, restructuring the gas flow. This configuration induces asymmetric accretion, in which the inner planet becomes starved as gap clearing suppresses its gas supply, while the outer planet continues to accrete from the high-density region at the outer gap edge. Consequently, the system naturally evolves toward mass-ratio convergence, and in many cases produces an inversion of the initial core-mass hierarchy. We further show that migration outcomes are highly sensitive to initial conditions. Systems with initially more massive inner cores tend to diverge, whereas steeper surface density profiles and more massive outer cores favor convergent migration and subsequent resonance capture. Overall, our results identify common-gap-driven asymmetric accretion as a unified mechanism linking orbital architecture, resonant capture, and the observed mass-ratio demographics of giant planet pairs.

items.title: The Second Catalog of Low-energy Fermi-LAT Sources
items.abstract: Abstract We used 14 yr of Fermi-Large Area Telescope (LAT) data to derive a catalog of sources detected between 20 MeV and 200 MeV. For each source, we provide localization, spectral, and association information. The Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT sources (2FLE) contains 450 sources detected at TS > 25, with median energy flux of F 20−200 MeV = 1.9 × 10 −11 erg cm −2 s −1 . Using a Bayesian and likelihood-ratio method, we associate 377 2FLE sources with a known counterpart. Of the 325 objects associated with extragalactic sources, the dominant source class represented in the 2FLE is flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Additionally, 52 sources are associated with Galactic sources. Three associated sources have not been previously detected in any γ -ray catalog and represent new γ -ray sources of known origin. We find that 387 2FLE sources have a positional cross-match with the 4FGL-DR4 sources. For the sources with a 4FGL counterpart, we compare the spectrum of the 2FLE source to the 4FGL spectral energy distributions. Of the 73 2FLE sources without multiwavelength associations, 13 have a 4FGL counterpart that lacks classification, while 60 are newly discovered γ -ray sources. Among these 60 sources, 51 are found at high latitudes (∣ b ∣ > 10°), and 38 are detected at >10 σ . Additionally, we find that out of the 450 2FLE sources, 45 are TeV emitters, and six are spatially coincident with a 1LHAASO source. The 2FLE helps us pave the way for reducing the “MeV gap,” and provides the most sensitive catalog between 20 and 200 MeV to date.

items.title: PDRs4All. XXIII. JWST-MIRI template spectra of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the Orion Bar obtained with blind signal separation
items.abstract: The aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) are observed in a wide variety of astrophysical sources, and now in unprecedented detail by the Space Telescope (JWST). These bands are generally attributed to the emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Our aim is to extract mid-infrared AIB template spectra from JWST observations of the Orion Bar photo-dissociation region that can be used to derive PAH properties from observations of other objects. We used the JWST MIRI-MRS observations from the PDRs4All program. We first isolated the AIBs from the data using a multi-component fitting approach. We then applied a nonnegative matrix factorization to the isolated AIB spectra and extracted two templates, named James Webb and following previous work. The spatial distribution and spectral characteristics of these two spectra suggest that they originate from two chemically distinct populations. We interpret as emission originating from a PAH population strongly exposed to ultraviolet (UV) radiation and mainly composed of large, compact ionized PAHs. Conversely, is interpreted as originating from a more shielded population of PAHs, which is less exposed to the UV by being more embedded in the cloud. This population consists of small, asymmetric, and mainly neutral PAHs with bonded aliphatic side groups. These templates can serve to analyze PAH emission in a wide variety of objects observed with MIRI-MRS.

items.title: SPICY 30021: An embedded bona fide FU Orionis star with a mid-infrared precursor
items.abstract: The unstable mass accretion process in young stellar objects often leads to observable outbursts. These episodic accretion bursts play a key role in the stellar mass assembly during the pre-main-sequence evolution. The outbursts with the highest amplitude and longest duration are commonly identified as FU Orionis stars (FUors). Only ∼50 FUor events were confirmed until recently. Most of these eruptive events occur in embedded protostars, which are difficult to monitor from optical surveys. We present photometric and spectroscopic observations of an eruptive young star (SPICY 30021) originally discovered from the mid-infrared time series. We constructed the spectral energy distribution and physically characterised the eruptive nature of SPICY 30021. NEOWISE We gathered multi-wavelength photometric time series from , VVV, and the recently established VVV-RENEW surveys. We also conducted photometric and spectroscopic observations during the outburst using instruments on the SOAR, Magellan, and VLT telescopes, including data from the ESO public survey VVVX-GalCen. We first identified the location of the outbursting source and disentangled it from nearby companions. We then measured the line-of-sight extinction by comparing spectroscopic features. The stellar parameters were then estimated from radial velocity, proper motions, and stellar evolution models. NEOWISE We found that SPICY 30021 is an optically obscured FUor with a line-of-sight (interstellar and circumstellar) extinction of A_V = 12.5 mag. The spectrum of SPICY 30021 closely resembles the spectra of classical FUors. Using various methods, we measured the distance of SPICY 30021 as 1.7 = 30 ̊m L_⊙, which is moderate for FUors. The quiescent near-infrared photometry is consistent with a young, 0.9 ̊m M_⊙ progenitor, although the mass remains dependent on the model and distance. kpc. The accretion luminosity of the outburst is L_ ̊m acc We confirm that SPICY 30021 is a bona fide FUor event. The mid-infrared precursor suggests an outside-in triggering mechanism.

items.title: Broad-line Regions behind a Haze. II. A Three-dimensional Electron-scattering Model of the Broad Br γ Line in NGC 3783
items.abstract: Abstract We investigate the broad Br γ line in the Type 1 active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 3783 using three-dimensional Monte Carlo electron-scattering radiative transfer with SKIRT. Paper I reproduced the observed smooth core and broad wings by convolving an intrinsic Keplerian profile with the analytic electron-scattering kernel of A. Laor. Here we instead transport photons through explicit source and scattering geometries. For a partially covered Keplerian source, three-dimensional transfer broadens only the scattered photons and leaves an unscattered double-peaked core. For the thin Keplerian source motivated by Paper I, a comparison of four scattering-geometry classes shows that neither a disklike scatterer nor the tested halo variants reproduce both the core and wings. We therefore construct a two-component-source (2CS) model containing an inner Keplerian source disk, a rotating disk haze, a nearly spherical halo haze, and direct emission from a slower outer disk. A reference 2CS calculation gives χ 2 / ν = 1.154 at i = 15°. Polar cones with an input radial optical depth τ hole = 0.1 preserve the line profile and give a measured Thomson-thin sight line. The preferred low redistribution width, full-column ionization, and weak recombination emission cannot all be realized by a uniform thermal halo. The 2CS model is therefore a physically motivated parametric description whose medium must ultimately be tested with self-consistent radiative transfer, ionization, and dynamics.

items.title: A Comprehensive X-Ray Characterization of the Pulsar Wind Nebula CTB 87: Evidence for Reverse-shock Interaction from Its X-Ray and Broadband Emissions
items.abstract: Abstract We present a comprehensive X-ray study of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) CTB 87, utilizing new NuSTAR observations and archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data. Our joint analysis reveals that the PWN’s X-ray spectrum exhibits significant curvature, well described by a broken or cutoff power law. The broken power-law fit yields photon indices Γ 1 = 1.89 ± 0.05 and Γ 2 = 2.73 ± 0.10 below and above a break energy of E b = 5.12 ± 0.26 keV, respectively, while the cutoff power-law fit gives Γ = 1.23 ± 0.10 and E c = 5.29 ± 0.67 keV. Spatially resolved spectroscopy confirms a previously observed radial softening of Γ, indicating significant synchrotron cooling as electrons move outward from the pulsar. We employed leptonic emission scenarios to model the broadband emission from CTB 87, focusing on the measured X-ray spectrum and the radial profiles. While an evolutionary one-zone model can explain the general features of the broadband spectral energy distribution (SED), its predictions do not fully reproduce the observed X-ray spectrum. Our multizone modeling demonstrates that the hard electron distribution required to explain the X-ray spectrum cannot account for the observed gamma-ray SED. This discrepancy suggests the presence of an additional electron population, possibly linked to the reverse shock interaction, and highlights CTB 87 as an evolved PWN whose broadband emission cannot be captured by these simple SED models. We discuss the potential origins for this second electron population and its implications for understanding the evolution of PWNe.

items.title: EP J062132.0+623837: A Multiwavelength Study of a Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Discovered by Einstein Probe
items.abstract: Abstract EP J062132.0+623837 is a new X-ray source identified in 14 day binned survey data from the Wide-field X-ray Telescope on board the Einstein Probe (EP). Subsequent X-ray observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board EP localized the source to the central region of the galaxy 2MASX J06213207+6238390 at z = 0.084. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the multiwavelength data for this object. During the FXT and Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory/X-Ray Telescope follow-up, the source remained X-ray active, with observed luminosities of (3–9) × 10 43 erg s −1 , and its X-ray spectra were well described by power-law models with photon indices of Γ ∼ 1.5. The optical spectrum of the host galaxy clearly reveals a broad-line active galactic nucleus (AGN) exhibiting significantly enhanced broad Balmer emission lines compared to an archival spectrum obtained 4 yr earlier, thereby marking a changing-look transition from Type 1.8 to Type 1.5. Furthermore, long-term optical and mid-IR light curves indicate that the nucleus underwent dramatic brightening around 2010 and has since shown substantial variability. Given the spatial coincidence and multiwavelength behavior, we identify EP J062132.0+623837 as a changing-look AGN, initially detected by EP and subsequently confirmed to exhibit large-amplitude variability across multiple bands. This case study demonstrates the great potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys for discovering changing-look AGNs, paving a new avenue for their systematic identification as a powerful complement to ongoing optical surveys.

items.title: Optical–Infrared Extinction Variation in Nearby Molecular Clouds
items.abstract: Abstract The dust extinction curve is an important probe of the properties of dust grains, particularly their size distribution. The properties of dust grains are expected to change significantly in dense molecular clouds due to shielding from interstellar radiation and an increased frequency of grain–grain and grain–gas collisions. We measure the dust extinction-curve shape parameter R ( V ) in nine nearby dense molecular clouds using data from the Apache Point Observatory (APO) Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) spectroscopic survey, in combination with 10-band photometry from the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (PS1), the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). We analyze the results to determine how the extinction curve varies in nearby molecular clouds. We find that most molecular clouds show a positive correlation between R ( V ) and E ( B − V ), but the strength of the correlation varies significantly between clouds. In addition, we find that the clouds with the strongest correlation tend to have very high dispersion in R ( V ) at fixed E ( B − V ), which tightens dramatically when the clouds are subdivided into separate regions. This suggests that local environmental conditions beyond density shape the R ( V )– E ( B − V ) relation.

items.title: EXPRESS: Blood-free full quantification of dynamic TSPO PET imaging with [11C]PBR28.
items.abstract: Quantitative dynamic PET imaging requires metabolite-corrected arterial input functions, traditionally obtained through invasive arterial blood sampling, limiting broader adoption of quantitative kinetic modelling. Achieving generalisability across datasets, scanners, and imaging centres remains a major challenge for data-driven alternatives. We developed ASTRA, a deep-learning-based framework for arterial input function estimation from dynamic brain TSPO PET. ASTRA was developed and validated using arterial measurements in one dataset (n=90), then transfer-learned and evaluated against arterial measurements at a second centre (n=52). Building upon this, ASTRA was applied to an independent clinical cohort (n=32) from the second site but without arterial reference data, where quantitative analyses had therefore not been performed, to assess whether it could reproduce previously reported semi-quantitative cross-sectional group differences. Robustness to altered tracer kinetics was evaluated in an out-of-distribution pharmacological blockade cohort (n=5). ASTRA-derived quantitative estimates agreed with arterial measurements (VT: CCC=0.658-0.805), with higher uncertainty associated with greater error. In the clinical cohort, ASTRA reproduced SUVR-based group differences using DVR (p<0.001), except in the pituitary gland (p=0.12). Finally, ASTRA yielded receptor occupancy estimates (0.92±0.17) closely matching arterial values (0.94±0.12) in the blocking cohort. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of multi-site, non-invasive quantitative TSPO PET.

items.title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals.
items.abstract: Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Sex-specific meta-analyses revealed 115 independent loci (12 of which were new) among males (n = 583,066) and 12 loci (2 of which were new) among females (n = 241,266). Multi-omic gene prioritization analyses highlighted 490 genes associated with MP through their effects on brain-specific and blood-specific regulation. Mendelian randomization analyses showed causal associations between MP and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and C-reactive protein levels. MP variants also showed pleiotropic associations with several brain imaging-derived phenotypes. This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

items.title: Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging.
items.abstract: Implantation remains the most inaccessible stage of mammalian development. Consequently, we know remarkably little about how the embryo coordinates the cellular transitions that establish the body plan and initiate placental formation, despite this being the period when most pregnancies are lost. Here we combine single-cell transcriptomics, live imaging and functional experiments to define these transitions at cellular resolution. Our results identify an intermediate state bridging naive and primed pluripotency in the embryonic lineage, trace anterior-posterior axis specification origins in the extraembryonic endoderm, and reveal trophectoderm bifurcation into distinct placental progenitors. Strikingly, we find that the placenta arises from two sources: the classically recognized polar trophectoderm and a previously unrecognized population of mural trophectoderm that migrates from the polar-mural border. Human mural trophectoderm shows similar region-specific behaviour and may include invasive-trophoblast-biased progenitors. These findings open new directions for improving stem-cell-derived embryo models and uncovering the early determinants of pregnancy success.

items.title: Social determinants of health and the exposome shape aging and dementia across global populations.
items.abstract: Social determinants of health, the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, shape brain aging and dementia. Yet evidence is dominated by Global North populations and often relies on single indicators (for example, education or income), limiting risk characterization and generalizability across settings. This Perspective provides a global, integrative overview of multidimensional, multilevel and life-course approaches to social determinants of health and exposome research in brain health. We examine composite indices and social-exposomal factors, their need for harmonization, contextual adaptation and local validation, and biological embedding through stress-related, inflammatory, metabolic, vascular and epigenetic pathways. We also discuss interactions with genetic susceptibility and the analytical challenges of modeling cumulative, time-varying and nonlinear exposures. These advances require feasible, policy-relevant implementation in resource-constrained settings. Moving beyond static, single-domain proxies towards context-sensitive measures and multilevel designs can improve risk characterization and support more equitable, globally relevant strategies for dementia prevention and precision public health.

items.title: Exercise is medicine: Translating exercise-induced cognitive benefits into rehabilitation practice.
items.abstract: Background Exercise is one of the most impactful activities we can do to support physical, cognitive, and mental health across the lifespan and within both healthy and clinical populations. There is robust evidence that exercise promotes cognitive function, enhancing our ability to plan, think, and execute goal-directed behaviours. These cognitive benefits directly support patients in rehabilitation contexts to understand, follow, and safely apply clinical recommendations. Purpose In this expert review, we provide an overview of the exercise neuroscience literature, highlighting key findings for the effects of exercise on cognition and brain health, followed by an overview of proposed mechanisms for these findings. Next, we translate these findings and offer a perspective in how they may be beneficial in rehabilitation settings, including special considerations for different populations experiencing cognitive decline. Finally, we end with a discussion of the limitations and future directions of this work, with special attention to equity, diversity, and inclusion to ensure that this knowledge remains accessible to all. Conclusions Our goal is to provide clinicians and researchers with the background knowledge that will equip them with what, how, and why exercise should be part of usual care for all types of patients in rehabilitation settings.

items.title: ERN-RITA/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis, classification, monitoring, and treatment of childhood idiopathic (primary) angiitis of the central nervous system.
items.abstract: Objectives Childhood central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis is a rare and serious disease for which no evidence-based consensus guidance, standardised terminology, or definitions of treatment response exist. We aimed to develop the first international recommendations for the diagnosis, classification, monitoring, and treatment of CNS vasculitis in children. Methods Adapting the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology standardised operating procedures, an international multidisciplinary panel of 42 experts from 15 countries was assembled through the European Reference Network on Rare Immunodeficiency, Autoinflammatory, Autoimmune and Paediatric Rheumatic Diseases, and the Paediatric Rheumatology European Society. A systematic literature review across 4 databases identified 182 eligible studies, graded per the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine hierarchy. A modified Delphi survey (42 respondents) was followed by a 2-day face-to-face consensus conference (26 voting members; ≥70% agreement required). Results The panel formulated 83 consensus statements (3 overarching principles, 14 principles, and 66 recommendations) across 7 clinical domains. Of 182 included articles, 152 (83.5%) reported paediatric data; no level 1 evidence was identified. Key advances include an 8-domain nomenclature system replacing the 'primary/secondary' dichotomy with 'idiopathic/disease-associated' terminology, a paediatric-specific vessel wall imaging interpretive principle, a prospective risk-stratification model for disease progression, genome-wide sequencing as the preferred genetic testing approach, and formal definitions of remission, relapse, and refractory disease. None of these elements had been previously codified for childhood CNS vasculitis. Conclusions These recommendations establish a comprehensive, evidence-graded framework for childhood CNS vasculitis. The absence of level 1 evidence across all domains points to the need for an international prospective registry and collaborative clinical trials.

items.title: Reelin Deficiency Alters the Directional Orientation, Apical Localization and Length of Primary Cilia in Principal Neurons in the Cerebral Cortex.
items.abstract: The primary cilia of pyramidal neurons in inside-out laminated regions are oriented predominantly toward the pia, a pattern reflecting reverse soma movement during postnatal neurodevelopment. However, the mechanisms that regulate the directional cilia orientation remain unknown. Here we show that the primary cilia of neocortical pyramidal neurons in male and female mice are localized at the base of the apical dendrites and aligned distally and opposite to the axon initial segment (AIS). However, this pattern is not observed in atypical pyramidal neurons in the deep neocortex, excitatory neurons in non-laminated regions, or interneurons, where cilia are randomly positioned around the nuclei and lack preferred orientation. In Reelin-deficient mice ( reeler ), the directional orientation and apical location of cilia in late-born neocortical and CA1 neurons are altered. However, the initial impairments are partially corrected during early postnatal development. In contrast, Reelin deficiency disrupts the directional orientation and apical localization of primary cilia in early-born neocortical neurons and principal neurons in evolutionarily conserved laminated regions, where lack postnatal correction. Reelin deficiency also increases the cilia length in principal neurons across the cerebral cortex at a developmental stage when cilia length stabilizes in wild-type mice. In contrast, cilia elongation is not observed in interneurons, GFAP-positive astrocytes, or excitatory neurons in non-laminated regions of reeler Together, Reelin regulates the directional orientation, apical localization, and length of primary cilia in principal neurons in the cerebral cortex. This study underscores the cilium as a key apical domain, particularly prominent in late-born pyramidal neurons. Significance Statement While primary cilia are implicated in various brain disorders, their physiological functions in the postnatal brain remain poorly understood. We show that the primary cilia in pyramidal neurons are localized at the base of the apical dendrites and aligned distally and opposite to the axon initial segment (AIS), forming a prominent "cilia-at-apical and axon-at-basal" pattern. Reelin deficiency alters the directional orientation, apical localization, and length of these cilia. Interestingly, late-born pyramidal neurons exhibit partial restoration under Reelin deficiency, whereas early-born neurons and those in evolutionarily conserved cortical regions do not. These findings identify primary cilia as a crucial apical domain and reveal an unrecognized Reelin-cilia functional crosstalk, which may enhance the polarity of pyramidal neurons.

items.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
items.abstract: Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions. Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.
