items.title: PARP1 deficiency induces aging-associated cardiac failure via activation of Akt signalling.
items.abstract: PARP1, a major poly-ADP-ribose transferase, plays a critical role in maintaining genomic stability, transcription, cellular energy metabolism, and cell death. In the heart, PARP1 inhibition protects cardiomyocytes against oxidative and genotoxic stress and attenuates ischemia-reperfusion injury caused by myocardial infarction. However, the role of PARP1 in aging-associated heart failure remains unexplored. In this study, we demonstrate the crucial role of PARP1 in regulating aging-associated cardiac remodelling and failure. The levels of PARP1 are down-regulated in aging mouse hearts, and PARP1 deficiency induces aging-related cardiac remodelling and contractile dysfunction in mice. The RNA-seq analysis revealed hyperactivation of Akt signalling, a major signalling pathway involved in aging, in PARP1-deficient hearts. In the heart, PARP1 deficiency spontaneously activates the Akt signalling pathway, leading to the development of aging-related cardiac hypertrophy and failure. Our findings reveal two distinct mechanisms by which PARP1 regulates Akt signalling, involving the direct interaction of PARP1 with Akt and the transcriptional regulation of phosphatases, including the expression of PTEN by PARP1. Mechanistically, PARP1 binds to the PTEN promoter and might transcriptionally promote its expression. In addition, PARP1 binds and inhibits Akt by poly-ADP-ribosylating Akt at the PH domain, which impairs Akt plasma membrane recruitment and subsequent activation. Inhibition of Akt reversed hypertrophy in PARP1-depleted cardiomyocytes and improved the contractile dysfunction in PARP1-deficient hearts. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized regulatory role for PARP1 in aging-associated cardiac failure.

items.title: Arid1b haploinsufficiency weakens excitatory synaptic input to inhibitory interneurons beginning during early development.
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents with diverse cognitive and behavioral abnormalities that begin during early development and persist into adulthood. Although the circuit mechanisms remain unclear, recent work suggests pathology in inhibitory interneurons (INs) plays a crucial role. Neocortical and hippocampal INs are generated from a common progenitor pool during embryogenesis and develop into similar major subtypes in both brain structures. Thus, dysfunction of ASD risk genes in IN progenitors may broadly impact neural circuit function. Here, we used transgenic mice to conditionally knockout one copy of the ASD risk gene Arid1b from the progenitors of parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking (PV-FS) INs, which provide perisomatic inhibition to control spike timing, and somatostatin-expressing non-fast-spiking (SST-NFS) INs, which inhibit dendrites to control synaptic integration and plasticity. We then investigated the physiology of their synaptic connections with excitatory pyramidal cells (PCs) in slices of neocortex and CA1 hippocampus from both neonatal and adolescent mice. Surprisingly, excitatory synapses from PCs to INs were weakened throughout development in both brain regions but inhibitory synapses from INs to PCs were normal. During early development, we found that weak excitatory drive to INs impaired the generation of spontaneous network events that contribute to circuit maturation. During later development, excitatory synapses to SST-NFS INs remained weak in both neocortex and CA1, which is expected to impair their participation in canonical inhibitory circuits necessary for proper encoding of sensory and spatial information by PCs. Our data show that impaired IN excitation is an important mechanism underlying circuit deficits in Arid1b haploinsufficiency.

items.title: The basic C-terminal tail of CXCL9/Mig, not its N-terminal chemokine domain, is necessary and sufficient for its neurotrophic activity.
items.abstract: CXCL9/Mig is unique among the CXCR3 ligands in carrying an extended, basic C-terminal tail that is absent from both CXCL10 and CXCL11. We previously found that CXCL9, but not CXCL10 or CXCL11, promotes neurite outgrowth and survival of PC12 cells and rescues NGF-deprived sympathetic neurons independently of CXCR3. Here, using an eight-member panel of CXCL9-related proteins and peptides that uncouples the N-terminal chemokine core from the C-terminal tail, we show that constructs lacking the C-terminal tail lose all neurotrophic activity and fail to activate ERK1/2 and Akt, whereas the isolated tail - whether expressed as a GST fusion or as a short synthesized peptide - fully reproduces neurite outgrowth, PC12 cell survival, and sympathetic neuron rescue. GST alone was inactive in every assay. These results map CXCL9's neurotrophic activity to its basic C-terminal tail, independent of its canonical N-terminal chemokine domain.

items.title: Vericiguat attenuates cardiac inflammation and oxidative stress in an obese postmenopausal rat model with concurrent modulation of PKG-I, TGF-β1, and NF-κB.
items.abstract: Background Inflammation and oxidative stress are implicated in cardiometabolic changes associated with menopause and obesity. This study investigated the effects of Vericiguat (VER) alone and in combination with estradiol (E2) on oxidative, inflammatory, atherogenic and fibrosis-related markers in cardiac tissue in an ovariectomized rat model of diet-induced obesity. Materials and methods Female Wistar rats were divided into sham and ovariectomized (OVX) groups and fed a standard diet (SD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 4 months, followed by 4 weeks of treatment with E2, two doses of VER, or their combination. Body weight, malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), plasma atherogenic index (AIP), cardiac risk indices I and II (CRI-I and CRI-II), cardiac hydroxyproline, and expression of cardiac PKG-I, NF-κB, and TGF-β1 proteins were assessed. Results OVX and HFD were associated with increased body weight, AIP, CRI-I, CRI-II, MDA, cardiac NF-κB and TGF-β1 expression, and hydroxyproline content, along with decreased TAC, TAC/MDA ratio, and PKG-I expression. E2 and VER treatments improved these alterations, as evidenced by reductions in AIP, CRI-I, CRI-II, MDA, NF-κB, TGF-β1, and hydroxyproline, as well as increases in TAC, TAC/MDA ratio, and PKG-I expression. Combined treatment with E2 and VER, compared to treatment with E2 alone, significantly improved all these parameters, with the exception of CRI-I and CRI-II. There were significant interactions between E2 and VER treatments were observed for TAC/MDA, hydroxyproline content, and TGF-β1 expression. Conclusion VER and E2 ameliorated several oxidative, inflammatory, atherogenic, and fibrosis-related changes in this model.

items.title: Targeting Astrocyte-Neuron Crosstalk in Depression: From Synaptic Mechanisms to Therapeutic Strategies.
items.abstract: Depression is a leading cause of global disability and imposes a substantial socioeconomic burden worldwide. While traditional theories, such as the monoamine hypothesis and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction, underpin current treatments, existing antidepressants are limited by their delayed onset of action. The tripartite synapse concept contributes to reframing depression, as glia contribute to synaptic dysfunction. Within this framework, astrocytes engage in bidirectional communication with neurons via gliotransmission and modulate synaptic plasticity as integral synaptic components. Postmortem studies have revealed a significant reduction in astrocyte density in the brains of patients with depression, a pathology closely linked to compromised synaptic integrity and loss. In this narrative review, we examine the structural and functional roles of astrocytes in maintaining synaptic homeostasis and explore how astrocytic dysregulation contributes to the pathogenesis of depression. Furthermore, we propose novel therapeutic strategies targeting astrocytes for antidepressant development.

items.title: Activation of GLP-1 receptors in the middle part of the paraventricular nucleus of thalamus suppresses alcohol-related responses.
items.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major public health challenge, and identifying the brain circuits through which pharmacological interventions act is central to developing more effective treatments. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists suppress alcohol-related behaviors in rodents and reduce alcohol consumption in clinical populations with AUD, yet the neuroanatomical substrates mediating these effects remain only partly mapped. One candidate region implicated in addiction is the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), particularly its middle part (mid-PVT), which modulates mesolimbic dopamine signaling, has been implicated in addiction-related processes including alcohol use, and expresses GLP-1R. Whether activation of GLP-1R in the mid-PVT influences alcohol-related responses had not been examined, and that was the aim of the present study. Here, we found that local GLP-1R antagonism in the mid-PVT with exendin-3(9-39) (Ex9) attenuated the suppressive effect of systemically administered GLP-1R agonist exendin-4 (Ex4) on alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation, implicating this region in the central actions of GLP-1R agonists. Intra-mid-PVT Ex4 also attenuated alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation and accumbal dopamine release in male mice, without altering the expression of alcohol-induced conditioned place preference. We further showed that Ex4 into the mid-PVT reduced alcohol intake in male and female rats, although a higher dose was required in females. In a separate cohort of alcohol-consuming, treatment-naive rats, Glp1r mRNA in the PVT did not differ between the sexes. Together, these findings indicate that GLP-1R in the mid-PVT contributes to alcohol-related responses, extending the neuroanatomical map of circuits through which GLP-1R agonists may suppress alcohol intake.

items.title: Quinolinic acid as a central immunometabolic mediator of inflammation, neurodegeneration, and disease pathogenesis.
items.abstract: Quinolinic acid (QA), a downstream metabolite of the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway, has emerged as a critical immunometabolic molecule linking immune activation, inflammation, and tissue pathology across diverse diseases. Recent evidence demonstrates that altered QA production is associated with chronic inflammatory disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, infections, cancer, and immune dysregulation. In the central nervous system (CNS), pathological accumulation of QA has been associated with excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor activation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and excitotoxicity, contributing to neuronal injury and neuroinflammatory pathology. In inflammatory skin diseases such as psoriasis, microbiota-derived QA modulates NOD-, LRR-, and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activity through aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)-dependent mechanisms, highlighting a regulatory role in cutaneous immunity. Studies further identified microglial-derived QA as both a biomarker and mediator of depressive-like behavior, with reductions in QA predicting therapeutic response to ketamine. Beyond inflammatory and neurological disorders, QA and related kynurenine metabolites exhibit anti-proliferative effects in melanoma cells by inducing apoptosis and inhibiting cell-survival signaling pathways. Therapeutic interventions targeting QA-mediated pathways, including microbiota-derived metabolites such as butyrate, have demonstrated neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in experimental models. Understanding the mechanisms governing QA production and signaling may facilitate the development of novel biomarkers and targeted therapies for inflammatory, neurodegenerative, infectious, and malignant diseases.

items.title: Hydrogen sulfide alleviates pyroptosis and cognitive dysfunction in diabetic encephalopathy by inhibiting ferroptosis.
items.abstract: Diabetic encephalopathy (DE) is a serious diabetic complication, primarily characterized by cognitive dysfunction. Ferroptosis and pyroptosis have been implicated as key contributors in neurodegenerative diseases. Although ferroptosis and pyroptosis have been demonstrated to be associated with DE respectively, it remains unclear whether they coexist and the intrinsic relationship between them in DE. Ferroptosis is able to induce the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). Coincidentally, mtROS is recognized as a critical signal that promotes pyroptosis. Nevertheless, there is still insufficient evidence to demonstrate that ferroptosis-associated mtROS act as a key factor in promoting pyroptosis in DE. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S), an endogenous gasotransmitter with known cytoprotective effects, is capable of reducing mtROS. However, it remains to be determined whether H2S can inhibit ferroptosis to reduce mtROS and ultimately alleviate pyroptosis in DE. In this study, both ferroptosis and pyroptosis were found activated in high glucose (HG)-induced HT-22 cells and in C57BL/6J diabetic mice. Interestingly, in HG-induced HT-22 cells, ferroptosis-related changes and mtROS accumulation occurred earlier than pyroptosis, suggesting that ferroptosis-associated mtROS may contribute to pyroptosis. The ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) not only suppressed ferroptosis but also reduced mtROS and attenuated pyroptosis-related signaling. Furthermore, H2S was observed to exert effects analogous to Fer-1, effectively suppressing both ferroptosis and pyroptosis, preserving mitochondrial function, and ameliorating cognitive dysfunction in vivo. These findings suggest that ferroptosis-associated mtROS accumulation may contribute to pyroptosis in DE, and that H2S attenuates ferroptosis, mtROS and pyroptosis while ameliorating cognitive dysfunction, presenting a promising preclinical strategy for DE.

items.title: Automated detection of blink reflexes evoked by optogenetic stimulation of TRPV1-lineage corneal afferents in transgenic mice.
items.abstract: Conventional rodent models for the study of corneal pain commonly evoke eye blink reflex using methods that indiscriminately activate polymodal nociceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors at temporal resolutions that don't closely match the sub-second timescale of underlying neural dynamics. We introduce a novel automated behavioral paradigm for detecting blink reflexes in transgenic TRPV1-ChR2-EYFP mice, enabled by millisecond-precision optogenetic stimulation of TRPV1-lineage corneal afferents (490nm light). Multi-feature quantification enables univariate and multivariate classification. TRPV1-ChR2-EYFP mice (N=5) blinked in 86.3 ± 10.9% of trials following corneal stimulation with high-intensity (4.69 - 4.77mW/mm²) blue light (490nm, 10 ms pulses) versus 2.5 ± 2.5% at low intensity (<0.01 to 0.07mW/mm²). Red light (638nm) produced no intensity-dependent change. Wild-type mice (N=3) exhibited none or minimal blink responses to blue-light stimulation. Noxious air puff evoked blinks in 98.8% of all trials. DeepLabCut-based pose estimation extracted six features quantifying the blink reflex, enabling automated detection using univariate and multivariate classifiers, with performance varying by feature and thresholding method. Multivariate classification achieved 99.2% accuracy under four-fold cross-validation and 98.2% mean accuracy under leave-one-mouse-out cross-validation. Automated thresholds yielded classification accuracy comparable to manually-validated thresholds. Unlike conventional air puff paradigms, this optogenetic approach enables temporally precise stimulation of TRPV1-lineage corneal afferents and automated analysis of blink responses at sub-second resolution. This video-based method enables accurate, high-throughput, and observer-independent empirical assessment of stimulus-evoked blink reflexes, providing a quantitative platform for investigating corneal sensory responses relevant to ocular nociception.

items.title: Investigating Patient and Public Acceptability of Wearable Technology used during Surgery: An Exploratory Sequential Mixed Methods Survey.
items.abstract: Wearable technologies are increasingly being developed for surgeons to wear intraoperatively, to support decision-making, monitor surgeon performance, and aid training; yet there remains a lack of research into patient's perspectives on them. This study aims to explore patient and public understanding and acceptability of surgeon-worn intraoperative wearables. A two-stage, mixed-methods, cross-sectional study was conducted. In Stage 1, neurosurgical inpatients at a UK academic centre participated in semi-structured interviews, supported by an explanatory video; responses were thematically analysed to inform the development of a quantitative survey. In Stage 2, a survey disseminated via social media and patient groups presented six wearable vignettes, which participants rated for appropriateness and comfort. In Stage 1 (n=30), most participants (25/30) had never heard of wearables, yet after the video most (23/30) identified specific benefits, including improved safety and precision. Thirteen expressed no concerns, nine were unconcerned provided devices were tested, regulated, and used by well-trained surgeons, and eight raised specific concerns. In Stage 2 (n=123), 80-95% of participants rated each scenario appropriate, and 87-99% were not uncomfortable with it. Comfort differed significantly by device type (p<0.001), from body-worn (98%) through head-worn (92%) to robotic (87%) wearables. After correction for multiple comparisons, no demographic or familiarity variable, including self-reported understanding, predicted appropriateness or comfort. Patients and the public appear highly accepting of surgeon-worn intraoperative wearables, although acceptance varied by device type and, for some, was conditional on safeguards. Device-specific patient education and transparent communication of risks and benefits should accompany their introduction.

items.title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

items.title: UC Irvine's BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) Brain Procurement Program for the Center for Multiomic Human Brain Cell Atlas Project.
items.abstract: High-quality neurotypical postmortem human brain tissue is essential for constructing comprehensive human brain cell atlases, but it is difficult to obtain. Here, we describe the establishment of UC Irvine's Brain Procurement Program, a coordinated multi-institutional pipeline to collect and process neurotypical donor brains for multiomic mapping studies within the National Institute of Health (NIH) BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) consortium. Through partnerships with the Orange County (OC) coroner's office, UC Irvine's Willed Body Program, UC Irvine's Medical Center (UCIMC), and the Children's Hospital of Orange County, we have developed standardized workflows encompassing donor identification, postmortem brain recovery and processing, region-of-interest dissection, neurotypical donor selection, and data management. Our experience demonstrates the feasibility of a community-based, multi-institutional procurement framework while highlighting challenges in recruiting neurotypical donors and ensuring demographic representation reflective of Southern California. We further identify opportunities to strengthen outreach and donation pathways. This program provides a scalable model for advancing population-reflective, high-quality human brain cell atlas efforts.

items.title: PIANO enables generative modeling of gene expression and scales multi-omics integration to 100 million cells.
items.abstract: Single-cell RNA technologies enable the routine acquisition of transcriptomic atlases. However, these molecular profiles are influenced by overlapping sources of variation. Since these covariates confound comparisons, data integration is the first step in most analyses. Three challenges remain: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells, and modeling how covariates influence gene expression. To address these challenges, we developed PIANO, probabilistic inference autoencoder networks for multi-omics, a deep learning framework whose central feature is a generative model of gene expression data. Additionally, PIANO achieves robust integrations and trains 10× faster than previous methods. PIANO accurately integrates single-cell data across species and across single-cell and spatial transcriptomics modalities. As practical applications, PIANO models spatially resolved gene expression during Alzheimer's disease progression in human brains and integrates over 100 million cancer cells to model drug perturbations. In summary, PIANO's integration and generative modeling capabilities will empower novel insights for a wide range of future studies.

items.title: Temporal changes in subcellular localization of synaptic proteins in human inner ear organoids recapitulate ribbon synapse development.
items.abstract: Ribbon synapses in mechanosensitive hair cells of the inner ear are essential for transmitting mechanical stimulation to electrical signals in sensory neurons, allowing for precise and persistent neurotransmission. During hair cell development, synaptic ribbons increase in volume, while decreasing in number. Moreover, the number of synaptic vesicles tethered to ribbons increases, and synaptic proteins accumulate near the active zones. Little is known about whether ribbon synapses in organoid models recapitulate the dynamic changes in ribbon synapse development in vivo. By employing 3D high-resolution imaging, we demonstrate that CTBP2-positive presynaptic ribbons exhibit temporal changes in the number, size, and shape during hair cell maturation in human inner ear organoids. Additionally, the number of neuronal processes contacting hair cells decreases over time, suggesting projection refinement. Temporal and morphological changes are consistent with ribbon synapse maturation in mouse hair cells, suggesting equivalent ribbon assembly and refinement in human organoid hair cells.

items.title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling.
items.abstract: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition, yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to viable tissue, inconsistent cell-type definitions, and limited multimodal data. Although single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of cell type diversity, transcriptomic data alone cannot explain neuronal function. Here, we introduce a multimodal patch sequencing (patch-seq) resource of human neocortical glutamatergic neurons spanning cortical layers 2-6. Combining morphoelectric features with spatial transcriptomic data to provide laminar context, we sampled 39 of 42 transcriptomically defined glutamatergic neuron types. This systematic approach enabled the identification of unique phenotypes for understudied populations in the human neocortex including L4 intratelencephalic, L5/6 near-projecting, and diverse L6 neurons. Human, macaque, and mouse comparisons of transcriptomically homologous L5 neurons reveal that morphoelectric differences across species were subclass specific. This dataset provides a unified multimodal reference for studying human cortical circuitry and neuronal diversity.

items.title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.
items.abstract: Sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

items.title: A consensus spinal cord cell-type atlas across mouse, macaque, and human.
items.abstract: The spinal cord contains cell types critical for motor, sensory, and autonomic function, many of which are implicated in neurological disease and injury. Yet no shared molecular framework links human spinal cord cell types to the animal models used to study them. Here, we present a cross-species atlas integrating single-nucleus gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and spatial transcriptomics from over one million nuclei spanning cervical to sacral segments in human, macaque, and mouse. Consensus clustering resolves 111 cell type groups replicable across all three species, whose spatial distributions map spinal laminae and nuclei, including Clarke's column. Identity and laminar organization are highly conserved, yet abundance and expression are allometrically scaled, with the dorsal horn being the principal site of divergence, concentrated in neurotransmitter receptor genes and including a primate-specific glycine receptor subunit switch. Sequence models uncover a conserved transcription factor grammar and nominate motifs underlying enhancer-adeno-associated virus (AAV) access to a divergent dorsal horn population.

items.title: Rethinking Digital Outcome Measures for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Trials: Consensus Priorities for Actigraphy Harmonization, Validation, and Regulatory Readiness.
items.abstract: Unlabelled Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) clinical trials need outcome measures that complement established end points while capturing how people function in daily life. In this viewpoint, we draw on our collective experience in ALS research, clinical trials, digital-measure development, and regulatory science, together with published evidence, a preliminary patient survey, stakeholder discussions, and experience from multisite actigraphy studies. We argue that the field now has a substantial base of longitudinal data and candidate measures, but lacks the coordinated framework needed to compare, prioritize, and validate them across studies. We identify 4 linked priorities: adopt fit-for-purpose measures in stages and within defined contexts of use; harmonize data collection and analysis; use data to shortlist and validate measures across cohorts; and prepare actigraphy methods for trial adoption through early industry and regulatory engagement. Across these priorities, actigraphy should complement rather than replace established clinical outcomes, with its integration guided by patient relevance, ALS phenotypic heterogeneity, participant, and caregiver burden, and the intended context of use. Our central message is that progress now depends less on generating additional isolated datasets or measures than on coordinating the evaluation of existing assets, and aligning future evidence generation.

items.title: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide)-Grafted Hyaluronic Acid Semi-Gels for Localized Mitochondrial Transplantation in Spinal Cord Injuries.
items.abstract: Mitochondrial transplantation (MT) represents a promising strategy for treating conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, including neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic syndromes, and tissue regeneration scenarios such as spinal cord injury (SCI). Unlike conventional approaches that address symptoms, MT aims to restore cellular energy homeostasis by replacing impaired mitochondria with functional organelles. However, clinical translation has been limited by the short extracellular lifetime of isolated mitochondria and by their rapid dispersion from the injection site. To address these barriers, we developed a thermoresponsive carrier based on hyaluronic acid covalently grafted with poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (HA-PNIPAAm), which combines the biocompatibility and bioactivity of HA with the temperature-induced chain collapse of PNIPAAm. The copolymers form injectable semi-gels that thicken above the transition temperature, resist dispersion under flow, and dissolve over hours to release their cargo. We characterized their composition, phase transition behavior, viscoelasticity, and mitochondrial release kinetics, and showed that encapsulation preserved mitochondrial respiratory function and membrane potential relative to free mitochondria over the time window relevant to delivery. In a rat contusion SCI model, subdural delivery of mitochondria in HA-PNIPAAm semi-gels restored spinal cord mitochondrial respiration to uninjured levels at 48 h post-injury. These findings establish HA-PNIPAAm semi-gels as a tunable, injectable platform for localized, cell-compatible mitochondrial delivery and support further evaluation of MT for SCI and other conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction.

items.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Vascular Sphincters in the Brain.
items.abstract: Brain precapillary sphincters (PSs) are located at the point where the penetrating arteriole meets the first-order capillary. Sphincters link blood flow in the capillaries to arteriolar inflow. The sphincters are encircled by contractile mural cells that can control the length and width of the enclosed vessel segment in both directions. Hemodynamic consequences include the ability of PSs to generate the largest changes in cerebrovascular flow resistance of all brain vessel segments. Using two-photon microscopy and genetically encoded reporters, we have revealed the physiology of sphincters. Our work has shown that sphincters can increase their diameter by approximately 30% within a few seconds, enabling rapid control of capillary blood flow over a wide dynamic range. In this article, we discuss the morphology and functions of sphincters, outlining their central role in rapidly adjusting blood flow in the microcirculation and protecting brain tissue against blood pressure variations in the cardiac cycle.

items.title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise.
items.abstract: Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

items.title: TRIB2 supports a high glycolytic phenotype in melanoma cells.
items.abstract: Background Metabolic adaptation is a crucial driver of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. The pseudokinase Tribbles homolog 2 (TRIB2) is highly expressed in melanoma and is associated with poor outcomes and treatment resistance. However, its specific role in the metabolic profile of melanoma cells remained unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of TRIB2 on cellular metabolism, and its role in metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Materials and methods The study used UACC-62 human melanoma cells with high endogenous TRIB2 expression and isogenic TRIB2-knockout (KO) clones generated via CRISPR-Cas9. Cell proliferation was assessed using trypan blue exclusion assays under treatment with metabolic drugs including 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), and dichloroacetate (DCA). Metabolic phenotypes were evaluated by measuring glucose consumption, lactate production, and real-time analysis of glycolytic flux (ECAR) and mitochondrial respiration (OCR) using a Seahorse bioanalyzer. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence. Gene expression was analyzed by qPCR, and protein levels were determined by western blot. Citrate synthase activity was measured enzymatically. Results TRIB2-KO cells exhibited significantly reduced basal proliferation compared with wild-type (WT) cells. KO cells were also more sensitive to the glycolytic inhibitor 2-DG. Conversely, WT cells were more susceptible to DCA treatment. Metabolic analyses confirmed that TRIB2-KO cells had lower glucose consumption, lactate production, and glycolytic capacity than WT cells. Mitochondrial respiratory function and the protein levels of key respiratory complexes were unchanged. Despite the reduction in glycolytic activity, TRIB2 depletion did not increase mitochondrial respiratory capacity and was associated with elevated basal intracellular superoxide levels. Among the molecular alterations identified, PDK4 was consistently reduced at both the mRNA and protein levels, whereas citrate synthase activity was significantly decreased despite preserved protein abundance, indicating selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. Conclusions TRIB2 expression promotes a glycolytic phenotype and contributes to metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Loss of TRIB2 does not induce a metabolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation but instead results in broader metabolic rewiring characterized by reduced glycolysis together with selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. These findings identify the TRIB2-PDK4 axis as a previously unrecognized component of metabolic regulation in melanoma and provide a rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential.

items.title: Comamonas aquatica diet inhibits TIR-1/SARM1-induced axon degeneration by providing vitamin B12.
items.abstract: Emerging evidence suggests the microbiome critically influences the onset and progression of neurodegenerative diseases; however, the identity of neuroprotective bacteria and the molecular mechanisms that respond within the host remain largely unknown. Here, we leverage Caenorhabditis elegans' well-characterized nervous system and ability to eat uni-bacterial diets to determine how metabolites and neuroprotective molecules from single species of bacteria suppress degeneration of motor neurons. We find that Comamonas aquatica significantly protects against degeneration induced by overexpressing a key regulator of axon degeneration, TIR-1/SARM1. Genetic analyses and metabolomics reveal Comamonas protects against neurodegeneration by providing sufficient vitamin B12 to activate METR-1/MTR methionine synthase in the intestine, which then lowers toxic levels of homocysteine in TIR-1-expressing animals. Defining a molecular pathway between Comamonas and neurodegeneration adds significantly to our understanding of gut-brain interactions and, given the prominent role of homocysteine in neurodegenerative disorders, reveals how such a bacterium could protect against disease.

items.title: A multiple Arc tagging approach for tracking neuronal ensembles across experiences.
items.abstract: Engrams, or memory traces, are the neuronal ensembles that collectively store individual experiences. Genetic strategies based on immediate early genes (IEGs), such as Arc/Arg3.1, allow for the ensembles active during memory encoding to be tagged and compared to those active during retrieval. However, these strategies only allow for the tagging of one neural ensemble. Here, we developed a multiple Arc (mArc) system that allows for the tagging of two Arc+ ensembles. We validated this system by investigating how context, time, and valence influence neuronal ensemble reactivation in the dentate gyrus (DG). We report that similar contextual and valenced experiences are encoded in overlapping DG ensembles and that ensembles are modulated by time, where experiences closer in time are encoded in more overlapping ensembles. These results highlight the dynamic nature of DG ensembles and show that the mArc system provides a powerful approach for investigating multiple memories in the brain.

items.title: Acarbose ameliorates age-related spatial learning and memory deficits in a mouse model of normal aging but not Alzheimer's disease.
items.abstract: Declines in function occur in both "normal" aging (in the absence of disease) and age-related pathological contexts, like Alzheimer's disease (AD). Whether "anti-aging" interventions (that extend lifespan) also promote cognitive function in aging and AD remains largely unexplored. We assessed the effect of acarbose (1000 ppm from 4 months of age) on spatial learning and memory using the Morris water maze in young adult (6 mo), mid-aged (12 mo), or aged (24 mo) cohorts of normal aging (Ntg-HET3) and AD-relevant (5xFAD-HET3) genetically heterogeneous mice. In middle-aged and aged Ntg-HET3 mice, acarbose (ACA) treatment moderately improved age-related deficits in spatial learning and robustly ameliorated impairments in spatial memory, maintaining performance at levels equivalent to young adults, with a progressively greater effect at older ages. Conversely, ACA failed to improve progressively worsening AD-related cognitive impairments in 5xFAD-HET3 mice. This work demonstrates that anti-aging interventions can also promote cognitive longevity in normal aging. Further, it highlights that AD does not simply reflect an accelerated aging process and requires therapies beyond anti-aging interventions that target its unique molecular and cellular drivers.

items.title: Sleep and Memory: Consolidation, Updating, and State-Dependent Control.
items.abstract: This review synthesizes recent evidence on the role of sleep in memory consolidation and updating, focusing on the underlying neural mechanisms and their control. Recent literature demonstrates that memory encoding is followed by a labile window during which memory traces are subject not only to consolidation but also to updating. Sleep after single-shot learning can stabilize or enhance memory, rendering it resistant to subsequent natural forgetting. In addition, sleep following multiple experiences supports further forms of memory processing, including reconsolidation, extinction, integration, and differentiation. These processes are mediated by neural circuitry dynamics coupled with electrophysiological oscillations and neuromodulatory rhythms across sleep states. Furthermore, memory processing during sleep can be experimentally controlled by manipulating these internal fluctuations or through targeted memory reactivation. Sleep-dependent processing of existing and newly acquired memories is governed by dissociable state-specific mechanisms, which are increasingly amenable to experimental control.

items.title: Latent Representation Learning from 3D Brain MRI for Latent Analysis and Prediction in Multiple Sclerosis.
items.abstract: Neurological diseases can lead to significant cognitive impairment. Linking magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived measures of brain structure with clinical assessments of cognitive function remains challenging, as conventional statistical methods and traditional machine learning approaches may struggle to capture complex relationships between brain structure and cognitive outcomes, hindering the development of reliable imaging biomarkers. Although deep learning methods offer greater predictive capabilities, their black-box nature limits interpretability, posing a major obstacle to clinical translation. Latent representation learning via generative models can provide informative representations and support deeper analysis and cognitive biomarker prediction. While standard generative adversarial networks and diffusion models primarily focus on generating images from random noise, variational autoencoders offer compact, probabilistic latent representations that are well suited for downstream tasks. In this study, we propose InfoVAE-Med3D, an adaptation of the InfoVAE framework for three-dimensional brain ​MRI to learn informative latent representations. By explicitly relaxing the mutual information regularization penalty between inputs and latent representations, our method aims to capture richer information from input MRI data, facilitating the analysis of brain-related characteristics and downstream prediction. We evaluate InfoVAE-Med3D on two datasets: a healthy control dataset ([Formula: see text]) containing chronological age and sex information, and a Multiple Sclerosis (MS) dataset ([Formula: see text]) collected from the Multiple Sclerosis Center of the First Medical Faculty, Charles University, Prague, containing chronological age, sex, and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) scores. The learned latent representations capture information related to sex and brain volumetric features, including grey and white matter volumes, as reflected in sex-related clustering and smooth transitions in brain volume measures in two-dimensional visualizations. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that InfoVAE-Med3D learns more informative latent representations, especially when the mutual information regularization penalty is completely removed. In this setting, the model generally outperforms other variational autoencoder variants in both MRI reconstruction and prediction of brain age and SDMT scores using support vector regression, while remaining competitive with deep learning-based predictive models, particularly on the MS dataset. InfoVAE-Med3D provides informative latent representations from brain MRI data of both healthy controls and patients with MS. By improving predictive performance and providing interpretable insights into the learned latent representations, the proposed framework offers a promising approach for advancing biomarker discovery and the analysis of cognitive impairment in neurological diseases, particularly ​MS.

items.title: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Unanswered Questions.
items.abstract: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) remains the leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality. While heterogeneous in its pathophysiology, a significant proportion of cases are likely attributable to cardiorespiratory collapse following a convulsive seizure. We synthesize recent mechanistic, biomarker, and prevention literature, moving from retrospective risk inference toward individualized action. Human and animal data support a multiple hit model, in which seizure-induced cardiorespiratory dysfunction is necessary but not necessarily sufficient for death: the environment, genetic susceptibility, sleep and circadian state, and potentially as yet unidentified factors determine which seizures prove fatal. The Mortality in Epilepsy Monitoring Units study (MORTEMUS) provided key insights into SUDEP pathophysiology, while multicenter prospective studies continue to examine SUDEP risk factors and mechanisms, and elucidate candidate biomarkers for individual risk stratification. Prevention is slowly moving beyond mainstays of nocturnal supervision and antiseizure therapies, guided by data from animal models of seizure-associated death. Emerging technologies such as seizure detection devices are being widely deployed to enhance protection, though none has been shown in a randomized trial to reduce SUDEP. Efforts toward universal SUDEP education and counseling not only address legal and moral disclosure responsibilities, but encourage patient autonomy and informed decision-making for individual risk reduction. The decade following publication of the MORTEMUS study continues to provide new insights into SUDEP pathophysiology, propose novel candidate biomarkers and offer potential intervention targets. While obstacles remain in the replication of putative clinical biomarkers and the translation of promising findings from animal models, enhancing SUDEP knowledge and effective patient counseling are critical to improving outcomes and saving lives.

items.title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
items.abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

items.title: High cortical lesion burden moderates the association between brain networks and processing speed in older adults with multiple sclerosis.
items.abstract: Cortical lesions (CL) are common in older adults with multiple sclerosis (OAMS), but their influence on the relationship between resting-state network strength (RSNS) and cognitive function in OAMS remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether CL moderates associations between RSNS and processing speed in OAMS. 82 OAMS participants (mean age: 64.4 ± 4.1 years; males/females: 26/56) were scanned in a 3T scanner. Identification of CL on double inversion-recovery (DIR) MRI images in this study was performed using established consensus recommendations. We estimated functional brain networks using a data-driven procedure to extract seven intrinsic resting-state networks. The Symbol-Digit-Modalities Test (SDMT), an established test of processing speed and working memory, served as the cognitive outcome measure. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, examined the relationship between RSNS and SDMT performance with CL (three levels: no CL, 1-2 CL, and ≥ 3 CL) as a moderator. Significant CL-by-network interactions in models adjusted for sociodemographic covariates and white matter lesion load indicated that high-burden CL vs. no CL moderated the association between RSNS and SDMT in the auditory network (AUD) (p = 0.030), dorsal attention network (DAN) (p = 0.033), left frontoparietal network (LFPN) (p = 0.030), and posterior DMN (pDMN) (p = 0.030). Conditional effects showed that high-burden CLs attenuated positive associations between specific brain networks and SDMT performance. These findings suggest that higher CL burden restricts the functional brain support for processing speed and working memory performance in OAMS.

items.title: Haploinsufficiency of PLXNB3 Impairs Neuronal Migration and Contributes to Cerebral Palsy.
items.abstract: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common motor disability in children, with a significant male predisposition. The identification of genetic causes provides numerous benefits for CP patients and their families; however, the underlying genetic aetiology remains largely unknown. Here, we identified six hemizygous clinical variants in the X-linked PLXNB3 (NM_001163257) (c.C373T[p.R125C], c.G775C[p.G259R], c.G3718A[p.A1240T], c.G4546A[p.V1516M], c.A4996T[p.N1666Y] and c.5024delA[p.E1675Gfs*10]) in six unrelated boys with CP, as well as the c.C3148T[p.R1050W] variant in one boy with global developmental delay. Among them, the variants p.R1050W, p.A1240T, p.N1666Y, and p.E1675Gfs*10 led to decreased protein expression, whereas the p.R125C variant reduced the interaction between PLXNB3 and its binding partner SEMA4A without significantly affecting protein expression. In vivo knockdown of Plxnb3 in the mouse embryonic brain disrupted neuronal migration and caused abnormal neuronal distribution in the cortical plate; these phenotypic effects were significantly rescued by co-injection of a dominant negative Rac1. Collectively, these findings provide genetic and functional evidence establishing the causal association between PLXNB3 variants and CP, and reveal that the underlying mechanism involves abnormal neuronal migration in Plxnb3-deficient mice, driven by enhanced Rac1 activity.

items.title: GOntact: using chromatin contacts to infer target genes and Gene Ontology enrichments for cis-regulatory elements.
items.abstract: Cis -regulatory elements (CREs) can be efficiently predicted genome-wide, but identifying their target genes remains challenging. Regulatory interactions between genes and CREs can take place over long genomic distances, often bypassing genes. Inferring CRE targets based on genomic proximity, as traditionally done in genomic studies, can thus be misleading. Thanks to chromosome conformation capture techniques, chromatin contacts between CREs and gene promoters can be assayed at the genome-wide scale, thus permitting more accurate predictions of CRE target genes. Here, we present a standalone computational tool and webserver named GOntact, which infers CRE target genes using chromosome conformation capture data. GOntact can be used to derive Gene Ontology (GO) enrichments for CRE sets, thus providing a basis for functional interpretation. We apply GOntact on enhancers active in several embryonic tissues, using Promoter Capture Hi-C data to infer chromatin contacts between genes and CREs. We show that GOntact predicts functional annotations that are coherent with enhancer activity. Compared to genomic proximity, GOntact predicts consistent but more specific functional annotations. With the increasing availability of high-resolution chromatin contact data, we believe that GOntact can provide better-informed target genes and functional predictions for CREs. GOntact is available at https://gontact.univ-lyon1.fr (webserver) and https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/anamaria.necsulea/GOntact (standalone command-line tool).

items.title: Carbon monoxide utilisation by Thermanaeromonas species and description of Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov.
items.abstract: Syngas fermentation by carbon monoxide (CO)-utilising acetogens offers a sustainable route for converting gasified waste materials into value-added chemicals. In this study, we isolated a novel thermophilic CO-utilising bacterium, strain AZ2, from marine hydrothermal sediment collected on the island of São Miguel, Azores, Portugal. Strain AZ2 is an obligately anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) analyses indicate that strain AZ2 represents a novel species within a previously uncharacterised lineage represented by the GTDB placeholder genus UBA 12545 in Neomoorellaceae. It is also the first cultured representative of this genus. Strain AZ2 was able to consume CO, producing acetate. We further demonstrated that its closest isolated relatives-Thermanaeromonas toyohensis and Thermanaeromonas sp. strain 9S-are capable of utilising CO, producing either acetate or hydrogen gas (H2). Additionally, we unveiled the genomic potential for CO utilisation within other members of the GTDB placeholder class DSM-521 (previously Moorellia) to which our isolate belongs, expanding the list of possible thermophilic CO-utilising acetogens. We propose that strain AZ2T represents the type strain of a novel genus and species, named Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov. (= DSM 121889T = JCM 39698T).

items.title: The global distribution of plant diversity.
items.abstract: Recent developments in biodiversity research have considerably advanced our understanding of the global distribution of plant diversity. This synthesis reviews current knowledge on plant distribution patterns and their drivers, highlighting methodological innovations such as remote sensing, artificial intelligence, machine learning and mechanistic modelling for quantifying plant diversity and uncovering its causes. Combined with new global datasets, these tools reveal how biogeographical history, environmental factors, functional traits and biotic interactions jointly shape plant diversity patterns. However, major uncertainties still hamper biodiversity research, including gaps and biases in species distribution data as well as incomplete taxonomic, trait, interaction and phylogenetic information, demonstrating that technological progress alone cannot resolve these challenges. Comprehensive efforts that integrate improved data collection and mobilization, analytical techniques, and collaborative international research will be essential to close these knowledge gaps and to advance our understanding and conservation of plant diversity amid ongoing anthropogenic environmental change.

items.title: One battle after another: orthoflavivirus receptors start to be revealed.
items.abstract: Orthoflaviviruses, members of the genus Orthoflavivirus in the family Flaviviridae, include major arthropod-borne pathogens, such as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis, and West Nile viruses. Their continued emergence and re-emergence are shaped by viral evolution, vector ecology, urbanization, climate change, human mobility, and uneven population immunity. Understanding the infection biology of these viruses will pave the way for developing therapeutic and preventive countermeasures. Recent discoveries identifying members of the low-density lipoprotein receptor family as functional entry receptors for yellow fever virus and tick-borne encephalitis virus have reshaped our understanding of orthoflavivirus entry. In this review, we analyze these new developments in the context of prior knowledge of orthoflavivirus receptors. We also discuss the evolutionary implications of receptor usage and how receptor identification may accelerate the development of antiviral drugs and vaccines. We propose a framework of orthoflavivirus-host receptor evolution that can be tested experimentally and can guide the development of prediction tools for comprehensive viral receptor usage.

items.title: Resistance fuels biological invasions while offering new avenues for RNAi-based pest management.
items.abstract: Global trade and climate change have accelerated the spread of invasive agricultural pests while intensifying insecticide resistance. In the sweet potato whitefly, Bemisia tabaci, 2 decades of nationwide monitoring efforts revealed rapid displacement of one population, B/MEAM1, by another, Q/MED, illustrating an 'invasion treadmill' driven by competitive asymmetry between invasive lineages. In this research article, we identify the cytochrome P450 CYP6CX3 as a key contributor to imidacloprid resistance and exploit it as a molecular target for mechanism-informed spray-induced gene silencing. Functional analyses demonstrated that CYP6CX3 overexpression and allelic variation contribute to resistance, while semi-enclosed greenhouse trials showed that topical double-stranded RNA delivery enhanced insecticide sensitivity and mitigated host damage from both herbivory and sooty mold. These findings connect invasion dynamics with resistance evolution and establish detoxification genes as practical RNAi targets for sustainable pest management and integrated pest management programs by reducing chemical inputs while maintaining or restoring the efficacy of conventional insecticides.

items.title: The role of biotic permeability in species' range dynamics.
items.abstract: Environmental changes are predominant drivers of species range dynamics, bringing new species into contact and forming novel biotic interactions. Yet we know little about how novel interactions affect range changes. We propose that biotic permeability-the degree to which species assemblages are permeable to individuals of a range-shifting species-may help anticipate range changes. Biotic permeability balances biotic resistance from negative interactions and biotic potential from positive interactions. We present a trait-based approach to estimate biotic permeability and to infer a theoretical biotic range limit where resistance and potential are balanced. Mapping biotic permeability reveals areas where future range expansions, contractions, and shifts are likely, enabling predictions about the direction and intensity of range changes.

items.title: Predicting Post-TOP Assay PFCA Burdens in Soil and Water Using Machine Learning: A Precursor-to-Product Modeling Approach.
items.abstract: The total oxidizable precursor (TOP) assay is widely used to reveal oxidizable per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) precursors that are not detected by conventional targeted analysis, but its labor- and cost-intensive nature limits large-scale monitoring. This study presents the first machine learning framework for predicting summed post-TOP perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acid (PFCA) concentrations from pre-oxidation PFCA profiles, enabling data-driven estimation of hidden precursor characteristics. Four tree-based ensemble models were trained using literature-derived datasets covering aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) and non-AFFF contamination in water and soil. Six routinely measured PFCAs (C4-C9) were evaluated under unified, source-specific, and source- plus matrix-specific grouping strategies. Source-based grouping provided little improvement over the unified model (test R 2 = 0.77-0.78), whereas incorporating environmental matrix substantially influenced prediction accuracy. The highest performance was achieved for non-AFFF water (R 2 = 0.954) and AFFF-contaminated soil (R 2 = 0.932), whereas lower predictive performance was observed for AFFF water and particular non-AFFF soil, indicating subgroup-dependent applicability. All tree-based ML models outperformed conventional linear baselines for the entire dataset (test R 2 = 0.727-0.768 versus 0.396-0.410). Feature importance analysis suggested that PFHxA may be associated with fluorotelomer-derived precursors in water, while PFOA may be related to PFAS retention characteristics in soils. Performance was largely retained with three input PFCAs in the evaluated groups, suggesting a potential screening utility primarily for AFFF soil and non-AFFF water, while requiring caution for AFFF water and non-AFFF soil.

items.title: Decoupling the effects of carrier type and operational conditions on nitrification performance and N<sub>2</sub>O emissions in MBBRs.
items.abstract: This study systematically investigated whether carrier type and operational conditions regulate N 2 O emissions in moving bed biofilm reactors (MBBRs) through identical or distinct pathways. Four carrier configurations (K1, multi-hollow-sphere, and ilmenite carriers, plus a carrier-free activated-sludge control) and seven operational conditions were evaluated using batch experiments combined with 16S rRNA sequencing. The multi-hollow sphere achieved the best performance, with an NH 4 + -N removal efficiency of 98.9%, an ammonia oxidation rate of 63.6 mg N/(L·h), and the lowest total N 2 O emission factor (EF = 0.89%). Its specific surface area was approximately half that of K1, suggesting that biofilm-development quality, rather than surface area alone, is a key factor affecting nitrification efficiency. Among the conditions sustaining effective nitrification, the combination of a DO of 5 ± 0.5 mg/L and an airflow of 0.5 L/min gave the lowest EF (0.78%) while maintaining NH 4 + -N removal above 90%. 16S rRNA sequencing indicated a trend toward decoupled regulation, in which the AOB/NOB balance showed a positive trend with EF across the four carriers (Pearson's r = 0.87) but varied inversely with EF across the seven conditions (Pearson's r = -0.71), where atmospheric N 2 O release was consistent with control by gas-liquid mass transfer. The exploratory correlation analysis, integrated with microbial-community and mass-transfer analyses, supports a proposed decoupling framework. The multi-hollow-sphere carrier combined with a DO set-point of 5 mg/L and an airflow of 0.5 L/min represents a promising operational strategy for MBBR to achieve efficient NH 4 + -N removal coupled with low N 2 O emissions in this study.

items.title: Epidemic-phase-dependent selection within clades contributes to punctuated SARS-CoV-2 evolution.
items.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 evolution is characterized by punctuated lineage replacement, with successor variants often show substantial antigenic shifts. However, immune evasion alone does not ensure spread, as many immune-evasive variants are rapidly lost, underscoring the complex selective constraints shaping SARS-CoV-2 evolution that remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the dynamics of prevalence, viral population diversity, and haplotype fitness across eight major SARS-CoV-2 clades, and their associations with functional metrics of transmissibility and immune evasion. We show that the viral fitness landscape within individual clades is modulated by epidemic phase: selection initially favors transmissibility but progressively shifts toward immune escape after the epidemic peak. This reveals an evolutionary asynchrony between viral diversification and selection: the transmission surge generates the greatest viral diversity, yet selection during this phase differs from that encountered later. As a result, immune-evasive variants favored late may be suppressed earlier, creating a mismatch that constrains continuous within-clade adaptation. Furthermore, incorporating epidemic progression into fitness prediction substantially improves predictive performance, emphasizing the importance of accounting for dynamic selection. Our findings connect macroscopic epidemiology with microscopic viral evolution, providing a conceptual framework for understanding and forecasting the evolutionary trajectories of epidemic viruses.

items.title: High-Precision and High-Throughput Screening in Environmental Samples Enabled by Secondary Mass Spectrometry Prediction: A Case Study on PPCPs.
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) has been extensively studied and developed for mass spectrometry prediction in recent years. However, a research gap exists regarding the integration of secondary mass spectrometry (MS 2 ) prediction models with suspect screening for environmental samples analysis. To address this, we developed a high-throughput, high-precision (HTHP) screening strategy that integrates MS2 prediction with suspect screening for environmental sample analysis. The cosine similarity of the proposed model reached 0.8. Taking pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) as the research object, we employed the message passing neural network (MPNN) architecture, a typical variant of graph neural network (GNN), to predict the MS2 information of compounds with unknown mass spectrometry profiles. In this study, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS) was utilized for the screening in environmental samples. Concurrently, we established screening filtering criteria requiring a fragment match count of 19 or higher and a retention time deviation (|ΔRT|) value below 1.51 min. The HTHP strategy was applied to screen 38 target compounds and the results were compared with those obtained from targeted analysis achieving an overall identification accuracy of 87.5%, which is higher than the 78.6% accuracy of the suspect screening method. Ultimately, the HTHP screening strategy enabled the successful identification of 715 compounds, from which eight compounds were selected for confirmation using standard substances, successfully validating five compounds. This HTHP approach effectively enhanced the accuracy of suspect screening in environmental samples.

items.title: Evidence for Establishing an Ammonia Critical Level using Tropical Forest Lichens.
items.abstract: Nitrogen pollution is increasing globally. It is accelerating rapidly in South Asia, driven in large part by agricultural emissions of ammonia (NH 3 ) especially over the Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP). Integrated management of South Asia's NH 3 emissions would benefit from development of quantitative target-orientated goals, including definition of NH 3 'critical levels', i.e. concentrations above which adverse effects can be shown for bioindicators. Among the most important bioindicators in this regard are lichen epiphytes, which helped to define the NH 3 critical level of 1 μg m -3 applied within temperate ecosystems of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE). Here we describe a novel enhancement experiment to test the response of tropical lichen epiphytes to a carefully controlled dose and duration of atmospheric NH 3 under field conditions in Sri Lanka. Our results demonstrate that tropical lichen epiphyte communities are sensitive to enhanced NH 3 , but that the pattern of this response depends on initial community composition which can be difficult to predict under baseline, natural forest conditions. However, monitoring and statistical modelling of lichen epiphyte species and guilds indicates that adverse effects can occur at NH 3 concentrations of 1 μg m -3 . This initial experimental evidence using lichen bioindicators confirms that the UNECE critical level of 1 μg m -3 would be relevant in a South Asia context, in support of NH 3 management and air pollution policies.

items.title: The deeper, the more protected? Shallow soils and fractured aquifers override depth-based protection against progesterone contamination in groundwater: evidence from an agro-intensive region of southern Brazil (Santa Catarina).
items.abstract: Steroid hormones are increasingly recognized as environmentally relevant contaminants due to their endocrine-disrupting effects at trace concentrations, yet their occurrence in deep groundwater remains poorly characterized, particularly in fractured aquifer systems. Here, we investigated the occurrence and environmental controls of progesterone in surface waters and deep groundwater (100-282 m) across an agro-intensive landscape in southern Brazil characterized by shallow soils and fractured basaltic aquifers. Progesterone was quantified by solid-phase extraction coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry in selected ion monitoring mode (SPE-GC-MS/SIM). The hormone was detected in 41 of 72 samples (57%), with comparable mean concentrations in surface water (0.31 μg L -1 ) and groundwater (0.34 μg L -1 ) and a maximum of 1.32 μg L -1 in a 222-m-deep well. Mixed models showed that progesterone occurrence and concentrations were not explained by well depth or by individual physicochemical or socioeconomic predictors. Instead, multivariate analyses associated progesterone distribution with the convergence of shallow, weakly developed soils and pasture-dominated land use, indicating that surface-groundwater connectivity is mediated by preferential flow in fractured bedrock and limited attenuation in the vadose zone. The wells sampled supply public drinking water, and the concentrations measured exceed by one to two orders of magnitude those reported to alter gene transcription in aquatic organisms. Our findings challenge depth-based assumptions of groundwater protection and support vulnerability-oriented monitoring frameworks that incorporate endocrine-disrupting compounds in agroecosystems underlain by structurally connected aquifers.

items.title: Cadmium pollution reshapes collective migration and bacterial transport in the soil amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum.
items.abstract: Soil protists, including the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, are important components of terrestrial microbial food webs, yet their behavioral responses to heavy metal pollution remain poorly understood. During development, D. discoideum forms multicellular slugs that migrate phototactically, a collective behavior associated with habitat selection, fruiting body positioning, and population dispersal. Given the widespread occurrence of cadmium contamination in soils, understanding its impact on this essential collective behavior is ecologically important. This study investigated the effects of Cd on D. discoideum slug phototaxis. We quantified migration onset time, slug number, migration distance, slug length, and phototactic directionality across a range of Cd concentrations. Results showed that Cd exposure significantly altered slug migration performance, with increased migration distance at 5 mg/L and marked inhibition at 10 mg/L, suggesting a possible hormesis like response. However, slug length did not differ significantly among Cd treatments. In contrast, phototactic directionality remained largely stable across treatments, indicating that Cd had a greater effect on migration performance than on light directed orientation. Symbiont associated groups generally initiated migration earlier, whereas their effects on migration distance varied with symbiotic state and Cd concentration. Furthermore, RFP-labeled symbiotic bacteria were detected along slug migration trails even under Cd stress, indicating bacterial deposition along the migration path and a potential route for their spatial redistribution. These findings reveal the complex effects of Cd exposure on amoeba collective behavior and suggest potential implications for the spatial redistribution of associated bacteria in contaminated environments.

items.title: Geometric morphometric analysis reveals dynamic skull and brain shape changes during early postnatal development in Twist1 heterozygous mice.
items.abstract: Background Craniosynostosis is one of the most common congenital craniofacial disorders. Understanding the progression of cranial dysmorphology is essential for optimizing surgical timing and assessing brain compression. The Twist1 heterozygous mutant mouse (Twist1 +/- ), a model of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (SCS), shows premature fusion of the coronal suture but no other craniofacial sutures during early postnatal development. Method We performed geometric morphometric analyses of the skull and brain in Twist1 +/- mice on a C57BL/6J background from postnatal day (P) 0 to P14 to characterize morphological changes associated with Twist1 haploinsufficiency and premature coronal suture fusion. Results Coronal sutures remained patent in wild-type littermates, whereas all Twist1 +/- mice showed complete fusion by P14. At P0, Twist1 +/- mice showed rostro-caudal shortening of the cranial vault and zygomatic arch; by P7, a distinct brachycephalic phenotype emerged. These cranial changes were associated with marked separation of the lambdoid and interparietal-supraoccipital sutures. In the brain, prominent dorso-caudal protrusion of the parietal and occipital lobes became evident between P7 and P14, slightly delayed relative to those in the skull. The brain deformation likely reflects rostral cerebral compression associated with coronal synostosis and may contribute to caudal suture separation. The separated sutures were later normalized through compensatory growth of the interparietal bone. Conclusions These findings define an early postnatal window during which cranial and brain phenotypes characteristic of SCS are established, providing clinical insight into the progression of craniofacial and brain dysmorphology in patients with SCS.

items.title: Metabolic rate and torpor use in Carollia perspicillata males with alternative reproductive tactics.
items.abstract: The costs associated with monopolizing access to fertile females may render sneaking copulations advantageous and promote the evolution of alternative reproductive tactics. In particular, males of the Seba's short-tailed bat (Carollia perspicillata) can be described either as sneakers or as harem males. Bats exhibiting these different reproductive tactics diverge neither in size nor in weight. This study investigated whether energetic adjustments underlie alternative reproductive tactics in male C. perspicillata, focusing on resting metabolic rate within and below the thermoneutral zone, on metabolic rate in torpor, and on the propensity to enter torpor during an energetic challenge. In a large captive colony, we compared 15 harem and 31 sneaker males to test whether social status influences resting and torpor energy expenditure or torpor use. Contrary to predictions, no differences were found among social statuses in any of these traits under standardised conditions. This suggests that, despite engaging in energetically costly territorial and courtship behaviours, harem males maintain resting energetics similar to those of sneakers. The bimodality in metabolic rates below the thermoneutral zone supported distinct torpid and euthermic states, with torpor propensity increasing over time rather than being temperature-driven. These results provide new insights into the interplay between social behaviour and energetics in heterothermic mammals and highlight the need for further research into intraspecific variation in energy management among alternative reproductive tactics.
