items.title: Measurement invariance of the Clinician Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 between trauma-exposed non-Western refugee patients and Dutch patients seeking treatment for PTSD.
items.abstract: Background: The Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) is the gold standard to assess post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Although the CAPS-5 was developed and validated primarily in Western samples, it is often used to assess PTSD in non-Western refugees.Objective: This study investigated whether PTSD as assessed with the CAPS-5 has the same factor structure, item-factor relationships and symptom severity scores across trauma-exposed, treatment-seeking individuals with either a Dutch (i.e. Western) background or a non-Western refugee background.Methods: We evaluated four DSM-5 PTSD models and tested different levels of measurement invariance in non-Western refugee (nWr) patients (N = 710) and Dutch patients (N = 1162) using confirmatory factor analyses (CFA).Results: CFAs showed that the Hybrid model of PTSD fit the data best in the nWr group, the Dutch group, and in the combined sample, indicating that configural invariance was met. The model representing scalar invariance showed a worse fit compared to the model representing configural invariance, indicating that item-factor relationships and/or thresholds (representing the value above which an individual endorses the next symptom severity category) differed between the subsamples. Further exploration showed that this result could likely be attributed to nWr patients generally receiving higher symptom severity ratings on the CAPS-5 items than Dutch patients with similar underlying symptom severity levels.Conclusions: NWr patients showed a similar factor structure of DSM-5 PTSD symptoms as Dutch patients. Furthermore, the relative contribution of the majority of symptoms to its belonging symptom cluster was similar between nWr patients and Dutch patients, indicating that item-factor relationships were similar across groups. However, nWr patients generally received higher symptom severity ratings than Dutch patients.

items.title: Dynamic Prognostic Treatment Planning in Dental Traumatology: A Conceptual Framework for Longitudinal Decision Making.
items.abstract: Traumatic dental injuries are characterized by complex biological responses involving the pulp, periodontal ligament, cementum, alveolar bone, and surrounding tissues. Post-traumatic findings such as pulp necrosis, pulp canal obliteration, external inflammatory resorption, external replacement resorption, ankylosis, and disturbances in root development have traditionally been used to characterize prognosis and treatment outcome. Contemporary biological understanding suggests that many of these complications represent manifestations of the initial tissue damage and subsequent healing processes rather than isolated adverse events. However, a complication does not necessarily imply that a traumatized tooth has ceased to provide clinical value, particularly in growing patients in whom temporary tooth retention may preserve function, esthetics, alveolar ridge preservation, and future rehabilitation options. The heterogeneity and unpredictability of trauma outcomes also challenge traditional prognostic concepts. Prognosis after traumatic dental injuries is therefore better understood as multidimensional and time-dependent rather than as a fixed categorical label. This conceptual narrative review examines the biological basis of post-traumatic outcomes and proposes Dynamic Prognostic Treatment Planning, a framework for longitudinal clinical decision-making. This integrates six domains associated with prognosis: biological prognosis, tooth survival, its function, growth and development, patient-reported priorities including the treatment burden and risk, and future rehabilitation options. At each clinically relevant decision point, these domains are reassessed and the management pathway is continued, modified, deferred, or changed. The framework does not replace injury-specific guidelines; rather, it is intended to structure the decisions that occur between and beyond guideline-defined interventions. It also introduces the concept of time-limited success: preservation may be worthwhile when a tooth provides meaningful developmental, functional, esthetic, psychosocial, or rehabilitative benefit during a critical period, even if eventual tooth loss is anticipated. The proposed framework requires expert consensus and prospective validation before its clinical effectiveness can be established.

items.title: Understanding the Partner Landscape for Zoonotic Diseases and Public Health Emergency Preparedness Capacity Strengthening Efforts in Ethiopia.
items.abstract: Multisectoral collaboration is critical for improving global health security; however, little has been known about how it occurs in order to strengthen public health capacities in low-income settings. We used a multiple case study design to explore multisectoral collaboration in Ethiopia for strengthening public health capacities in 2 cases: public health emergency preparedness and zoonotic diseases. Document analysis and in-depth interviews identified partners for each case and examined partner roles and responsibilities. Partners perceived Ethiopian government entities as leading capacity development, and multisectoral collaboration as important to efforts. Platforms convening sectors and partners, such as the National One Health Steering Committee, were important collaboration facilitators. Institutionalizing multisectoral collaboration can improve leadership awareness and commitment to collaboration. A common understanding of roles and responsibilities in collaboration efforts can also improve accountability, sustainability, and trust. Research findings can improve understanding of how multisectoral collaboration occurs in Ethiopia for public health capacity development. Findings can also provide considerations for strengthening and leveraging multisectoral collaboration to improve public health capacities and systems in other low-income settings. Additional research can expand the evidence base for how multisectoral collaboration increases global health security.

items.title: Evidence-based policy improvements for lipid lowering therapy: a focus on reducing clinical inertia and improving cardiovascular outcomes.
items.abstract: Despite substantial evidence linking low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) reduction to improved cardiovascular outcomes, a significant implementation gap persists. Clinical inertia, defined as failure to initiate or intensify therapy despite suboptimal control, remains a key barrier to achieving guideline-recommended LDL-C goals, particularly in high-risk populations. This review analyses systemic drivers of clinical inertia in lipid management, with emphasis on modifiable policy and organizational barriers. These include restrictive access and reimbursement policies, suboptimal health information technology and workflow design, misaligned quality metrics, and fragmented care delivery models. Evidence-based strategies to address these barriers are evaluated, including administrative reform, financial incentives, integrated clinical decision support, team-based care, and structured care pathways. The principal challenge is not therapeutic efficacy but effective implementation. Translating evidence into population benefit requires a shift from isolated prescribing to system-level optimization. Key priorities include harmonizing access policies with guidelines, embedding outcome-based accountability, and scaling multidisciplinary care models. Sustained adherence also depends on addressing patient-level beliefs, treatment tolerability and burden, and broader socio-economic barriers, including social determinants of health. Over the next five years, progress will depend on integrating implementation science, digital tools, and value-based frameworks to enable proactive, equitable, and sustainable lipid control.

items.title: Barriers to Complementary and Integrative Health Use Among Veterans on Long-Term Opioid Therapy.
items.abstract: Complementary and integrative health (CIH) therapies are increasingly promoted within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) as nonpharmacologic approaches and adjuncts to long-term opioid therapy (LTOT) for chronic pain. However, uptake remains modest, and barriers to initiation and continuation are poorly understood. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 126 Veterans with chronic pain on LTOT who had no CIH utilization documented in VHA electronic health records between July 1, 2017, and December 31, 2022. Participants were sampled from a national VHA cohort of over 280,000 Veterans. Respondents reported familiarity with nine CIH services-acupuncture, biofeedback, guided imagery, clinical hypnosis, therapeutic massage, meditation, tai chi/qi gong, yoga, and chiropractic care-as well as prior use and reasons for non-use or discontinuation. Barriers were summarized overall and stratified by age, sex, and race. Fewer than 10% of Veterans reported regular use of most modalities, with chiropractic care as the exception (23% regular use). Common reasons for non-use included lack of knowledge about eligibility, uncertainty about how to begin, and skepticism about effectiveness. Discontinuation was most often attributed to perceived ineffectiveness, cost, and logistical challenges. Younger Veterans more frequently reported not knowing they were eligible or how to start, while White Veterans more often cited doubts about effectiveness, and Black Veterans reported discomfort with particular modalities. Self-practice therapies (yoga and meditation) were more commonly practiced at home; whereas hands-on therapies (acupuncture, chiropractic care, and massage) were largely accessed in community settings where cost and logistics were prominent barriers. Substantial barriers remain to CIH service engagement among Veterans on LTOT, spanning awareness, logistics, and personal comfort. Targeted education, streamlined referrals, and strategies to manage early expectations may improve uptake and sustainment.

items.title: Perceived Social-Media Health Misinformation Predicts Lower Trust and Weaker Patient-Clinician Communication, Not Broad Digital-Health Withdrawal, in HINTS 2022 and 2024.
items.abstract: Concerns about false or misleading health information on social media may matter less for broad digital-health withdrawal than for trust and communication. Using pooled HINTS 6 (2022) and HINTS 7 (2024) public-use data, we examined whether two perceptions of social-media misinformation were associated with trust in the health-care system, patient-centered communication, telehealth use, patient-portal use, online health-information seeking, and clinician discussion of social-media health information among U.S. adults. The analytic sample included 10,818 respondents with substantive values on both focal measures. Adjusted pooled models used the official merged 100-replicate HINTS weight construction with jackknife replicate-weight variance estimation. Respondents perceiving less misleading social-media health information were more likely to discuss such information with clinicians, reported better patient-centered communication, and in some contrasts reported higher trust. Perceived misinformation was not associated with telehealth and was weakly related to portal use. Online health-information seeking did not show a simple withdrawal pattern. Overall, perceived social-media health misinformation was linked less to uniform digital-health withdrawal than to trust, patient-centered communication, and clinician discussion.

items.title: miR-486-3p knockdown induces testicular ferroptosis by upregulating Acsl4 in mice: a novel molecular target for non-lethal fertility control of rodent pests.
items.abstract: Rodent population outbreaks pose serious threats to public health and agricultural production. Traditional lethal rodenticides can cause environmental contamination and poisoning of nontarget organisms, while raising animal welfare concerns, creating an urgent demand for environmentally friendly, nonlethal control strategies. Fertility control through intervention at key molecular targets enables population regulation while preserving ecological integrity, making it a promising nonlethal alternative. Ferroptosis-mediated impairment of testicular function provides a theoretical basis for male fertility control. Nevertheless, key regulatory targets in this pathway remain poorly defined. Here, we used mice as a model to investigate a potential molecular target for inducing male reproductive impairment, laying the foundation for future applications in rodent pest population control. We found that miR-486-3p targets the ferroptosis-associated gene encoding acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (Acsl4) and inhibits its expression. miR-486-3p overexpression alleviated peroxide accumulation induced by RAS selective lethal 3 in Sertoli cells and testicular tissue, reducing sensitivity to ferroptosis and indicating that miR-486-3p plays a critical role in regulating ferroptosis. Local knockdown of miR-486-3p in the testis induced peroxide accumulation and ferroptosis, disrupted the seminiferous tubule structure, and caused a 10.8% reduction in testicular weight and a 78.2% reduction in epididymal sperm count. Our results suggest that miR-486-3p knockdown induces ferroptosis-associated testicular damage by upregulating Acsl4, providing a candidate target for developing nonlethal interventions for rodent pest population management via male fertility control. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

items.title: Learning after referral: referral outcome review as a post-referral diagnostic teaching method in GP specialty training.
items.abstract: Delayed diagnosis in primary care is usually discovered after the consultation has moved on: when a referral is accepted, redirected, rejected, delayed, or returned with an unexpected diagnosis. This Teaching Exchange describes the Referral Outcome Review, a tutorial method for GP specialty trainees that starts after the referral outcome has arrived rather than at the first consultation. The method was developed from routine one-to-one supervision and uses anonymised recent cases. Each case is discussed through six questions: (i) what was the initial diagnostic frame, (ii) what referral question was asked, (iii) what response came back, (iv) what uncertainty remained, (v) who owned the next step, and (vi) what patient-facing wording would be used next time? The approach is deliberately not an audit, dataset, complaint review or learning or significant event analysis. It is a formative educational conversation designed to reveal the diagnostic afterlife of referrals. By focusing on rejected referrals, normal investigations, advice-and-guidance replies, non-attendance and specialist discharge, the method helps trainees recognise false closure, referral drift and missed re-entry points. It offers a practical, low-cost way to teach diagnostic safety as a longitudinal primary care skill within routine supervision, without formal data collection or additional infrastructure and without waiting for rare adverse events.

items.title: 'A well-laid plan is half a cure': using aphorisms to promote pattern recognition, practical wisdom and intergenerational learning in undergraduate general practice.
items.abstract: General practice placements offer opportunities for undergraduate students to immerse themselves in apprenticeship learning under an experienced supervisor. Historically, apprenticeship teaching went hand-in-hand with learning of medical aphorisms. An aphorism is 'a short pithy saying expressing a general truth' and seeks to communicate pattern recognition, clinical safety and practical wisdom. The art of learning through aphorisms has largely been lost from undergraduate medical education. To address this, we introduced teaching on aphorisms as part of our year four in-house preparation for placement in general practice.Aphorisms are drip-fed to students across two days of general practice teaching. This culminates in a 15-minute 'aphorism quiz', where student groups must interpret twelve aphorisms and then decide whether each is the product of 'ancient wisdom', 'artificial intelligence' or written by their lecturers. Aphorism teaching receives positive quantitative feedback. Free text comments are scarce, and informal chats suggest that this is because students are completely unfamiliar with learning through sayings and maxims. Aphorisms are best revealed to students in their clinical context rather than as a list. Aphorisms promote intergenerational learning of practical wisdom, and their decline in medical education reflects a growing shift away from apprenticeship and vocational learning. Aphorisms constitute historical attempts at constructing overarching principles for learning the practice of medicine. Their survival highlights the enduring challenges of being a doctor. Aphorisms offer a solution to 'guideline paralysis' and serve to counterbalance the 'science' of the Medical Licensing Assessment by promoting an understanding of the 'art' of medicine.

items.title: Prospective associations between diet quality, frailty and incident cognitive impairment in the health and retirement study.
items.abstract: Diet quality is a modifiable determinant of healthy aging, potentially influencing physical and cognitive functioning through inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Although healthier dietary patterns have been linked to reduced frailty and cognitive decline, findings remain inconsistent. The interrelationships among diet quality, physical frailty, and incident cognitive impairment, including potential modification by specific dietary components, remain poorly understood. We analyzed 1,636 cognitively normal participants in 2016 from the Health and Retirement Study, a longitudinal study of adults in the United States (U.S.), with diet assessed in 2013, frailty in 2016, and cognitive follow-up through 2022. Cognitive impairment was assessed with cognitive tests and used the Langa-Weir classification; diet quality was measured using the Healthy Eating Index-2015 (HEI-2015); and physical frailty used a modified Fried phenotype. Survey-weighted regression, Cox models, four-way decomposition, competing-risk and multistate models, and additive Bayesian network (ABN)-informed generalized structural equation models (GSEM) were applied. Higher HEI-2015 scores were associated with lower frailty (β = -0.13, P < 0.001), but not with incident cognitive impairment. Frailty was associated with higher cognitive risk in minimally adjusted models (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 2.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.56-3.32), with attenuation after full adjustment. Exploratory analyses identified 13 nominally significant food-item associations with composite cognitive impairment, including higher risks associated with selected dairy products, processed meats, and beverages, and an inverse association with red wine (HR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.66-0.89). None survived FDR correction. Five dietary associations with probable dementia alone survived FDR correction but remained exploratory. Four-way decomposition provided limited evidence of dietary mediation or interaction, while sensitivity analyses supported attenuation of frailty-cognition associations. Higher diet quality was associated with lower physical frailty but not independently with incident cognitive impairment. Food-specific associations were heterogeneous and largely did not survive multiple-testing correction. Findings warrant replication before drawing dietary recommendations for cognitive health.

items.title: A non-IMiD multi-target degrader reactivates fetal hemoglobin.
items.abstract: Reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is a validated therapeutic strategy for sickle cell disease (SCD) and β-thalassemia. Cereblon (CRBN)-dependent molecular-glue degraders of HbF repressors are advancing clinically, but all share an immunomodulatory imide drug (IMiD) backbone and its class liabilities. We show that SH6, a non-IMiD small-molecule degrader, consistently induces HbF in erythroid cell lines, primary healthy-donor, SCD, and β-thalassemia CD34⁺-derived erythroid cells, and humanized NBSGW mice, at nanomolar to low-micromolar concentrations. When all compounds were tested at a matched 0.25µM concentration, HbF induction by SH6 was comparable to that of decitabine and greater than that of hydroxyurea, pomalidomide or thalidomide. HbF induction is CRBN/proteasome-dependent and associated with simultaneous degradation of the γ-globin repressors ZBTB7A and BCL11A. These findings provide proof of concept for IMiD-independent pharmacologic HbF reactivation and support further study of SH6 as a mechanistically distinct tool compound.

items.title: Reported use of participatory methods in health research with transgender and gender diverse populations: a scoping review.
items.abstract: It is well established that health promotion is most effective when informed by the community it targets, through participatory methods. Transgender and gender diverse peoples have been marginalized and experience worse health and lower levels of service access when compared with cisgender individuals. The use of participatory methods in health research to address these issues is of high importance to help rectify this. The aim of this scoping review was to document the reported use of participatory methods in health research with transgender and gender diverse samples to map the current applications of these research frame works and priorities for future studies. The inclusion criteria for articles were published January 2014-February 2025, peer-reviewed, health research, transgender and gender diverse populations, English language, and participatory methods. Three databases were searched: CINAHL complete, MEDLINE complete and LGBTQ+ source. Articles were independently screened for eligibility. Consensus meetings were held to synthesize results. Forty-two papers were identified in the search that met inclusion criteria. The majority of studies were conducted in the United States (n = 23, 54.76%) and other high-income countries, ranging in time duration from several weeks to years, and commonly had as their research topic gender affirming care (n = 9, 21.42%), mental health and wellbeing (n = 9, 21.42%) and healthcare experiences (n = 8, 19.04%). Whilst most studies employed numerous strategies of community participation, a significant proportion (n = 14, 33.33%) of studies did not report having a community reference group. The aims of studies could be clustered under three broader categories; to understand or describe; to develop or evaluate; and research priority setting. Studies were heterogeneous and more rigorous application of participatory principles and reporting of methods is needed. Research with transgender and gender diverse populations must include their meaningful participation from inception to completion. Greater detail and clarity in reporting is necessary to aid future studies who can build on the successes and shortfalls of previous studies.

items.title: Air pollution exposure during urban running in Frankfurt, Germany: a randomized crossover comparison of particulate matter levels on park, roadside, and residential routes across morning and early afternoon hours.
items.abstract: In urban environments, physical activity-induced health effects may be diminished by exposure to air pollution. Typical avoidance strategies, such as running through green spaces or avoiding major roads and rush hours, have not yet been adequately validated. This study quantified particulate matter exposure during running across three adjacent urban microenvironments: a major roadside, a residential area, and an urban park, accounting for diurnal variation. Mobile measurements of particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters ≤ 10 μm (PM10), ≤ 2.5 μm (PM2.5), and ≤ 1 μm (PM1) as well as local urban background concentrations of PM2.5 and PM10 were collected during 2 km runs (n = 60, pace 8:02-4:31 min/km). Runs on major roads (n = 20), residential streets (n = 20), or in an urban park (n = 20), as well as runs in the morning (n = 30) and in the early afternoon (n = 30), were equally distributed. Differences between routes, incorporating the effects of daytime and meteorological factors, on particulate matter concentrations were analysed using linear mixed-effects models. The lowest concentrations across PM fractions occurred during early-afternoon runs in the park, whereas the highest exposure to PM10 across all environments was reached during morning runs on the same route. In line with the urban background levels, exposure across all routes was lower during early-afternoon than during morning runs. Humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and temperature were associated with particulate matter exposure during running. A sensitivity analysis using run-level means (n = 60) did not confirm the route or route×daytime effects as statistically significant, indicating that these patterns require confirmation in larger samples. Running in parks in the early afternoon and avoiding busy morning hours may help reduce fine and submicron particle exposure, particularly during calm, humid, and high-pressure conditions when pollutant dispersion is limited. ​However, park routes did not reduce, and at times increased, coarse-particle (PM10) exposure, especially in the morning. These route- and daytime-related differences were not confirmed in a run-level sensitivity analysis and should therefore be regarded as preliminary.

items.title: Socioeconomic inequalities in healthcare utilization among older adults in Indonesia: social network mediation and dynamics before and after Universal Health Coverage.
items.abstract: Socioeconomic inequalities in healthcare utilization (HCU) remain widespread in many low- and middle-income countries, even following major health system reforms. Social networks may influence individuals' ability to access healthcare by providing information, resources, and support, yet their role in shaping socioeconomic inequalities in HCU remains poorly understood. This study examined whether social networks and their dynamics over time mediate the relationship between socioeconomic position (SEP) and HCU among older adults in Indonesia across periods before and during the implementation of Universal Health Coverage. Data were drawn from the fourth (2007-2008) and fifth (2014-2015) waves of the Indonesian Family Life Survey, including 7,964 and 7,986 adults aged 50 and older, respectively. HCU outcomes included outpatient service use and participation in the posyandu lansia programme during the previous four weeks. SEP was modelled as a latent construct based on education, household expenditure, and wealth indicators. Social networks were conceptualized across four ecological levels (individual, family, community, and societal), and social network dynamics were assessed using a panel sample of 4,411 individuals participating in both waves. Causal mediation analysis was applied to estimate the proportion of the SEP-HCU relationship mediated by social network characteristics. HCU was higher in IFLS-5 than in IFLS-4, with outpatient service use rising from 16.9% to 24.6% and posyandu participation from 2.5% to 6.7%. Socioeconomic inequalities persisted, with higher SEP groups more likely to use outpatient services. Social network dynamics were common, with 36% of respondents experiencing changes over time, and were socially patterned, with lower SEP groups more likely to show increasing network trajectories. Loneliness and marital status mediated up to 7.3% of the association between SEP and outpatient service use, while community-level social networks mediated up to 21.7% of the relationship with posyandu participation. Social networks contribute to explaining socioeconomic inequalities in HCU among older adults in Indonesia. The findings highlight the importance of both structural health system reforms and informal social support systems in shaping HCU. Strengthening community networks and addressing social isolation may complement improvements in formal healthcare coverage and help promote more equitable HCU in ageing populations.

items.title: Suicide in youth and its prevention: a public health priority.
items.abstract: Suicide is a major public mental health problem in young people. Effective suicide prevention requires a public health approach that address both individual and social determinants. The articles published in this collection sought to better understand the factors that contribute to youth suicide and potential preventative approaches. Four studies reported on either the development or evaluation of suicide prevention approaches, including school-based mental health promotion, risk factor identification, multi-modal strategies comprising assessment, referral, and intervention, gate-keeper training. Development of suicide prevention approaches that can be tested and implemented at scale, and importantly, in low- or middle-income countries is necessary in the future.

items.title: When the Body Becomes Ministry: African American Clergy, Theological Meaning-Making, and Obesity Intervention in Black Faith Communities in the USA.
items.abstract: Obesity continues to drive chronic disease disparities in the USA, disproportionately affecting African American communities. Faith-based settings have been used to support health promotion, yet limited research has examined how clergy interpret and implement obesity-related interventions within congregational life. This study examines how African American clergy involved in weight loss initiatives address obesity within Black faith communities in Houston, Texas. This interpretive phenomenological study used semi-structured interviews with ten African American clergy involved in congregational health programming. Inductive thematic analysis identified five themes that were subsequently interpreted using the transtheoretical model. Clergy framed health as an extension of pastoral responsibility, integrating spiritual teachings with practical guidance while addressing stigma, resource constraints, and mistrust of health systems. Participants described using sermons, group programs, and informal counseling to promote behavior change, emphasizing relational influence, lived example, and congregational accountability. Messaging was adapted to align with faith traditions, cultural norms, and existing patterns of fellowship. Participants described obesity as a shared community concern and emphasized culturally and spiritually responsive approaches to congregational health promotion. These findings underscore the importance of culturally and spiritually responsive approaches that position clergy as central actors in community-based health efforts. Integrating faith leadership into intervention design may strengthen engagement and contribute to more effective strategies for addressing obesity disparities in Black faith communities.

items.title: Social Deprivation, not Rurality, is Associated with Receipt of Guideline-concordant Care for Pancreatic Cancer in North Carolina, USA.
items.abstract: Rural-dwelling patients with pancreatic cancer (PC) and a higher Social Deprivation Index (SDI) score may be less likely to receive guideline-concordant care (GCC) than patients living in urban areas. We hypothesized that SDI score and rurality would affect the receipt of GCC among patients with PC. The North Carolina Central Cancer Registry was queried to identify patients with PC from 2004 to 2019. GCC was defined by National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines for PC/Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results staging as localized disease (surgery/chemotherapy), regional disease (at least chemotherapy), or distant disease (chemotherapy and/or palliative care). Multivariable regression assessed the impact of patient-level factors, SDI score, and geographic location on the receipt of GCC. The cohort included 3595 patients with PC: 2532 (70%) urban and 1063 (30%) rural dwellers. Most had regional disease at diagnosis (n = 1871; 52%), were aged 65-79 years (n = 2021; 56%), were female (n = 1891; 53%), were non-Hispanic white (n = 2619; 73%), and had a medium SDI score (n = 1767; 49%), a Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 0 (n = 987; 27.5%), and a Frailty Index of 3+ (n = 976; 27%). GCC was received by 151 (32%) patients with localized disease, 1533 (82%) with regional, and 886 (71%) with distant disease. Across all stages, high (odds ratio [OR] 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.55-0.92) and medium (OR 0.82; 95% CI 0.67-1.00) SDI scores were associated with a decreased likelihood of receiving GCC. Among localized patients, those with high (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.21-0.85) and medium (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.27-0.81) SDI scores had decreased GCC. There was no association between SDI score and GCC among patients with regionalized and distant disease. Across all stages, there was no association between GCC and geographic location. Social deprivation, not rurality, was associated with a decreased receipt of GCC for patients with PC. Multilevel interventions are needed to modify barriers and facilitators of GCC receipt at a state level.

items.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia.
items.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers1,2. However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples3, collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

items.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts.
items.abstract: In 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status1. Here we report the comparative performance of this framework versus conventional BMI-based classification using prevalence, incidence and mortality data from 844,108 adults across four cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain. Complementing BMI with waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio data showed that BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2-3.1% and underestimated it in 5.2-8.6% of participants across cohorts. The combined anthropometric definition increased overall obesity prevalence by 3.3-7.4% relative to BMI-based classification. Clinical obesity accounted for 22.7-31.3% of total obesity, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6-10.9%. A large proportion of individuals (between 77.4% and 91.3%) with preclinical obesity at baseline showed no progression to clinical obesity over 10 years. Increased mortality risk was associated with the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, but not with BMI-only obesity. Clinical obesity was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.64-1.73), whereas preclinical obesity conferred only modest risk (1.19, 1.14-1.24). These findings support the global adoption of the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework to improve obesity care and policy.

items.title: The Dual Burden of Depression Severity and Barriers to Care: Findings From the 2019-2023 National Health Interview Survey.
items.abstract: Low-income adults experience a disproportionate burden of depression and greater need for mental health services, yet face disparities in access to timely and adequate care. This cross-sectional study analyzed 2019-2023 National Health Interview Survey data among low-income adults with household income < 200% of the federal poverty level (N = 16,406; weighted to 140,227,433). Depressive symptom severity was classified using the Patient Health Questionnaire - 8 as none/minimal (reference group), mild, moderate, or severe. Survey-weighted logistic regression models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for financial and non-financial barriers to care, adjusting for demographic characteristics, anxiety, and other comorbid health conditions. Approximately one quarter of low-income adults reported depressive symptoms, including 16.5% with mild, 6.7% with moderate, and 5.2% with severe symptoms. Greater depressive symptom severity was associated with progressively greater barriers to care. Compared with the reference group, those with severe symptoms had substantially higher odds of needing but being unable to afford mental health services (aOR, 16.66 [95% CI, 12.70-21.86]) and experiencing cost-related delays in mental healthcare (aOR, 16.13 [95% CI, 12.18-21.37]). Similar patterns were observed for non-financial barriers, particularly limited provider availability (aOR, 8.65 [95% CI, 6.06-12.33]) and lack of transportation (aOR, 5.24 [95% CI, 3.76-7.32]). Overall, these findings suggest a "dual burden" wherein low-income adults with the greatest depressive symptom severity, who may also have the greatest need for treatment, experience greater financial and non-financial barriers to accessing care. Addressing these barriers will require multifaceted interventions, including expanding insurance coverage, provider networks, transportation access, and mental health treatment infrastructure.

items.title: Penetration of avian and human influenza A viruses through mucus gel networks in vitro.
items.abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAVs) remain a public-health concern because of their continuous evolution and zoonotic transmission. Respiratory mucus is the first extracellular barrier encountered by inhaled viruses, yet standardized approaches for studying influenza virus passage through mucus and the infectivity of transferred virus populations remain limited. Here, we established an in vitro virus-mucus penetration assay to analyze IAV interactions with standardized mucin-containing matrices. We used mucus from human Calu-3 airway epithelial cells cultured under air-liquid interface conditions and bovine submaxillary mucin as surrogate matrices. Preparations were normalized by total protein and characterized using biochemical and biophysical methods. We compared a human seasonal H1N1pdm virus with a highly-pathogenic avian H5N1 virus. Viral genome transfer was quantified by RT-qPCR, while retained infectivity was assessed in susceptible cells. Both mucin-containing matrices restricted viral passage compared with control solutions. Viral RNA transfer and retained infectivity varied by matrix and virus, although no statistically significant difference between H1N1pdm and H5N1 was detected within either matrix. Together, these results establish a framework integrating mucus characterization with complementary measurements of viral transfer and infectivity. This approach provides a basis for investigating influenza virus-mucus interactions under controlled conditions and can be extended to other IAV strains and physiologically relevant mucus sources.

items.title: Association of inflammatory burden index with sex steroid hormones in U.S. children and adolescents.
items.abstract: Evidence linking the inflammatory burden index (IBI) to sex hormone profiles during development remains limited. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine associations between IBI and testosterone, estradiol, and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). Restricted cubic spline analyzes (RCS) assessed nonlinear relationships. Stratified and sensitivity analyzes were performed. After full adjustment, higher IBI was associated with lower testosterone (β = -0.143, 95% CI: -0.190 to -0.096) and, among adolescents, lower estradiol (β = -0.113, 95% CI: -0.155 to -0.071). Participants in the highest IBI quartile had markedly reduced testosterone (β = -0.587, 95% CI: -0.807 to -0.366) and, among adolescents, estradiol (β = -0.477, 95% CI: -0.684 to -0.270). For SHBG, significant inverse associations were observed in the second and third IBI quartiles. RCS analyzes showed a nonlinear inverse association with testosterone, a nonlinear inverse association with estradiol among adolescents, and a U-shaped relationship with SHBG. Stratified analyzes suggested potential differences in associations across developmental stages and sexes. Results were robust in sensitivity analyzes. Higher IBI was associated with lower testosterone in children and adolescents and lower estradiol among adolescents, whereas SHBG showed a U-shaped association. Further prospective studies are needed to clarify temporality and clinical relevance. Higher inflammatory burden index is associated with lower testosterone in children and adolescents and lower estradiol among adolescents, with evidence of nonlinear relationships, particularly a U-shaped association with sex hormone-binding globulin. This study is among the first to evaluate a composite inflammatory index in relation to sex steroid hormones in a nationally representative pediatric population, highlighting age- and sex-specific heterogeneity. These findings suggest that systemic inflammation may play a role in endocrine regulation during critical developmental periods, providing novel epidemiological insights into the relationship between systemic inflammation and endocrine regulation during development.

items.title: Balancing harm minimization and oncological safety in MRI-informed prostate cancer screening.
items.abstract: Risk-adapted prostate cancer screening is endorsed by international healthcare organizations. However, oncological safety and harm minimization in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-informed screening lack validation. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic utility of an MRI-first screening strategy for detecting grade group (GG) ≥ 2 prostate cancer. This prospective, multi-site study recruited men between the ages of 50 and 69 from three public service providers in Berlin. Eligible participants underwent MRI and serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing at two imaging centers. Prostate biopsy was recommended following MRI positivity (score 4-5) or serum PSA ≥ 4 ng/mL (high-risk). MRI-negative men (score 1-2) with PSA < 3 ng/mL were discharged (low-risk), while men with an MRI score of 3 or a PSA of 3-4 ng/mL were actively followed and invited to repeat screening after 1 year (indeterminate-risk). The primary outcome was the proportion of risk groups and GG ≥ 2 prostate cancer detected using MRI alone or combined with PSA. Of 587 screened men, 566 (mean age, 57.2 ± 4.7 years [SD]; range: 50-69 years) were eligible, and 552 underwent both screening tests. Of these, 78/552 (14.1%; 95% CI: 11.5-17.3), 51/552 (9.2%; 95% CI: 7.1-11.9), and 423/552 (76.6%; 95% CI: 72.9-80.0) were classified as high-, indeterminate-, and low-risk, respectively. PSA testing alone would have missed 9/18 (50.0%) and 7/18 (38.9%) of screen-detected GG ≥ 2 prostate cancers at ≥ 4 and ≥ 3 ng/mL thresholds. Biopsying MRI-positive men detected 17/18 (94.4%) of GG ≥ 2 prostate cancers. A PSA-gated (≥ 3 ng/mL) MRI-informed strategy demonstrated excellent strategy compliance (13/13 [100.0%]), could protect 24/27 (88.9%) from unproductive biopsies and GG1 overdiagnosis, and detect 10/18 (55.6%) of GG ≥ 2 prostate cancers. MRI-first screening demonstrates high oncological safety for GG ≥ 2 prostate cancer but increases overdiagnosis and biopsy rates. PSA-gated MRI-informed strategies may reduce harm while maintaining acceptable detection rates.

items.title: Technology-enhanced, group-based (TEG) model of hand therapy management versus usual care following carpal tunnel release surgery: A feasibility and pilot randomized controlled trial.
items.abstract: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is the most common entrapment neuropathy resulting in high volume carpal tunnel release (CTR) surgeries. Usual hand therapy following CTR typically is offered in-person, in one-to-one sessions. Technology-enhanced, group-based hand therapy (TEG) may potentially reduce costs and increase access. To determine the feasibility of the TEG approach and a future randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing the clinical and cost-effectiveness of TEG versus usual care. Single-centre feasibility and pilot RCT comparing TEG (group-based, app-based home-program, telehealth follow-up) versus usual care (one-to-one, paper-based home-program, in-person follow-up). Outcomes included acceptability, feasibility, adherence, numbers screened/eligible/approached/randomized, follow-up rate and data completeness. Costs were calculated for both groups, and value of information analysis was conducted to assess the value of future research. Exploratory clinical outcomes included symptoms, pain and quality of life at baseline and 6-weeks follow-up. Patients' experiences were explored via survey. Of 61 patients screened, 40 were eligible and approached, 33 randomized, 1 withdrew, resulting in 32 participants. 15 received usual care (M=53 years;73% female) and 17 received TEG (M=61 years;59% female). Acceptability (TEG M=4.33, usual care M=4.38) and feasibility (TEG M=4.47, usual care M=4.43) were high for both groups. TEG appointment attendance was 97% and home program completion 100% (n=4 missing). Most felt comfortable with the group format and valued peer interactions. Ease and convenience of the app-based home-program and telehealth follow-up were highly valued. Mean cost per participant for TEG was $68 and $110 for usual care. Symptoms improved in both groups similarly. Value of information analysis showed a future large RCT is expected to be cost-effective. The TEG model was feasible and acceptable. Results indicate TEG is likely to lead to non-inferior clinical outcomes compared to usual care and has potential to save costs, justifying a future fully powered, multi-centre RCT.

items.title: Mosquito vector abundance, spatial distribution and arboviral transmission risk in high-traffic cross-border zones of Tanzania.
items.abstract: Arboviral diseases remain a major global public health challenge because mosquito vectors continue to expand their geographical range through increasing international travel, urbanization and climate change. This study aimed to assess the abundance, spatial distribution and larval indices of mosquito vectors of medical importance in a cross-border setting. A comprehensive entomological survey, using multiple collection techniques, was conducted between October and November 2024 at high-traffic cross-border zones at Mutukula ground crossing connecting Tanzania and Uganda and Namanga ground crossing connecting Tanzania and Kenya. Adult mosquitoes were collected using BG-Pro traps, CDC light traps and Prokopack aspirators, while larval surveys were conducted through cross-sectional household inspections of potential breeding habitats. Data were summarized using descriptive statistics, and associations between variables were assessed using the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Binomial and Poisson regression models were used to identify factors associated with mosquito abundance and breeding site occurrence, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. A total of 6952 mosquitoes were collected, comprising Culex quinquefasciatus (84.7%, n = 5895), Aedes aegypti (10.0%, n = 689) and Anopheles gambiae s.l. (5.3%, n = 369). Significantly higher abundance of Aedes spp. and Anopheles funestus s.l was recorded in hamlets located within 400 m of the international border (p < 0.0001), whereas Culex quinquefasciatus predominated in hamlets situated beyond 400 m from the border (χ2 = 1938, p < 0.000001). One female Aedes albopictus was detected among the adult Aedes collections, suggesting the potential introduction of this invasive vector. Four of the 10 hamlets surveyed had larval indices exceeding recommended thresholds, indicating an elevated risk of arboviral transmission. This study revealed a high prevalence of Aedes aegypti within the cross-border buffer zone and a broader distribution of Culex species beyond this zone. These findings underscore the urgent need for sustained vector control interventions and strengthened entomological surveillance and control beyond the International Health Regulations (2005) as amended in 2024, which recommended a 400 m buffer zone at points of entry to mitigate the risk of arboviral disease transmission and potential epidemics.

items.title: Who will I find behind the door? Perspectives of chronically ill patients after the loss of their regular general practitioner in southern Spain.
items.abstract: Background Relational continuity is a key element of quality Primary Health Care (PHC). In the current global PCH crisis, this dimension is hampered by professional instability. Aim To explore the consequences of professional instability for chronically ill patients without a regular general practitioner (RGP) in southern Spain and its relationship with PHC functioning and quality. Design and Setting Qualitative study conducted in PHC settings in the province of Granada, Spain, throughout 2024. Method 26 semi-structured interviews with chronically ill patients without an RGP were conducted. The interviews were analysed using a Grounded Theory approach to capture the subjective experiences and meanings attributed to PHC. Results Faced with frequent professional turnover, patients reported distrust, frustration, and feelings of abandonment. Being seen by a different doctor each time and repeatedly discussing their health problems with different professionals was perceived as undermining their healthcare experience. Patients recalled the value of having an RGP, describing higher-quality and more efficient care, with fewer access barriers, as well as psychological and emotional support that they could no longer find. Conclusion Limited continuity may hinder the development of doctor-patient bonds, which participants associated with greater support, increased trust, and a more responsive PHC experience. In this context, professional instability may contribute to frustration, dissatisfaction, and reduced trust in care. These findings suggest that professional stability is important for sustaining accessible, supportive, and clinically reliable primary care for patients with chronic conditions. Keywords General Practice; Relational Continuity of Care; Professional-Patient Relations.

items.title: Serum Metabolomic Profiling and Clinical Phenotypes in Parkinson's Disease: A Case-Control Study.
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by heterogeneous motor and non-motor symptoms, but serum metabolic features related to this variability remain unclear. To address this, this small-scale study investigated serum metabolic alterations in patients with PD and explored their relationships with clinical features. Serum samples from 9 patients with PD and 9 age- and sex-matched normal controls were analyzed using untargeted UPLC-MS/MS metabolomics. OPLS-DA was used for exploratory group discrimination. Candidate metabolites were selected according to OPLS-DA-derived variable importance in projection (VIP) values, nominal p values, and fold-change criteria (VIP > 1.0, nominal p 0.585). In addition, pathway enrichment analysis and exploratory correlation and regression analyses were performed to evaluate the relationships between metabolite changes and clinical characteristics. Using these nominal screening criteria, 169 candidate metabolites were identified, including 84 upregulated and 85 downregulated metabolites. Pathway analysis suggested potential involvement of steroid hormone biosynthesis, bile secretion, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction. Within these pathways, candidate metabolites, including docosahexaenoic acid, 8Z,11Z,14Z-eicosatrienoic acid, 5α-dihydrotestosterone, 2-methoxyestradiol, cortisol, chenodeoxycholic acid, deoxycholate, and adrenic acid, showed exploratory associations with clinical features related to gastrointestinal symptoms, non-motor manifestations, and motor-related clinical features. Overall, this study suggests that alterations in serum steroid hormones, bile acids, and unsaturated fatty acids may be related to clinical manifestations of PD, although these findings require validation in larger cohorts.

items.title: Longitudinal Kidney Function Trajectories and Their Association With Hemoglobin and Transfusion Phenotype in Adults With β-Thalassemia.
items.abstract: Renal functional trajectories and their associations with hemoglobin exposure remain incompletely characterized in adults with β-thalassemia. We analyzed 994 adults (806 transfusion-dependent thalassemia [TDT], 188 non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia [NTDT]) followed in the Italian Webthal network for up to 16 years. eGFR was estimated using CKD-EPI 2021 and analyzed using mixed-effects models. Baseline hyperfiltration was present in 22%, but was not associated with significantly faster subsequent eGFR decline. Overall eGFR declined by -1.13 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (95% CI, -1.20 to -1.07), with a steeper trajectory in TDT than NTDT. In 877 patients (5529 observations), models incorporating one-year-lagged, time-varying hemoglobin and baseline eGFR showed that hemoglobin-eGFR associations differed across transfusion phenotypes. Among phenoconverted patients, higher lagged hemoglobin was associated with a more negative age-related eGFR slope, persisting in sensitivity analyses accounting for baseline eGFR. Adjustment for hemoglobin did not eliminate phenotype-related differences in slopes. Chelation regimen was not associated with slope differences in the selected long-term monotherapy subgroup. Thus, renal trajectories vary by transfusion phenotype, and their associations with hemoglobin exposure are heterogeneous. Whether declining eGFR reflects attenuation of hyperfiltration or progressive renal injury cannot be established from these observational data.

items.title: Clinicogenomic determinants of early progression on first-line osimertinib in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
items.abstract: With the recent approvals of the FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA regimens in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), identifying clinico-genomic features predictive of suboptimal outcomes with first-line osimertinib monotherapy is critical in guiding upfront treatment selections. This is a multicenter retrospective study enrolling patients with advanced NSCLC harboring common EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletions [ex19del], L858R) treated with first-line osimertinib monotherapy across 13 centers (Clinical cohort). Comprehensive baseline genomic data on tumor tissue were available for DFCI and MSKCC (Genomic cohort). The association of clinicogenomic features with real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) was investigated. Caris Life Science cohort was used for RNA-sequencing analysis. A total of 1488 patients were enrolled in the clinical cohort; at median follow-up of 43.3 months, median rwPFS was 16.3 months (95%CI 15.3-17.4), median overall survival was 36.7 months (95%CI 34.8-39.4). TP53 mutated (TP53MUT) was independently associated with shorter rwPFS compared with TP53 wild-type (TP53WT), specifically in EGFR ex19del (adjusted HR [aHR] 1.68, p<0.001) than in L858R subgroup (aHR 1.18, p=0.2). Using a survROC model for rwPFS, PD-L1 was the variable with greatest impact on risk of progression at 6 (ΔAUC=0.0549) and 12 (ΔAUC=0.0348) months. In the genomic cohort, patients with TSGMUT (RBM10, CREBBP, ATM, RB1, KMT2D, TSC2, PTEN) had shorted rwPFS compared to TSGWT (aHR 1.5, p=0.01), specifically in L858R subgroup (aHR 1.8, p=0.02). Combining TP53 with TSG, pts with TP53MUT plus at least one TSGMUT and pts with TP53WT-TSGMUT had shorter rwPFS compared to TP53WT-TSGWT and TP53MUT-TSGWT. In the genomic cohort, PD-L1 TPS was the strongest predictor of very-early rwPFS (ΔAUC=0.16), followed by TP53-TSG (ΔAUC=0.08). PD-L1 was associated with higher MET mRNA and immunohistochemistry expression and transcriptional program enriched for proliferative, inflammatory, and metabolic signaling pathways. In this multicenter real-world cohort, baseline PD-L1 and TP53 combined with TSG predict very-early progression to first-line osimertinib, with EGFR subtype-specific prognostic impact of genomic co-alterations.

items.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
items.abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

items.title: A disease-contextualized atlas of proteome-scale molecular influences of natural products
items.abstract: Understanding the system-wide molecular effects of natural products remains challenging because chemical knowledge is fragmented, proteomic coverage is incomplete, and experimental perturbation data are scarce, particularly for multicomponent medicinal herbs. Here we present an integrative framework for modeling molecular influences of natural compounds and medicinal herbs in disease-specific contexts. We harmonized three herbal medicine databases to establish a standardized atlas of 46,422 chemical entities, 12,459 medicinal herbs, and 156,588 herb-compound associations. We integrated high-confidence protein-protein interactions with proteomic and transcriptomic data to reconstruct molecular networks across nine cancers. By prioritizing protein-level evidence and using transcriptomic associations to extend coverage, these networks capture disease-associated interaction rewiring beyond differential expression. We coupled AI-inferred compound-target interactions with signed random walks with restart to model the propagation of molecular influences from sparse direct targets to directional, genome-scale network profiles. Using gastric cancer as an in-depth case study, we generated profiles for 45,418 compounds across 16,899 molecular nodes and explored multicomponent herbal interventions. We further applied the framework to eight additional cancers and retrospectively compared selected profiles with published drug-perturbation proteomics. This atlas provides a scalable basis for systems-level modeling of natural-product interventions and mechanism-guided drug discovery.

items.title: Optogenetic Modulation Fraction: A Robust Opsin-Presence Effect and an Unresolved Cell-Type Question, by Censoring-Aware Survival Analysis of Public Neuropixels Data
items.abstract: Expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in an interneuron population substantially raises the fraction of locally recorded units whose spike timing is altered by light, relative to no-opsin controls, under every method tried. Establishing that result rigorously, and retracting two secondary claims that did not survive the same rigor, is this paper's actual content. We reanalyze eight public Allen Institute Neuropixels sessions (4,112 units), modeling light-to-first-spike latency as a right-censored time-to-event outcome, with a Cox model, pooled FDR correction, and a small-cluster-robust test (logistic regression plus an exact wild cluster bootstrap, since only eight session clusters exist). We report an unrestricted modulation fraction and a restricted direct-responder fraction (evoked latency under 10 ms, an explicit, literature-grounded threshold). ChR2-expressing Sst/Pvalb sessions show a large, bootstrap-confirmed elevation over control under both metrics. Two further claims, each initially suggested by a standard test, did not survive the exact bootstrap or a direct formal check, and we report both retractions as results in their own right. Vip-ChR2's apparent elevation over control is not confirmed by the bootstrap and becomes non-significant once restricted to direct responders. A second pattern, that among modulated units Vip sessions had a higher proportion of direct responses than Sst/Pvalb, opposite the raw ordering, evaporated under the same bootstrap test: no genotype contrast approaches significance, and control has the highest proportion of all three, which cannot be biological. Per-session rates vary enormously within one genotype. With two earlier corrections (a session-composition artifact and a standard-versus-exact-bootstrap discrepancy), this is a four-correction paper: pooled estimates and secondary patterns deserve the same scrutiny as a headline claim.

items.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
items.abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

items.title: The impact of DNA replication on the timing of cellular events
items.abstract: Cellular timing often relies on the accumulation of a regulatory protein to a threshold. For a stable protein produced at a constant rate, the threshold alone sets timing precision: the squared coefficient of variation of the first-passage time is the inverse of the threshold number of molecules. This counting limit appears to be a fundamental constraint. However, production rates vary across the cell cycle. By solving exactly a stochastic model coupling DNA replication and protein accumulation, we show that when a gene replicates at an optimal time, precision exceeds the counting limit.

items.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
items.abstract: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.

items.title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
items.abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

items.title: PathwayDesigner: an interactive SBML/KEGG/Reactome/Escher compatible editor for biochemical network diagrams
items.abstract: PathwayDesigner is an interactive editor for biochemical network diagrams. A network can be drawn directly on the screen, or described as an Antimony model, which PathwayDesigner then lays out and draws. PathwayDesigner reads and writes SBML using the Layout and Render packages, writing Render in a form that other tools can interpret correctly. PathwayDesigner can read and write a diagram's layout and appearance using either Antimony's own layout statements or in a new, more concise format that we propose. PathwayDesigner can also open Escher maps, KEGG maps and Reactome's SBML-based maps. Other components of the model, such as events, rules, functions, and units, are kept and can be edited within the application. Species and reactions can be annotated with references to any database, and PathwayDesigner can find and add annotation references automatically by searching the BiGG, ChEBI, PubChem, and Rhea databases with a component's Id or Display Name, or contextually with a reaction's reactants and products. The network's stoichiometry matrix, conservation laws, and flux null space are computed and visualized on the diagram. The visual style of a diagram can be set with named styles or themes, saved and reused across models. One built-in theme follows the Escher style. The software is written in pure Rust as one code base for Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web browser, where it runs as WebAssembly. The web version is hosted on a GitHub page so that a user doesn't need to manually install code. All 1,062 curated BioModels models and the 1,823 semantic cases of the SBML Test Suite were read and written back without change. Diagrams were exchanged in both directions with COPASI and SBMLNetwork. PathwayDesigner is released as open source with MIT licence, at https://github.com/sys-bio/PathwayDesigner-rs, and runs in the browser at https://sys-bio.github.io/PathwayDesigner-rs/.

items.title: Dynamical stability of double planets in compact multiplanetary systems
items.abstract: The "peas-in-a-pod" architecture of planetary systems, where planets are roughly evenly sized and log-spaced, is pervasive throughout known exoplanetary systems. However, many systems deviate slightly from this trend in that they have a "gap" where no planet has been detected, where one might have otherwise expected one to exist. There are many common explanations for the existence of these gaps, including the existence of as-yet-undiscovered planets lurking in these gaps; however, we propose that one potential explanation for some of these gaps is that they are filled by binary planets, a pair of gravitationally bound planets orbiting a common center of mass outside of both bodies. Specifically, in this work, we investigate the dynamical stability of these binary planets as compared to the more conventionally assumed single planets using Monte Carlo N-body simulations. We find that binary planets are slightly less stable than single planets. Overall, we find that binary planets and their cousins in exomoons provide a plausible explanation, at least from a stability perspective, for the existence of some dynamical gaps.

items.title: Desorption of water from cosmic silicates
items.abstract: Recent JWST and ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks have identified water reservoirs in the inner regions of the disks. This would provide terrestrial planets forming therein access to a water reservoir. In situ formation of water molecules on grain surfaces was proposed as one possible formation process in the PDS 70 system, but transport by small silicate particles coupled to the gas could be another mechanism. Laboratory experiments on the thermally induced desorption of water molecules from different water-containing silicates at elevated temperatures provide another possibility for the enrichment of water molecules in the inner disk. Physically and chemically bound water in silicates can be released upon annealing processes. Water that is physically bound undergoes desorption at temperatures up to 473 K. In contrast, chemically bound water in form of different silanol or Mg-OH groups in amorphous silicates or phyllosilicates, can be released at higher temperatures, ranging from 773 to 923 K. The relevant temperatures are sufficient to trigger the solid-state recrystallization of amorphous silicates to Mg-rich orthopyroxene and olivine. The existence of these crystalline silicates has been substantiated through Spitzer and JWST-MIRI observations. Based on the experimental results, we postulate that the desorption of bound hydroxyl groups may serve as a mechanism for the formation of the water reservoir at temperatures up to 900 K, much higher than the water sublimation temperature of 100 to 200 K.

items.title: A Bright L4 Neptune Trojan Found by Stacking Archival ZTF Images
items.abstract: We report a Neptune Trojan found by a shift-and-stack search of archival Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) difference images of 2019 October, and recovered in public images of seven other telescopes back to 2008. The orbit uses 88 positions on 54 nights from 2008 to 2025, a 17.22-year arc, all measured on our own Gaia DR3 plate solutions. Its heliocentric osculating elements at JD 2460000.5 are a = 30.2158 +/- 0.0004 au, e = 0.0661 and i = 20.32 deg; a fit of the same positions with the independent orbit code Find_Orb agrees within 0.4 sigma in every element. The nominal orbit librates about Neptune's leading Lagrange point L4 with a period of 9.25 kyr and an amplitude of 8.7 deg over the next Myr, and 84 +/- 2% of 500 clones of the orbit remain L4 Trojans for 4.5 Gyr. Its absolute magnitude is H_V = 6.96 +/- 0.10 (linear phase law), or 6.81 +/- 0.06 on the H, G convention of the Minor Planet Center's list of Neptune Trojans, whose brightest L4 member has H = 7.26, so the object is possibly the brightest known L4 Neptune Trojan. Its color, g-r = 0.52 +/- 0.05, lies in the g-r range of the red Neptune Trojans, and for albedos of 0.05-0.15 its diameter is about 140-240 km.

items.title: Crater Scaling Relationships for Gas Impingement on Planetary Regolith
items.abstract: Plume-surface interaction (PSI) effects remains a major uncertainty for operations on regolith-covered planetary bodies. Although spacecraft exhaust can erode surfaces, form craters, and accelerate ejecta, existing PSI relationships are largely derived for scenario-specific lunar and Martian landing conditions and are not yet reliably generalizable. Resolving this problem is important not only for spacecraft safety, but also because controlled thruster interactions could provide an active geotechnical experiment during asteroid reconnaissance. Measurements of thruster-formed craters and ejecta may constrain regolith density, strength, porosity, and particle properties that are otherwise difficult to determine remotely. Such information is particularly relevant to planetary defense, where uncertainty in near-surface properties can strongly affect the outcome of kinetic-impact mitigation and the interpretation of momentum transfer. We investigate gas-driven excavation using near-vacuum, pulsed-N$_2$ experiments in a cohesionless asteroid regolith analog and comparisons with a low-gravity drop-tower experiment and historical chemical-thruster tests. We adapt projectile-cratering $π$-scaling, and find that these relationships can describe gas crater volume as a function of gas, target, gravity, and nozzle properties. A common gravity-regime relationship describes the laboratory data and is consistent with an experimental low-gravity result. Generalizing the $π$-scaling relationship for cohesive targets shows consistency with Apollo-era chemical-thruster cases. These results provide a framework for using spacecraft thrusters as active geotechnical tools during small-body reconnaissance.

items.title: Magellan PFS Discovery of a Cold Gas Giant Exoplanet Likely Formed by a Gas Disk Gravitational Instability
items.abstract: Using the Planet Finder Spectrograph (PFS) on the 6.5-m Magellan Clay Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory we have discovered a cold gas giant exoplanet orbiting the K7V dwarf star HIP88962. 16 yrs of PFS observations imply an exoplanet with an orbital period of $\approx$ 19.3 yrs and a radial velocity semiamplitude (K) of 94.9 m s$^{-1}$. With a host star mass of 0.62 $M_\odot$, this implies a planet mass $M_p sin(i) \sim 5 M_{Jup}$. While stable M dwarfs have a PFS RMS of $\approx$ 3 m s$^{-1}$, the single Keplerian fit for HIP88962 has an RMS of $\approx$ 6 m s$^{-1}$, hinting at a second exoplanet. The best double planet Keplerian fit, with a 4.113 d period, still results in a RMS of $\approx$ 5 m s$^{-1}$. HIP88962 has Ca II H lines with twice the emission of four stable stars, implying that stellar activity may contribute to the RMS jitter error for the single Keplerian fit. When combined with Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry, HIP88962 b has a nearly edge-on orbit with inclination 91 $\pm$ 22 deg, true planet mass $4.83$ M$_{Jup}$, semimajor axis 6.15 $\pm$ 0.5 au, and eccentricity 0.718 $\pm$ 0.02. Including a PFS jitter of $\approx$ 7 m s$^{-1}$ yields $χ^2 = 0.995$ for the combined solution. A massive gas giant orbiting at $\approx$ 6 au around a 0.62 $M_\odot$ star is incompatible with published core accretion population synthesis models, but consistent with formation by gas disk gravitational instability.
