items.title: Making sense of sensation: a framework of interoceptive attribution and appraisal with clinical applications
items.abstract: Abstract Interoception provides a link between bodily states and cognitive and affective processes across both unconscious and conscious domains and is fundamental for a coherent sense of self. While previous research linking interoception to mental health has predominantly focused on interoceptive accuracy, attention, self-beliefs and insight, we argue that the higher-order interpretation of consciously perceived bodily signals plays a fundamental and underexplored role in this relationship. We propose a framework delineating two higher-order processes—interoceptive attribution and appraisal—which constitute the interpretation of interoceptive sensations that reach conscious awareness. We outline key factors that modulate attention, attribution and appraisal, and evidence the relevance of this framework to mental health conditions. Given that these processes are accessible to cognition, they represent an important target for existing psychotherapeutic interventions. We integrate such interventions within our framework, highlighting their potential to enhance interoception-based therapeutic approaches. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.

items.title: How does the developing mind construct a self?
items.abstract: Abstract Our capacity to think about ourselves is a developmental achievement that, when it emerges, profoundly changes cognition. Currently, there are few, if any mechanistic accounts of where a concept of self could come from, and empirical investigation within contemporary developmental science is surprisingly absent. Drawing on a wealth of data from cognitive neuroscience and developmental psychology, I propose a new mechanistic account of the ontogeny of our reflective self-awareness anchored in infants' interoceptive signals. This is a social cognitive account in which infants' expectations about others' attention are deeply entwined with the modulating effect that others' attention has on infants' awareness of their interoceptive state, together providing the impetus for infants to generate a conceptual representation of self de novo. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.

items.title: Testing for interactions in multivariate data
items.abstract: Factorial designs are a mainstay of the scientific paradigm, allowing the effects of multiple experimental factors and their interactions to be efficiently studied within a single experiment. In brain imaging, however, multivariate data analyses commonly proceed using multivariate decoding and we argue that the standard “difference of accuracies” test is not a true test of interactions. To remedy this situation we propose an encoding method based on a Bayesian multivariate linear model which is ideally suited to the factorial analysis of such data. We show how it can be used to test for multivariate main effects and interactions using data from EEG studies of reward learning and declarative memory. This approach additionally allows for null hypotheses to be accepted and allows one to infer whether multivariate effects are driven by collections of univariate effects or voxel dependencies. We also propose that those wishing to pursue tests for interactions using decoding methods use an “accuracy of differences” test.

items.title: The representational geometry of cognitive maps under cognitive control
items.abstract: Abstract Recent work has shown that the brain abstracts non-spatial relationships between entities or task states into representations called cognitive maps. Here, we investigate how cognitive control enables flexible top-down selection of goal-relevant information from multidimensional cognitive maps retrieved from memory. We examine the relationship between cognitive control and representational geometry by conducting parallel analyses of functional magnetic resonance imaging data and recurrent neural network models trained to perform the same task. We find both stable map-like representations in a medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortical network that reflect both task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions and context-dependent, orthogonal representations of only task-relevant dimensions in a frontoparietal network. These representational motifs also emerge with distinct temporal profiles over the course of training in the recurrent neural network, with map-like representations appearing first. We further show that increasing control demands due to incongruence (conflicting responses) between current task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions impact the geometry of subjective representations, and the degree of this effect further accounts for individual differences in cognitive control. Taken together, our findings show how complementary representational geometries balance stability and behavioral flexibility, and reveal an intricate relationship between cognitive control and cognitive map geometry.

items.title: CARE-Drive: A method for evaluating reason-responsiveness of vision–language models in automated driving
items.abstract: Foundation models, including vision language models, are increasingly used in automated driving to interpret scenes, recommend actions, and generate natural language explanations. However, existing evaluation methods primarily assess outcome based performance, such as safety and trajectory accuracy, without determining whether model decisions reflect human relevant considerations. As a result, it remains unclear whether explanations produced by such models correspond to genuine reason responsive decision making or merely post hoc rationalizations. This limitation is especially significant in safety critical domains because it can create false confidence. To address this gap, we propose CARE Drive, Context Aware Reasons Evaluation for Driving, a model agnostic framework for evaluating reason responsiveness in vision language models applied to automated driving. CARE Drive compares baseline and reason augmented model decisions under controlled contextual variation to assess whether human reasons causally influence decision behavior. The framework employs a two stage evaluation process. Prompt calibration ensures stable outputs. Systematic contextual perturbation then measures decision sensitivity to human reasons such as safety margins, social pressure, and efficiency constraints. We demonstrate CARE Drive in a cyclist overtaking scenario involving competing normative considerations. Results show that explicit human reasons significantly influence model decisions, improving alignment with expert recommended behavior. However, responsiveness varies across contextual factors, indicating uneven sensitivity to different types of reasons. These findings provide empirical evidence that reason responsiveness in foundation models can be systematically evaluated without modifying model parameters.

items.title: Typicality biases in interpreting unmarked sentences: an artificial language learning experiment on differential argument marking
items.abstract: Many languages exhibit differential argument marking (DAM), in which nouns are marked for their grammatical role only in certain contexts. DAM manifests as differential object marking (DOM) and differential subject marking (DSM), both of which are conditioned by factors such as animacy and hypothesized to arise via ambiguity avoidance and tendencies to mark atypical situations. While previous studies have primarily focused on production, this study employs artificial language learning to investigate comprehension of ambiguous (unmarked) sentences in both DOM and DSM, examining whether learners rely on typicality biases for grammatical role assignment, and whether the type of marking they have learned affects their interpretation. Results indicate a strong givenness effect and a potential smaller animacy effect, with no significant differences between DOM and DSM conditions. These findings suggest that typicality biases play a key role in shaping DAM systems—particularly information structure—and that their emergence might be best understood as a communicative phenomenon shaped by listener expectations.

items.title: Exploring the roles of gender identity and neurodivergence in the development of eating disorders among neurodivergent trans and gender diverse people – a large-scale qualitative study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people experience disproportionately high rates of eating disorders and are more likely to be autistic and/or have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) than their cisgender peers. Qualitative research shedding light on the mechanisms underlying these intersections remains limited. This study explored how gender identity, autism, and ADHD intersect to shape the development and lived experience of eating disorders in neurodivergent TGD people. Methods We conducted an online survey with 260 neurodivergent TGD adults (75.4% assigned female at birth; M age = 28.0 years) in the UK, all with current and/or past experience of an eating disorder. Participants responded to two open-ended questions about factors contributing to their eating disorder. Responses were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Participants’ accounts are represented in one theme: ‘Eating disorders function as a way of managing both internal experiences and external challenges’. Within this theme, we discuss four subthemes that represent unique and intersecting contributors to distress for neurodivergent TGD adults with lived experiences of eating disorders: (1) Gaining control in an overwhelming world (2), Living in a body that does not reflect your gender (3), Negotiating identity and belonging in a cisnormative and neuronormative society, and (4) Managing bodily presentation for safety. Conclusions Findings highlight the heterogeneity of eating disorder experiences in neurodivergent TGD people and the roles of autism and ADHD. They situate eating disorders within a complex interplay of sociocultural and interpersonal environments that all impact on experiences of distress and capacity to cope with this distress. Plain english summary Trans and gender diverse people, whose gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth, are more likely than cisgender people to experience eating disorders. They are also more likely to be autistic or have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, we do not fully understand how gender identity, autism, and ADHD affect people’s experiences of eating disorders. We analysed written responses from 260 trans and gender diverse adults in the UK who were also autistic or had ADHD and a current or past experience of an eating disorder. Participants answered open-ended questions about the factors they thought contributed to their eating disorder via an online survey. Participants described their eating disorder as a way of coping with challenges they faced. Some of these challenges were linked to their gender diversity, autism, and/or ADHD. These challenges included feeling overwhelmed by sensory experiences, feeling uncomfortable in their body, struggling to fit into others’ expectations, feeling isolated and different to others, as well as worries about being judged or targeted, or feeling unsafe. These findings show that there is no single reason why trans and gender diverse people develop eating disorders. Support and treatment need to take into account people’s identities, life experiences, and neurodivergent characteristics.

items.title: Epilepsy Online Social Support: Characterizing topics and challenges shared in the r/Epilepsy community
items.abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological conditions, and people living with epilepsy (PLWE) often use social media as a resource. However, a comprehensive understanding of the topics represented in epilepsy-specific communities where PLWE may be more honest is essential to designing better technologies to address epilepsy self-management. To understand the main topics and concerns of PLWE, we collected 23,944 r/Epilepsy subreddit posts and performed topic modeling, thematic, and psycho-linguistic analyses. We found five major themes for those topics: symptoms and triggers (e.g., mental health and memory, sleep/nocturnal, and photosensitivity), treatment and healthcare experience (e.g., medication, understanding epilepsy), daily functions ( e.g., perceived level of independence and finances), seizure activity (e.g., auras and ictal symptoms), and support for PLWE (assisting PLWE and support for PLWE). We highlight the top psycho-linguistic characteristics of posts across different topics. Our contributions include providing an understanding of the challenges of an online epilepsy community and their social support needs, and implications for designing technologies.

items.title: Gesture, Not Speech, Distinguishes Autistic and Neurotypical Children’s Narratives Across Toy and Human Listener Contexts
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Toy- and play-based interactions are used in developmental, educational, and clinical settings to promote engagement and reduce social demands. Whether autistic and neurotypical children adapt speech and gesture across listener contexts remains unclear. We examined multimodal narratives addressed to toy or human listeners by diagnosis. METHODS: Fifty-two children (28 autistic: Mage = 106.50 months, SD = 30.88; 24 neurotypical: Mage = 85.04 months, SD = 28.25) completed a task based on the ADOS-2 Monkey Story. Speech and gesture amount, diversity, and complexity were analyzed using negative binomial and linear regression with robust standard errors, controlling for age and nonverbal IQ. RESULTS: Neither diagnosis nor listener type predicted speech production. Age was associated with greater lexical diversity but not speech amount or mean utterance length. In the human-listener condition, autistic children produced more complex gesture-speech combinations than neurotypical children. Gesture amount showed a trend-level diagnosis effect (p = 0.053), whereas gesture diversity did not differ reliably. Among autistic children, listener type was unrelated to speech or gesture measures. No Diagnosis × Listener Type interactions were detected. CONCLUSION: Diagnosis-related differences emerged in gesture more than speech, with no reliable effects of listener type. Greater gesture​ complexity among autistic than neurotypical children in the​ human-listener condition underscores variability in autistic gesture use. These findings caution against characterizing autistic multimodal communication solely in terms of reduce​d gesture production. Examining gesture complexity and gesture-speech integration alongside production ​frequency may provide a more comprehensive understanding of autistic communication. Larger studies across communicative contexts are needed before translating findings into practice.

items.title: THE EFFECT OF A WELL-BEING PROMOTION PROGRAM ON DEPRESSION AMONG OLDER ADULTS IN THE COMMUNITY
items.abstract: This study aimed to: (1) evaluate the effect of a well-being promotion program on depressive symptoms among older adults in the community; (2) compare depression scores before and after the intervention in the experimental group; and (3) examine differences in depression score changes between the experimental and control groups. A quasi-experimental design with a pretest–posttest control group was employed. The sample consisted of 66 older adults. Research instruments included the 9-Item Depression Screening Questionnaire (9Q) and the Thai Geriatric Depression Scale (TGDS). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and independent and paired t-tests. The results indicated a significant reduction in depression levels, with greater improvement observed in the experimental group compared to the control group. These findings suggest that the well-being promotion program is effective in reducing depressive symptoms among older adults. The program may be applied as an alternative intervention in community mental health settings.

items.title: Global environmental genomics reveals vast uncultivated protist diversity and taxonomic blind spots
items.abstract: Protists, defined as eukaryotes distinct from plants, animals and fungi, comprise much of eukaryotic phylogenetic diversity and perform key ecological functions, yet most lineages remain uncultivated and poorly represented in reference databases. Amplicon-based 18S rRNA gene surveys have transformed protist ecology, but primer bias, PCR bias and marker length can limit recovery of divergent lineages. Here, we conduct a cultivation-independent, rDNA operon-centered survey of over 30,000 assembled metagenomes, protist single-cell genomes and 21 long-amplicon datasets spanning marine, freshwater and soil-associated environments. We recover 157,956 long 18S rRNA gene sequences (≥800 bp), which together with reference sequences cluster into 103,338 OTUs at 97% identity and 24,438 OTUs at 85% identity. After excluding non-protist groups and singletons, 81% of the remaining 9543 protist 85%-OTUs consist exclusively of environmental sequences with no described representative. A concatenated 18S-28S rRNA framework reveals strong underrepresentation of Amoebozoa, Discoba, and Rhizaria in current references and identifies 13 candidate deeply divergent lineages with little or no database representation, some of which we link to partial genomes recovered by single-cell genomics. We further characterize their ecosystem distributions and predict associations with bacteria and other eukaryotes. This study provides a global, cultivation-independent resource for targeted sampling and downstream genomic, ecological and experimental characterization. In this study, the authors analyze over 30,000 assembled metagenomes across ecosystems to uncover hidden protist diversity, including major novel uncultivated lineages, and reveal their habitats and connections to other microbes.

items.title: Global biodiversity models exhibit low predictive accuracy on local scales
items.abstract: Abstract Amid the global biodiversity crisis, there is high demand for spatially explicit biodiversity indicators. Global models that quantify human impacts on biodiversity provide important insights for conservation, but systematic testing of predictive performance has been lacking. Here, when evaluating alpha- and beta-diversity models using representative global data, we find that, despite land-use impacts in line with previous research, there is a challenging gap between effect size inference and local prediction. The results show that mixed models with study attributes as random effects, common in biodiversity meta-analysis and indicators, exhibit low predictive accuracy, driven by reliance on highly averaged fixed effects. Ecologically structured models that replace study random effects with biome, realm and taxonomic parameters show improved but still modest results in sampled contexts. Further, performance when extending predictions to other contexts remains low, related to distribution shifts in environmental conditions and biodiversity responses. Our results highlight a tension between high-resolution predictor availability and the granularity at which biodiversity responses can be reliably estimated. While models are essential for informed conservation efforts, their applicability is fundamentally constrained by current data availability, which includes geographic and taxonomic biases. Countries with extensive data can build higher-fidelity national indicators, but accelerated and systematic data collection is needed to support data-poor regions with localized, actionable biodiversity insights.

items.title: Evidence of impact of tire wear particles on a roadside plant community at environmentally relevant concentrations
items.abstract: Abstract Tire wear particles (TWPs) are recognized as a significant contributor of microplastic pollution, and recent research has shown their effects on plants using various types of crops. However, given the fact that abrasion of tire tread intensifies near roadways, roadside plant community should receive more attention. In this study, we established mono- and mixed-plant communities including four different species (, , , and ), and the effects of TWPs on each community were investigated across a range of concentrations (1 to 10,000 mg kg). We found the significant changes in the structure of mixed-plant community, which represented opposite growth patterns between two species ( and ), while there were no effects on each species in the mono-culture condition. Our results revealed that takes advantage in the mixed-culture condition, in terms of biomass, while experienced the negative effects on shoot mass. We measured electrical capacitances to understand plant-plant interactions in root system, and it aligned with the growth patterns ( and ) of TWP treatments. Soil pH varied depending on the cultivation of each species and TWP treatments. Consequently, we assumed that TWPs alter the soil process and plant-plant interactions. Roadside ecosystem provides ecological values, and the impacts of TWPs on roadside plant community might be crucial to sustain a wild range of environmental functions.

items.title: Transposable elements as drivers of reproductive isolation: A framework for testing hybridization-induced escalation of genetic conflicts
items.abstract: Abstract Contrary to long-held views, the exchange of genetic diversity between species by hybridization is now recognized as an important process contributing to the evolution of biodiversity. However, hybridization has molecular consequences beyond the exchange of genetic variation. The clash of divergent genomes upon hybridization can escalate genetic conflicts previously resolved in parental species—notably between transposable elements (TEs) and their repressors—and may unleash a cascade of molecular events inducing the evolution of chromosomal rearrangements (structural variants, SVs). Novel TE insertions and other SVs are often associated with cancer, reduced longevity, and genomic disorders, and usually inflict high fitness costs, thus they likely incur major constraints to gene flow among species and may constitute an integral component of reproductive isolation. Furthermore, in the presence of gene flow, certain SVs (e.g., inversions) may help protect beneficial combinations of alleles across genes from breaking up. By mediating an increased input of SVs, TE reactivation may therefore act as an architect of SVs underlying reproductive isolation. While the hypothesis of TE-related reproductive barriers is not new, tests of its predictions outside the context of hybrid dysgenesis remain scarce, especially in natural hybrid zones. With this perspective we aim to synthesize ideas and provide a roadmap to stimulate research targeted towards an increased understanding of hybridization-induced TE reactivation and its potential knock-on effects for the evolution of structural variation and reproductive isolation. We argue that technological advances now provide unprecedented opportunities to identify genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic signatures of such re-escalating genetic conflict upon hybridization and present a roadmap to guide research to investigate such genetic conflict in natural hybrid zones. While our perspective is predominantly focused on vertebrates, with adaptations to the taxon-specific TE biology, our roadmap represents a generalizable framework for the study of hybridization-induced escalations of TE-related genomic conflicts.

items.title: Range-wide genomics reveals deep divergence in peripheral populations of the streamside salamander (Ambystoma barbouri)
items.abstract: Abstract Peripheral populations often harbor unique evolutionary diversity yet face disproportionate conservation risk. The streamside salamander ( Ambystoma barbouri ) occurs primarily in the Ohio River basin in Kentucky, Indiana, and Ohio, but persists as isolated, disjunct populations in central Tennessee and western West Virginia, where rapid urbanization threatens remaining habitat. We combined mitochondrial DNA sequencing (~ 1,200 bp of the D-loop) and genome-wide SNP data to assess range-wide phylogeographic structure and fine-scale population differentiation across 89 populations throughout the contemporary geographic range of the species. Mitochondrial analyses revealed multiple deeply divergent lineages, whereas SNP-based analyses demonstrated strong nuclear differentiation between Tennessee populations and the species’ northern distribution in Kentucky, Indiana, Ohio, and West Virginia. Within Tennessee, genomic data identified three well-defined genetic clusters structured by watershed boundaries, with hierarchical AMOVA supporting significant differentiation among watersheds and among populations within watersheds. Together, these results indicate that Tennessee populations of A. barbouri represent a distinct and evolutionarily significant component of the species’ range and support their recognition as distinct conservation units.

items.title: Valley-bottom wetland agricultural conversion and recovery shape greenhouse gas dynamics and soil organic carbon stocks in an African tropical highland system
items.abstract: Tropical wetlands significantly impact global greenhouse gas (GHG) budgets and carbon storage; however, data from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) remain limited. Highland valley-bottom wetland (HVBW) agriculture supports millions, yet its effects on GHG emissions and carbon storage remain undocumented. This study quantified soil emissions of nitrous oxide (N 2 O), carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), and methane (CH 4 ) in the Taita Hills, Kenya, from 12 converted, 10 recovering, and one reference (intact) HVBW. Agricultural conversion shifted wetland emissions from CH 4 to N 2 O dominance. Converted HVBWs were N 2 O sources (1.6 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1), driven by elevated soil nitrate, whereas the intact HVBW was an N 2 O sink (−0.3 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1), with high soil moisture and a high soil C/NO3--N ratio suggesting complete denitrification. Recovering HVBWs showed intermediate N 2 O emissions (0.5 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1). CO 2 emissions were similar between converted and recovering HVBWs (9534 vs. 9610 kgCO2-Cha-1yr-1) but lower in the intact (2923 kgCO2-Cha-1yr-1). CH 4 emissions were highest in the intact HVBW (2757 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1), intermediate in recovering sites (781 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1), and lowest in converted sites (38 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1). The intact HVBW had an SOC stock of 224 Mg C ha −1 , indicating carbon loss rates of 2.7 MgCha-1yr-1 over 45 years for converted HVBWs. Comparing recovering with converted HVBWs suggests an SOC recovery of about 1.1 MgCha-1yr-1 after abandonment, offsetting ∼0.0005 % of Kenya's annual agricultural GHG emissions, or 9.8 % when scaled nationally. However, recovering HVBWs also emitted considerably more CH 4 , so their net climate effect cannot be derived from SOC stocks alone. These findings highlight trade-offs between GHG emissions and carbon storage in HVBWs, with wetland recovery promoting partial functional restoration and SOC recovery in SSA, but at the cost of increased CH 4 emissions.

items.title: RNA and proteins joined up at the origins of life: Persistence is the point
items.abstract: What drove nucleic acids (NA) into functional associations with proteins (PR) at the origins of life? We reason from polymer physics and the Central Dogma that the fitness value of cooperating through a division of labor—NA for replication fidelity and PR for functional fitness—is much higher than for either polymer alone. Our model shows a Pareto Front, where NA and PR can bootstrap each other to achieve autocatalytic cooperativity toward biology.

items.title: CO emissions and NO x ∕ CO ratios from the extreme 2025 Iberian wildfires: TROPOMI-based estimates and comparison with inventories
items.abstract: In summer 2025 the Iberian Peninsula experienced exceptional wildfire activity, with nearly 0.5 Mha of land burned and carbon emissions that broke European records since 2003. In this work, we quantify CO emission rates from 15 wildfires in northwestern Spain and northern Portugal during August 2025 using satellite observations from the Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI). Through a plume masking method that exploits the synergy between collocated NO 2 and CO TROPOMI observations in complex multi-fire scenes, we infer CO emission rates for 46 individual hotspots. The area studied represents about 70 % of the total burned area in the Iberian Peninsula during that period. The inferred TROPOMI-based emission rates are compared against three fire emission inventories: the Global Fire Assimilation System (GFAS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED) and the Fire Inventory from NCAR (FINN). Our results indicate that inventories systematically underestimate CO emissions by about a factor of 3 relative to TROPOMI-derived estimates, consistent with findings from previous studies on other extreme wildfire events. Additionally, we also investigate the NO x / CO mole density ratio (MDR; NO x = NO + NO 2 ) as a proxy for combustion efficiency. This estimate is obtained from TROPOMI NO 2 / CO MDR using literature-based NO 2 -to-NO x conversion factor. The TROPOMI-derived NO x / CO MDR values are consistently lower than those from inventories, with regional variability suggesting differences in combustion phase and fuel type across the study domain. These results highlight the potential of combined satellite observations to assess wildfire emissions in complex fire scenes, while also pointing to limitations in current fire emission inventories under such conditions.

items.title: Taxonomically standardized iNaturalist records reveal broad-scale patterns in documented polychaete diversity across U.S. coastlines
items.abstract: Abstract Citizen-science platforms are increasingly used to document biodiversity, but their value for taxonomically difficult marine invertebrates remains uncertain. Polychaete annelids are diverse, ecologically important, and often difficult to identify from photographs alone, raising questions about how community-science records should be interpreted. Here, we evaluated research-grade iNaturalist observations of Polychaeta across the continental United States. We retrieved 13,775 observations from iNaturalist, standardized names against a World Register of Marine Species-derived taxonomic backbone, assigned records to coastal regions using geographic coordinates, and analyzed observation-based richness, family composition, species overlap, rank-observation structure, and rarefaction patterns. After filtering, 12,539 observations representing 302 species, 54 families, and 4,027 observers were retained. Sampling effort was highly uneven, with the West Coast accounting for most observations, species, families, and observers. Species overlap among coasts was limited, and dominant families differed regionally, although tubiculous families such as the Serpulidae were prominent across all three coasts. Rank-observation curves showed that a small number of frequently documented species dominated each regional record, whereas many taxa were represented by few observations. Observation-based rarefaction indicated continued species accumulation, especially on the West Coast. These results show that taxonomically standardized iNaturalist records can reveal broad patterns in documented polychaete diversity while underscoring the need for expert validation, voucher-based taxonomy, and careful interpretation of observation-derived biodiversity data.

items.title: Preliminary tolerance distances of Sri Lankan deer to humans: The effect of species, landscape use, and proximity to buildings
items.abstract: Abstract Disturbance of wildlife by humans is common worldwide and is prevalent in areas where local economies rely on ecotourism, which promotes close encounters between people and charismatic megafauna, e.g., deer. When ecotourists approach wildlife, maintaining adequate separation distances minimizes impacts on focal mammals while enhancing the ecotourism experience. We propose suitable separation distances by measuring deer Flight-Initiation Distances (FIDs) in the tourism and biodiversity hotspot, Sri Lanka. FIDs ( n = 139 non-alert individuals) differed between four species: Spotted Deer Axis axis (µ ± SE, 23.74 ± 3.59 m), Barking Deer Muntiacus muntjak (15.36 ± 1.69 m), Sambar Rusa unicolor (12.11 ± 1.92 m) and Hog Deer A. porcinus (10.44 ± 2.32 m). Barking Deer, Sambar and Spotted Deer exhibited positive associations between Starting Distance (the distance between the observer and focal deer when an approach began) and FID. This relationship is almost always modelled as a linear effect in studies of wildlife FIDs, however for Sambar and Spotted Deer it was non-linear. Spotted Deer and Sambar had longer FIDs in wilderness compared with non-wilderness areas. Sambar at Horton Plains National Park, which are subjected to intense depredation by Leopard Panthera pardus kotiya , tended to have shorter FIDs within c. 300 m of human infrastructure, perhaps at least partly because Leopards avoid humans. Minimum human-deer separation distances (95th percentiles of FIDs collected in wilderness areas) were: 31 m for Spotted Deer; 64 m for Sambar; 23 m for Barking Deer; and 15 m for Hog Deer (with limited sampling). Prescriptions based on these could be implemented into tourism operations via codes of conduct, for future validation and fine-tuning.

items.title: PRELIMINARY MORPHOMOLECULAR CHARACTERISATION OF A CRYPTIC WEEVIL ASSOCIATED WITH YOUNG OIL PALMS IN MALAYSIA
items.abstract: A cryptic weevil associated with damaged young oil palms was detected in Tangkak, Johor, Malaysia.The specimen was initially suspected to be the red palm weevil, Rhynchophorus ferrugineus, but exhibited notable differences in body size and elytral markings.Morphometric analysis revealed morphological differences, prompting molecular identification using cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) and 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) gene markers.COI sequence analysis showed 84.94%-85.17%identity with Sphenophorus compressirostris, while 16S rRNA analysis showed 93.36% identity with Sparganobasis subcruciata and 91.94% with Sphenophorus sp.These results suggest a closer phylogenetic affinity to Sphenophorus-or Sparganobasis-like taxa than to Rhynchophorus, although they should be interpreted as preliminary indications rather than definitive taxonomic placement.This study provides preliminary evidence of an unusual weevil lineage associated with Malaysian oil palm systems.The findings highlight the limitations of morphology-based identification alone and emphasise the value of integrating molecular diagnostics in pest surveillance.Given that related taxa include basalboring species capable of damaging internal palm tissues, misidentification may result in inappropriate control strategies and overlooked infestations.Overall, this preliminary work underscores the importance of combining morphological and molecular approaches to improve diagnostic accuracy and support timely, evidence-based pest management in the oil palm industry.

items.title: Bats and People: Assessing Awareness, Threats, and Conservation Challenges in Three Selected Barangays in Naawan, Misamis Oriental
items.abstract: This study assessed community knowledge, perceptions, and attitudes toward bats in Barangays Patag, Mapulog, and Tagbalogo in Naawan, Misamis Oriental. Data were collected through surveys of 98 individuals and key informant interviews with eight local officials. Respondents reported awareness of the importance of forests and bats and expressed support for habitat protection, anti-poaching measures, and natural resource conservation. Knowledge gaps and uncertainty persisted regarding the ecological roles of bats and their interactions with people. Pesticide use, noise pollution, garbage dumping, quarrying, and illegal logging were among the most frequently reported potential disturbances. Interview responses indicated limited information about bat populations and uneven awareness of local conservation measures. The findings describe community perceptions and do not directly measure ecological threats, population trends, or policy implementation. They support targeted environmental education, biodiversity monitoring, coordination among local institutions, and opportunities for community participation in conservation.

items.title: Heritopolis—from Historic Urban Landscape to Metropolitan Heritage: rethinking heritage for the century of the metropolis
items.abstract: Abstract The 2011 UNESCO Recommendation on the Historic Urban Landscape marked a decisive shift in heritage thinking by extending conservation beyond monuments and historic centres to embrace the broader urban context. Since then, however, metropolitan regions have become the dominant spatial, demographic and economic form of human settlement, exposing conceptual and operational limitations in heritage frameworks still largely centred on the city. The metropolitan condition requires more than a spatial enlargement of heritage: it calls for a reconsideration of its conceptual foundations. Building upon the principles of the Historic Urban Landscape while engaging with debates on metropolitan governance, spatial sustainability and complexity, the paper proposes Metropolitan Heritage as an interpretative framework rather than a new heritage category. Metropolitan Heritage is defined as a dynamic system of relationships linking culture and nature, urban and rural territories, infrastructures, ecological processes and multiple identities across metropolitan regions. Drawing on the experience of the Heritopolis initiative, the paper argues that heritage can become a strategic framework for governing metropolitan territories while contributing to the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals and the New Urban Agenda.

items.title: Canonical assortativity: An application to multivariate mixing patterns in the international wildlife trade
items.abstract: Abstract The international wildlife trade is a leading cause of global biodiversity loss, and the spread of infectious diseases and invasive species. However, to date, there has been limited investigation into the multivariate effects and the asymmetric nature of the drivers of the wildlife trade. We present a method for calculating a multivariate assortativity metric for networks with vector-valued node attributes, which is then used to analyse the spatiotemporal influence of a wide range of trade drivers (inferred from a systematic review) on wild-caught, live, terrestrial vertebrate trade networks constructed from Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) data. This method may be used for the analysis of any real-world networks possessing multivariate node attributes for exploratory data analysis, structural analysis, or link prediction. We found that links in wildlife trade networks demonstrate strong asymmetric demand-side selectivity for biodiversity attributes and supply-side selectivity for economic and governance attributes. The trade of wild birds demonstrated a weaker structure, supporting evidence for the power of strong regional trade regulations, such as the EU Wild Bird Trade Ban. Novel network approaches provide important insights into the global supply chain of wildlife trade. In particular, the trade in terrestrial vertebrates was shown to be more consistently structured by demand than by supply, highlighting the inherently paradoxical nature of scarcity-driven demand in the wildlife trade and underscoring the critical role of trade regulations in importing countries.

items.title: Reflexive Monitoring for Urban Nature Planning: An Adaptive Evaluation Approach
items.abstract: Unlike grey infrastructure projects, which are generally thought of as being complete upon final construction, urban nature is dynamic and ever-changing through seasons and years. It’s important, therefore, that monitoring frameworks take into account long-term stewardship and growth phases that extend well beyond initial design and implementation. This chapter provides a methodological overview of Reflexive Monitoring (RM), and its application in European Cities involved in the development and on-going implementation of Urban Nature Plans. With its origins in transition management theory, RM provides an assessment approach designed to capture learning in real time [ 1 ]. It enables and supports urban practitioners to track progress, identify institutional barriers, leverage opportunities, and translate daily operational friction into shared organizational knowledge. The chapter presents a series of common challenges and barriers faced by city practitioners when it comes to long-term greening initiatives, including the limits of conventional indicators, institutional barriers and siloed governance, and the difficulty of planning for long-term outcomes. RM is positioned as a facilitating mechanism, providing the urban practitioners with the tools and knowledge to overcome these challenges by creating spaces for shared learning, and the identification of best practice learning outcomes. Key learnings from Barcelona, Paris, Burgas, Mannheim, and Belgrade are presented.

items.title: Genetic structure, inbreeding and effective population size in an endangered island cockatoo, following management-led recovery
items.abstract: Abstract Island populations are particularly vulnerable to genetic risk. The glossy black-cockatoo Calyptorhynchus lathami halmaturinus has been restricted to Kangaroo Island, South Australia, since the mid-20th century and had declined to a few hundred individuals before management-led recovery. To understand how this population bottleneck might have affected population structure, genetic diversity and inbreeding, we analyzed single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), principally generated from feather samples collected from nestlings during two breeding seasons. We investigated differences in genetic variability between population ‘flocks’ across the island. Overall F IS was 0.02 and mean allelic richness was 1.84. Low pairwise F ST values (-0.001-0.04) indicated genetic connectivity between the flocks, however, genetic differentiation (P ≤ 0.004) between all but the two eastern flocks suggests some limitations to gene flow. Seventeen per cent of individuals were highly inbred, with more than a third of these individuals from the most eastern flock. While there was no substantial population structure, analysis indicated some differentiation of the currently expanding eastern flock. Spatial autocorrelation found stronger than random relatedness amongst nestlings in nesting clusters, confirming suggestions from previous studies. The estimated effective population size ( N e ) was 122, above the minimum ( N e ≥ 50 ) commonly thought needed to avoid inbreeding depression in the short term, with N e values for two flocks also above this level. Our study highlights the importance of focussing on population genetics as well as numerical recovery when developing actions to manage threatened populations.

items.title: Seamounts from the Central Indian Ocean Basin as a guide to the likely geochemical characteristics of small volcanoes on Venus
items.abstract: Our comparative morphometric analysis indicates that the overall pattern of the diameter–frequency distribution for volcanoes on Venus resembles that of terrestrial seamount datasets. This suggests that smaller volcanic structures on Venus and seamounts on Earth may share certain underlying formational factors. The processes of forming small volcanoes seem to be controlled by similar conditions such as the size of magma chamber, duration of eruption, and magma compositions, despite the fact that the terrestrial-type plate tectonics is not operating on Venus. The Venusian lavas is also comparable with geochemical characteristics terrestrial of the mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) and is attributed to their production under anhydrous condition. Future investigations into the heights, volumes, tectonic environments, related lithospheric thickness and geoid heights of both Venusian volcanoes and terrestrial seamounts could help understand the similarities and distinctions between the geological formations on the two planets. India is aiming for future Venus Orbiter missions to capture the high-resolution surface images through synthetic aperture radar. New terrestrial analogue site and its Venusian equivalents will thus, offer better insights on comparative planetology and ground truth validation of the orbiter data. Graphical abstract

items.title: Productivity and economic benefits of intercropping buckwheat and green gram with chilli under the Northern transition zone of Karnataka
items.abstract: Intercropping systems improve agricultural resource efficiency and crop productivity, especially for spice crops like chilli. This research assessed the productivity and economic advantages of intercropping buckwheat and green gram with chilli. The study was conducted during the kharif seasons of 2022 and 2023 at the Main Agricultural Research Station, Dharwad, Karnataka. The experiment was laid out in a randomised complete block design (RCBD) with nine treatments and three replications, representing different row arrangements of chilli intercropped with buckwheat and green gram. Green gram was incorporated as an intercrop with chilli in this study, as it is recommended for the Northern Transition Zone of Karnataka, to facilitate a comparative analysis. The findings indicated that chilli (120 × 60 cm) + buckwheat (1:3 ratio, T3) and paired row chilli (60/120 × 60 cm) + buckwheat (2:3 ratio, T5) produced the highest chilli equivalent yield (818 and 819 kg ha-1 respectively), land equivalent ratio (1.64 and 1.43 respectively), area time equivalent ratio, income equivalent ratio and monetary yield advantage. These treatments also recorded higher gross returns, net returns and benefit-cost ratios compared with other treatments. The results indicate that intercropping buckwheat with chilli in 1:3 or 2:3 row ratios improved productivity and economic returns.

items.title: Mycogenic management of Pythium irregulare root rot and wilt in pepper via endophytic Aspergillus terreus MF3 and Mentha spicata extracts
items.abstract: Abstract Background Pepper ( Capsicum annuum L.) is a critically important crop for the global economy; however, its production is severely affected by harmful soil-borne pathogens such as Pythium irregulare , which causes root rot and wilting. This study aimed to evaluate a sustainable biological control strategy combining the halophytic endophytic fungus ( Aspergillus terreus MF3 ( A. terreus MF3)) isolated from Avicennia marina in South Sinai, Egypt and the methanolic leaf extract of Mentha spicata ( M. spicata ), with the goal of suppressing the disease, mitigating oxidative stress, and inducing defense responses in the host plant. Results GC–MS analysis of the M. spicata extract tentatively identified 11 phytochemical constituents, predominantly consisting of oxygenated monoterpenes, fatty acid esters, and phenolic derivatives, with key bioactive compounds including 1,2-Benzenedicarboxylic acid (46.32%), 9-Octadecenoic acid (Z) (12.53%), and Piperitenone oxide (6.01%). In vivo greenhouse experiments showed that P. irregulare infection resulted in a high disease index (85.1%) in untreated infected plants, whereas treatment with A. terreus MF3 fungal filtrate and M. spicata extract reduced the disease index to 40.1% and 45.0%, respectively. Both biological treatments partially alleviated pathogen-associated oxidative stress compared with the infected control, reducing MDA accumulation from 9.10 to 6.20 mg g −1 DW with A. terreus MF3 and to 7.50 mg g −1 DW with M. spicata , while H 2 O 2 levels decreased from 7.80 to 5.60 and 6.40 mg g −1 DW. Furthermore, the treatments improved photosynthetic pigment levels and enhanced biochemical defense responses, as reflected by increased free proline and total phenolic contents and enhanced activities of peroxidase (POD) and polyphenol oxidase (PPO). Conclusions This study introduces a novel, eco-friendly biocontrol strategy combining the halophytic endophytic fungus Aspergillus terreus MF3 and Mentha spicata leaf extract to combat Pythium irregulare in pepper. By effectively suppressing the disease, mitigating pathogen-induced oxidative stress, and stimulating host defense responses, this sustainable approach offers a valuable alternative to chemical pesticides for integrated disease management.

items.title: Assessing Urban Expansion and Land Use Transformation in Dehradun Using Geospatial Techniques
items.abstract: The spatial distribution of landuse pattern have undergone tremendous changes due to rapid urbanisation, which has become an identifiable aspect of development in modern times, particularly in environmentally sensitive regions. However, this research aims to investigate the changes in time and space in terms of Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) and urbanisation in Dehradun Planning Area between 2001 and 2026, focusing on understanding the extent and direction of the changes. The analysis was based on multi-temporal satellite images having a spatial resolution of 30 m, which were retrieved from Landsat missions in 2001, 2010, 2018, and 2026. In the accuracy assessment process, error matrices and kappa statistics have been used to ensure the reliability of the classification results. The findings depict a drastic shift in the surroundings, where built-up areas expand rapidly along with the reduction in cropland and vegetation. Cropland and vegetation decreased by 14.03% and 7.38%, respectively, from 2018 to 2026. While the settlement area (built-up) increased by 17.88%, becoming the dominant land cover with a value of 53.07%. There was a noticeable increase in barren and transitional land, while water bodies remained almost constant. The above changes reflect an unsustainable development trend of urban sprawl driven by infrastructure and population growth. To guarantee the sustainability of regional development and ecological balance, it is concluded that Dehradun is at a crucial stage of urban transition, which needs urgent action in land use management, green space conservation, and sustainable urban development.

items.title: Low prevalence of wolf-dog hybrids in the Iberian Peninsula
items.abstract: Abstract Wolf ( Canis lupus )—dog ( Canis familiaris ) hybrids are a widely recognized example of anthropogenic hybridization of conservation concern. In the Iberian Peninsula, wolves and dogs coexist in highly humanized landscapes, with many opportunities for interbreeding. Previous studies have documented wolf-dog hybridization here; however, their ability to estimate the frequency of this phenomenon was limited because of opportunistic, or geographically restricted sampling. Further, the use of non-standardized genetic markers limited comparability across studies. Here, we conducted a systematic non-invasive survey, collecting over 800 fecal samples across the species range in Iberia. Genetic analyses combined a mitochondrial DNA barcode for species identification, 13 autosomal microsatellites for individual identification, two sex markers, and a panel of 96 ancestry-informative SNP markers specifically developed for wolf-dog hybrid detection across Europe, which enables the assignment of hybrid classes up to second-generation backcrosses. Our results revealed a very low prevalence (< 2%) of wolf-dog hybrids in this population. Among 204 individually identified wolves, we detected three first-generation (F1) and one later-generation (F2/BCw) hybrids. Two of the identified hybrids were related, thus representing only three hybridization events, all located at the edge of the species distribution or in human disturbed areas. Simulations regarding the expected change in the genetic composition of the population with this prevalence of hybrids, and the observed underrepresentation of backcrosses, suggest reduced reproductive success in hybrids. The results imply that the risk of genetic swamping of wild wolves by domestic dogs is currently low in Iberia.

items.title: Temporal dynamics of coral bleaching and live coral cover at the Cayman Crown Reef, Gulf of Honduras (2016–2025)
items.abstract: Located in the Gulf of Honduras between Guatemala and southern Belize, Cayman Crown (Corona Caimán) is a recently documented offshore coral reef system of high geomorphological complexity lying at the terminus of the deep Cayman Trench. The reef is characterized by extensive spur-and-groove formations and steep vertical walls descending from 10–30 m to depths exceeding 300 m. Despite its offshore location, Cayman Crown has historically supported among the highest live coral cover recorded across the Mesoamerican Reef (24-50%), consistently corresponding to good (≥20%) to very good (≥40%) live coral cover, under the Reef Health Index. However, the reef has been exposed to intensifying thermal stress across three successive bleaching events. It remains unknown whether this offshore reef can retain its capacity to recover under repeated thermal stress, as multi-event, site-level records of bleaching and recovery are lacking for this reef system. Here, we assess bleaching severity, mortality, and recovery across four sites spanning three bleaching events from 2016 to 2025. The highest Bleaching Severity Index (BSI) values were recorded during the 3.5 Regional Coral Bleaching Event (RCBE), 2019–2021; with a BSI of 54–59% and peak DHW ~10 °C-weeks, followed by the Fourth Global Coral Bleaching Event (GCBE), 2023–2025; with a BSI: 25–41% and peak DHW ~19 °C-weeks, and moderate values during the Third GCBE, 2014–2017; with a BSI: 25–30% and peak DHW ~8 °C-weeks. Following the 2019 bleaching, corals recovered nearly completely, demonstrating strong short-term post-disturbance resilience. In contrast, consecutive bleaching during the Fourth GCBE resulted in approximately 29% overall coral mortality and persistent residual bleaching extending into the February 2025 post-disturbance survey (BSI: 4–10%). The 2023–24 bleaching caused pronounced live coral cover losses, particularly at Corona Caimán Valle de Aga CC01 (50.3% to 34.1%) and Corona Caimán Bajón GT008 (35.7% to 22.5%), while Corona Caimán 2 CC02 showed a slight increase (24.7% to 28.3%), indicating variability in site-level responses. These findings are consistent with projections of increasing marine heatwave frequency, under which reefs would experience repeated bleaching with shorter recovery windows. The transition from near-complete recovery following a single acute bleaching disturbance to measurable colony mortality under consecutive bleaching events suggests that repeated heat stress may erode the resilience of even offshore reefs.

items.title: Water and High-Altitude Mining in the Andes
items.abstract: Summary The high-altitude Andean landscape contains rich mineral deposits such as copper, silver, gold, zinc, and lithium, among others, frequently located near the basin headwaters. From pre-Columbian times to the present, diverse human groups have exploited these deposits, mobilizing specialized, forced, and voluntary labor and deploying metallurgical practices of Native American and Old World origin. Control of these operations has been equally varied, ranging from small communities and ethnic groups to the Inca and Spanish empires, as well as various private-sector actors, including owners of mines and water-powered stamp mills and large mega-mining corporations. The metallurgical techniques and the mining settlements have required the control of water for human consumption, hydraulic energy, and as a solvent in major mines such as Potosí, Oruro, Carangas, Cerro Pasco, and Huancavelica, among others. Consequently, pre-Columbian, colonial, and modern mining in the Altiplano has utilized and modified the waterscape through hydraulic infrastructure and mining technologies, profoundly altering the ecology and endangering biodiversity both at the extraction sites and in other ecological niches. Similarly, the availability of water during the summer rainy season and the challenges posed by groundwater that frequently caused mine flooding shaped the production cycles of silver, gold, and copper in the Andean environment. The interaction between mining and water bodies in the Andean mountains has been shaped by the impact of diverses production methods on the environment and the responses of Indigenous communities and other social actors to the modification and contamination of wetlands (bofedales), lagoons, lakes, and glaciers.

items.title: Calf-Snatching among Cetaceans? Interspecific Associations of Adult Bottlenose Dolphins with Common and Striped Dolphin Calves in Southern Portugal
items.abstract: Abstract Interspecific interactions among cetaceans are diverse and have been reported on numerous occasions. However, interspecific alloparental care (an adult exhibiting nurturant behavior towards a non-descendant young of a different species) is rarely documented. Here, we describe multiple calf-directed interspecific associations, including one apparent instance of prolonged interspecific alloparental care, along the southern coast of Portugal. This behavior was directed by adult common bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops truncatus ) towards six common dolphin ( Delphinus delphis ) calves and one striped dolphin ( Stenella coeruleoalba ) calf. Out of these calves five were classified as neonates. Observations occurred during both dedicated and opportunistic boat-based surveys. In total, 14 sightings were documented between 2016 and 2025. In 13 of these sightings, the heterospecific calf was observed swimming in echelon position alongside an adult bottlenose dolphin, and antagonistic behaviors by adult bottlenose dolphins towards the calves were observed during three encounters. Photo-identification confirmed the involvement of 94 adult bottlenose dolphins throughout all encounters, with the recurring presence of 39 individuals (41.5%). Three observations revealed a consistent pairing between one adult bottlenose dolphin and a common dolphin neonate, which persisted for nearly one month in 2024, with no other adult swimming with a heterospecific calf more than once. Although the exact reasons behind these interactions remain unclear, this study provides a unique insight into the social dynamics between different cetacean species, spanning from antagonistic to seemingly care-giving behavior. Moreover, it documents the first instance of prolonged interspecific alloparental care among cetaceans along the coast of mainland Portugal.

items.title: Spatial and seasonal distribution patterns of wild shrub vegetation along abiotic gradients in Jhelum District, Punjab, Pakistan
items.abstract: The spatial (habitat-based) and seasonal (phenological) distribution patterns of wild shrub vegetation in Jhelum District, Punjab, Pakistan, are significantly influenced by various abiotic factors. This study aimed to investigate the taxonomic richness, distribution patterns of shrubs in relation to habitat characteristics and environmental gradients in the Jhelum district. Field surveys were conducted from 2019 to 2021 using 120 randomly established transects, and vegetation data were analyzed using classification and ordination approaches. The study area was found to have 28 species of shrubs that constituted 15 families. The dominant families were Solanaceae (17.86%), followed by Apocynaceae and Leguminosae (14.29%). Nanophanerophyte (89.29%) was the dominant life form, followed by Chamaeophyte (7.14%) and Megaphanerophyte (3.57%). In Leaf size spectra Mesophyll (28.57%) then Nanophyll (25%). Phenology of most of the shrubs observed in August-September (25.00 percent) and then March-April (21.43%). The ecosystems characterized with the high levels of species diversity (∼27 species), richness (H' = 3.26; d = 7.67) were those of forest and hilly areas, whereas agricultural lands and home gardens had the lowest diversity levels (less than five species; H' = 1.10; d = 1.82). Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) indicated three big ecological clusters, i.e., Cluster 1- Dry and arid species ( Fagonia indica, Capparis decidua ), Cluster 2- Moisture-dependent and disturbed habitat species ( Ipomoea carnea, Lantana camara ), and Cluster 3- Forest and hilly region species (Datura metel, Dodonaea viscosa), associated with shaded, stable microclimates. Climatic constraints were reflected in flowering which was highest in spring and monsoon and less in winter and summer. The first two principal components explained 43.39% of the total variation, capturing major, though partial, patterns associated with habitat and seasonal characteristics. Diversity indices, including Shannon diversity, Simpson diversity, and richness measures, indicated higher diversity in forest habitats compared with agricultural habitats. These results are relevant to focus on the conservation of forests, their recovery, and afforestation in the urban areas to preserve ecological balance and increase the robustness of the biodiversity to changing climatic conditions.

items.title: Realizing the Potential of Urban Nature: Why Do Urban Nature Plans Need a “Plus”?
items.abstract: Cities are increasingly expected to use urban nature to address multiple, overlapping challenges, including biodiversity loss, climate adaptation, health and wellbeing, social inclusion, and urban resilience. Yet the presence of urban nature does not automatically guarantee that its potential will be realized, equitably distributed, or sustained over time. This chapter explains why Urban Nature Plans (UNPs) need a “plus”: an expanded approach that goes beyond preparing urban nature roadmaps to address the enabling and disabling conditions that shape implementation, maintenance, monitoring, and long-term benefit realization. Building on a Social-Ecological-Technological Systems perspective, the chapter identifies four sets of contextual factors—institutional, infrastructural, perceptional, and resources-and-competencies—that act as dynamic filters across urban nature planning processes. Drawing on examples from UNPplus cities, it shows how these factors can cascade across preparation, action planning, and implementation and monitoring phases, creating barriers or enabling conditions for urban nature ambitions. The chapter argues that UNPplus offers a diagnostic foundation for moving from fragmented greening initiatives towards more coordinated, adaptive, and durable urban nature planning processes. By clarifying mandates, strengthening co-creation, aligning resources, and embedding monitoring and stewardship, cities can better translate urban nature ambitions into realized, equitable, and lasting benefits.

items.title: Monitoring Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services in Urban Nature Planning
items.abstract: Biodiversity is essential for human wellbeing and has become a foundation component of sustainable and regenerative urban design. Urban Nature Plans (UNPs) are being championed in European cities to embed nature-positive practices and ecosystem service provision into strategic urban planning. To effectively embed UNPs that reverse biodiversity declines, drive social justice, and deliver healthy and liveable cities, there is a need to generate robust evidence through monitoring and impact evaluation (M&E). M&E forms the foundation of three Steps of UNPs: Step 5: Analyse the current state of nature and biodiversity; Step 6: Set indicators and targets; and Step 9: Establish a monitoring, reporting, and evaluation system. However, delivering M&E at a scale, and to a level that provides direct evidence of the impacts of a UNP, remains a challenge for many cities. Resource, capacity, technical, and expertise gaps, and the complexity of understanding the multifaceted drivers that influence biodiversity and ecosystem service patterns in urban areas, can all present difficulties for city authorities. City experiences, and established and emerging innovations, are presented here to support cities in developing M&E to underpin their UNP development and implementation.

items.title: Advancing Local-Regional Integration Through Urban Nature Plans
items.abstract: Urban Nature Plans (UNPs) are increasingly recognized as strategic instruments for mainstreaming biodiversity, enhancing climate resilience, and supporting sustainable urban transformation. However, the ecological processes and socio-environmental challenges they seek to address extend beyond municipal boundaries, requiring stronger integration across territorial scales and governance levels. This chapter examines the role of local-regional integration in enabling the effective development of UNPs. Drawing on spatial planning literature, it examines the organizational, procedural, and normative challenges that affect the alignment of local actions with broader regional strategies. The chapter analyses local-regional integration through three complementary sets of conditions: spatial and biophysical, institutional and societal, and financial. Empirical insights are drawn from a collaborative process involving five European cities, Barcelona, Paris, Belgrade, Burgas, and Mannheim. The Barcelona metropolitan context is presented as an illustrative example of multi-scale integration, while the experiences of the other cities are used to identify common opportunities, barriers, and emerging practices. The chapter concludes by arguing that local-regional integration is not merely a technical planning challenge, but plays a key role in advancing biodiversity mainstreaming and nature restoration within coherent territorial development strategies across scales.

items.title: Linear and nonlinear characteristics of high-frequency electrostatic drift waves in absence of collisions
items.abstract: Abstract High-frequency electrostatic drift wave modes are shown as hybrid modes generated by the linear mixing of drift and cyclotron dynamics growing at the expense of cyclotron modes via a reactive mode-coupling instability. The fundamental role of the density gradient is to break the symmetry between the two cyclotron branches. A sufficiently steep gradient causes the drift-modified branch to overlap with the cyclotron branch leading to energy distribution. The analysis is carried out within a cold-ion fluid model without invoking collisional, non-adiabatic or finite Larmor radius effects. Laboratory observations of localized high-frequency drift wave signatures provide qualitative and parametric support for the density gradient threshold and high frequency scaling identified by this hybrid mode-coupling model. A second order nonlinear equation with variable coefficients has been derived to show the wave characteristics in various parameter ranges.

items.title: Galaxy and Halo Root Systems: Fingerprints of Mass Assembly
items.abstract: Abstract We discuss what we call halo or galaxy root systems, collections of particle pathlines that show the infall of matter from the initial uniform distribution into a collapsed structure. The matter clumps as it falls in; projected through time, it produces filamentary density enhancements analogous to tree roots and branches, or branching river networks. This relates to the larger-scale cosmic web, but is defined locally about one of its nodes: a physical, geometric version of a merger tree. We find dark-matter-halo root systems on average to exhibit more roots and root branches for the largest cluster haloes than for small haloes, indicating their more complicated assembly, even in dark matter without gas physics. Also, we find that high spin manifests as curvier roots, and that many have mass contributions that start far away from central, compact protohalo cores. Root systems also show sensitivity to anisotropic infall, which we see some evidence for in a simulation with rather low box size.

items.title: Fast simulations of X-ray absorption spectroscopy for battery materials on a quantum computer
items.abstract: X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) is a leading technique for understanding structural changes in advanced battery materials such as lithium-excess cathodes. However, extracting critical information like oxidation states from the experimental spectra requires expensive and time-consuming simulations. Building upon a recent proposal to simulate XAS using quantum computers, this work proposes a highly-optimized implementation of the time-domain algorithm for X-ray absorption. Among a host of improvements to Hamiltonian representation, circuit implementation, and measurement strategies, three optimizations are key to the efficiency of the algorithm. The first is the use of product formulas with the compressed double factorized form of the Hamiltonian. The second is recognizing that for spectroscopy applications, it is sufficient to control the error in the eigenvalues of the (approximate) Hamiltonian being implemented by the product formula, rather than the generic error on the full time evolution operator. Using perturbation theory to estimate this eigenvalue error, we find that significantly fewer Trotter steps are needed than expected from the time evolution error bound. The third is the choice of an optimized distribution of samples that takes advantage of the exponentially decaying Lorentzian kernel. Through constant factor resource estimates, we show that a challenging model Li 4 Mn 2 O cluster system with 18 spatial orbitals and 22 electrons in the active space can be simulated with 100 logical qubits and less than 4 × 10 8 Toffoli gates per circuit. Finally, the algorithm is implemented on a simulator, and the reconstructed spectrum is verified against a classical computational reference. The low cost of our algorithm makes it attractive to use on fault-tolerant quantum devices to accelerate the development and commercialization of high-capacity battery cathodes.

items.title: NGDEEP: A New Nonparametric Measure of Local Star Formation and Attenuation at Cosmic Noon
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce a new nonparametric technique to quantify the spatially resolved relationship between the local star formation rate (SFR) and dust attenuation. We then apply it to 12 star-forming galaxies at 1.0 < z < 2.4 using JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy from the NGDEEP survey. First, we construct spatially resolved (∼1 kpc per pixel) Balmer decrement (H α /H β ) maps of these galaxies and derive their corresponding dust attenuation and intrinsic SFR maps. We then rank-order the map pixels by attenuation and construct a cumulative distribution curve of the total SFR as a function of increasing attenuation. We define A ( H α ) 10 % SFR , A ( H α ) 50 % SFR , and A ( H α ) 90 % SFR as the dust attenuation levels behind which 10%, 50%, and 90% of the total integrated SFR is screened, respectively. These metrics quantify the probability that a given star-forming region lies behind a given level of attenuation. Across the full sample, 50% of the local star formation occurs behind an attenuation of 2.9 mag or higher ( A ( H α ) 50 % SFR ) on average. This indicates that the bulk of star formation in these galaxies is significantly attenuated by dust. The value of A ( H α ) 10 % SFR equals 0.6 mag for the average profile, indicating that even the least attenuated star-forming regions are still highly attenuated. The globally measured attenuation more closely matches A ( H α ) 10 % SFR than A ( H α ) 50 % SFR . This suggests that the global value is weighted toward the least dust-obscured star-forming regions and significantly underestimates the typical attenuation a star-forming region encounters. items.title: How significant is the lensing interpretation of GW231123?
items.abstract: GW231123 is one of the most unusual gravitational-wave (GW) events, with exceptionally large inferred masses and near-extremal spins, offering an opportunity to test whether propagation effects contribute to these properties. We therefore examine whether the data support wave-optics microlensing embedded in a strong-lensing galaxy, whose detection becomes increasingly likely as observations accumulate, whether this interpretation can explain these properties, and how significant the preference remains under detector noise and waveform systematics. We compare six hypotheses: unlensed, isolated point mass, and embedded point-mass (EPM) and binary-lens (EB) effective models in Type-I (minimum) and Type-II (saddle) macro images. The EB Type-I model is most favored. For the most accurate waveform model NRSur7dq4, it gives $\log_{10}B^{\rm EB-I}_{\rm U}=2.60$, versus $0.89$ for Type II, indicating sensitivity to macro-image geometry. Within Type I, however, the binary improves over the point mass by only $\log_{10}B^{\rm EB-I}_{\rm EPM-I}=0.16$ and $Δ\ln\mathcal{L}_{\max}=0.56$, providing no clear evidence for structure beyond a single effective perturber. Moreover, under embedded lensing, waveform-template discrepancies and inferred masses and spins are reduced. However, real O4a backgrounds from numerical-relativity injections show that the apparent lensing evidence is sensitive to waveform systematics and realistic detector noise: although the commonly used waveform IMRPhenomXPHM gives the largest Bayes factor, $\log_{10}B^{\rm EB-I}_{\rm U}=4.52$, it is less exceptional relative to its own background, with a false-alarm probability of $6.5$--$8\%$, whereas NRSur7dq4 gives only $2$--$3\%$. Thus, waveform systematics can amplify apparent lensing evidence, but GW231123 remains an intriguing lensing candidate.

items.title: Constraining the dynamical Chern-Simons gravity with future gravitational-wave detectors
items.abstract: Dynamical Chern-Simons gravity, a parity-violating modification of general relativity, is regarded as a low-energy effective theory arising from string theory. Gravitational waves provide a powerful probe for testing its predictions. However, current gravitational wave observations are unable to place meaningful constraints on this theory through phase measurements, due to limitations from detector noise and the validity requirements of the waveform models. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of the prospects for constraining the dynamical Chern-Simons gravity with future gravitational-wave detectors using stellar mass black holes binary. We quantify how the constraining capacities vary across different detectors and source parameters, and identify the regions of parameter space that satisfy the small-coupling condition. Furthermore, by incorporating an astrophysically motivated mass distribution model for stellar mass black hole binaries, we estimate the potential of upcoming observatories.

items.title: Banana Split: Improved Cosmological Constraints with Two Light-curve-shape and Color Populations Using Union3.1+UNITY1.8
items.abstract: Abstract Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) have been used to provide key constraints on the equation-of-state parameter of dark energy. They are generally standardized under the assumption that they belong to a single population, with luminosities standardized in a continuous (roughly linear) fashion using the observed light-curve timescale. We update the Union3+UNITY1.5 supernova (SN) cosmology analysis in light of increasing evidence for at least two core populations of SNe Ia and apply this “UNITY1.8” model to the updated “Union3.1” compilation. In addition to finding evidence for two different light-curve-shape ( x 1 ) distributions, we also find that the color distributions are different, that the light-curve-shape/magnitude standardization relations are different, and that these populations have different distributions across host-galaxy stellar mass and redshift. Importantly, we find that the residual host-mass–luminosity step found in prior SN Ia cosmology analyses is now consistent with zero for unreddened SNe. We report a significantly tightened constraint on the split in the red-color standardization between SNe in low- and high-mass galaxies. We find that the estimated uncertainties shrink on cosmological parameters when fitting the same SNe assuming two modes versus one mode. We confirm similar trends in simulated data when running both versions of Unified Nonlinear Inference for Type Ia cosmologY (UNITY) on the same (two-mode) simulations. For a flat ΛCDM cosmology, we find Ω m = 0.33 4 − 0.024 + 0.025 from SNe alone; for a flat w 0 – w a cosmology, we find w 0 = − 0.76 0 − 0.082 + 0.084 and w a = − 0.7 9 − 0.30 + 0.28 when including SNe, baryon acoustic oscillation, and cosmic microwave background. In the 2D w 0 – w a plane, UNITY1.8 decreases the tension with flat ΛCDM by 0.1 σ to ∼3 σ compared to single-mode UNITY.

items.title: Quasinormal modes and tidal responses of black holes in generic anisotropic matter environments
items.abstract: We develop a perturbative framework for a black hole embedded in a generic, possibly anisotropic, matter environment under spherical symmetry. Our approach extends previous analyses restricted to vanishing radial pressure or to perturbative matter configurations. Within this framework, we derive an analytical generalization of the Einstein cluster that incorporates a polytropic radial pressure, and we investigate the properties of this solution. We show that both the geodesic structure and the axial quasinormal-mode spectrum remain predominantly governed by an overall gravitational redshift effect, while the radial pressure systematically enhances the environmental corrections. In contrast, the tidal Love numbers are substantially more sensitive, and can exhibit order-unity deviations, including vanishing and negative strictly static magnetic Love numbers for sufficiently large anisotropy. We present the full linearized equations, which can be applied to various extensions, including ringdown analysis and extreme-mass-ratio inspirals.

items.title: Charge Transfer from Ammonia Neutralizes Propylene Oxide Cations: Implications for the Astrochemistry of Chiral Molecules
items.abstract: Abstract Propylene oxide is the first of only two chiral species observed to date in the interstellar medium but little is known about the chemistry that leads to a detectable abundance of this molecule in Sagittarius B2. We used a glow-discharge ion source and a room-temperature ion trap to study the neutralization reactions necessary to convert propylene oxide cation (PpO+)─the assumed precursor for propylene oxide in space─into the observed astrochemical. We found that the charge-transfer reaction between PpO+ and ammonia (NH3) proceeds with a pressure-independent rate coefficient of (1.39 ± 0.03) × 10–12 cm3 s–1 to neutralize PpO+ and form the radical cation NH3+. Although this measured rate coefficient is much slower than that predicted by capture theories, the high abundance of NH3 in Sagittarius B2 motivates the inclusion of this reaction in astrochemical models. We hypothesize that the low ionization energies of many chiral molecules important to origin-of-life theories means these species may exist as cations in the interstellar medium.
