items.title: 2D/3D-QSAR-guided design of novel 1,2,4-triazole derivatives with predicted enhanced antimicrobial activity.
items.abstract: The present study demonstrates that the integration of structural descriptors, quantum-chemical parameters, regression modelling, and 3D contour map analysis within a hybrid QSAR framework represents an effective strategy for the rational design of bioactive 1,2,4-triazole derivatives with improved predicted antimicrobial properties. The work may also be regarded as a practical roadmap for further research on 1,2,4-triazole-3-thiols. Our dataset comprised previously synthesised 1,2,4-triazoles that had already shown broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, thereby ensuring a consistent structural core and reliable biological annotations. Structural, quantum-chemical, hybrid, and 3D-QSAR models were developed using structural and DFT-derived descriptors and were assessed by cross-validation, external validation, Y-randomization, and applicability-domain analysis. The best-performing model (hybrid QSAR; n = 28) achieved R 2 = 0.731, adjusted R 2 = 0.669, Q 2 = 0.621 (internal, PRESS-based), and mean Q ext 2 = 0.43 (100-repeat random-subsampling external validation). Despite its compact size and structural homogeneity, the dataset enabled transparent mechanistic interpretation and identified the difluoromethyl substituent at the C-5 position of the triazole ring, together with avoidance of naphthalimide-type fragments, as the statistically robust structural determinants of activity ( p = 0.001 and p = 0.022 respectively). A library of 20 CHF 2 -bearing candidates (D1-D20) was designed on this basis; fine-grained ranking among them is presented as an exploratory tiebreaker only, since it rests on electronic descriptors that were not statistically significant. These predictions remain to be validated experimentally and are intended to guide future synthesis and biological testing.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Cannibalism in Austro-Papuan Dragons (Lacertilia: Amphibolurinae), With a New Record of Cannibalism in the Peninsula Dragon (Ctenophorus fionni).
items.abstract: In 2012, one of us observed an adult male peninsula dragon ( Ctenophorus fionni ) predate a juvenile conspecific. This was noteworthy as we understood peninsula dragons to be primarily insectivorous and it prompted us to investigate cannibalism more generally using a systematic, comprehensive review of the literature. Cannibalism has never been reported in any wild, natural-living Australo-Papuan (i.e., Amphibolurine) agamid, except in the peninsula dragon. There are now three records of cannibalism in the peninsula dragon, all from populations of the central form. This raises the possibility that peninsula dragons, or certain populations thereof, may be unusually predisposed to cannibalism. However, the current data available are too sparse to draw firm conclusions and we encourage anyone with observations of cannibalism to publish them.

items.title: Fertilisation Success in Acanthaster cf. solaris and Acanthaster brevispinus and Reciprocal Hybrid Crosses Across a Range of Sperm Concentrations and Development to the Hybrid Juvenile.
items.abstract: Novel species interactions between resident and range shifting species in response to warming are posing challenges for conservation and management. This is especially the case when major predatory species are involved, as seen in the appearance of a mixed species outbreak of coral-eating crown-of-thorns sea stars Acanthaster cf. solaris (As) and the lesser-known Acanthaster brevispinus (Ab) in the tropical to subtropical transition zone in eastern Australia. The outbreak consisted of reproductively mature animals, and we investigated the potential for cross-species hybridisation in fertilisation experiments across a range of sperm concentrations to sperm limitation conditions (10 6 -10 2 sperm mL -1 ). Fertilisation was successful in all combinations of parents (As ♂ × As ♀, Ab ♂ × Ab ♀, Ab ♀ × As ♂, As ♀ × Ab ♂) with successful hybrid crosses in sperm dilutions as low as 10 2 sperm ml -1 . Development in conspecific and heterospecific crosses was similar through the bipinnaria and brachiolaria larval stages to the juvenile. Juvenile hybrids had typical juvenile Acanthaster spp. development with a stellate five-armed profile post metamorphosis, gaining arms after ~78 days. At no stage did the juvenile hybrids develop the distinctive pink colour trait that is characteristic of Acanthaster cf. solaris juveniles. Our results indicate that hybridisation is not restricted by sperm limitation conditions, with subsequent development of hybrids to the advanced juvenile stage. Our results highlight the potential for hybridisation and species introgression when range shifting species overlap with sister taxa. This may facilitate further range expansion or development of resilient hybrid progeny as a risk to vulnerable high latitude coral communities.

items.title: Massive inter-animal horizontal gene transfer contributes to stress tolerance in the fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila
items.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in animals is thought to be rare and largely restricted to transfers from non-animal sources. In contrast to this expectation, we discovered that 9.2% of the protein-coding genes in the genome of the dark-winged fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila (order: Diptera, family: Sciaridae) are of potential HGT origin. Most of these genes have phylogenetic affinity with sequences from other distantly related arthropods that inhabit a shared soil-dwelling niche with B. coprophila. We show that these findings are inconsistent with genomic contamination or widespread gene loss and instead suggest a level of inter-animal HGT that is, to our knowledge, unprecedented. Consistent with their potential functional importance, ~75% of putative B. coprophila horizontally transferred genes (HTGs) are transcribed, and nearly all are shared across multiple sciarid fungus gnat species that diverged tens of millions of years ago. Further, domain annotations suggest that HTGs participate in diverse processes potentially important to B. coprophila ecology. We tested the functions of eight putative B. coprophila HTGs through transgenic expression in the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and found evidence that HGT has likely endowed B. coprophila with the novel capability to biosynthesize NAD+, as well as enhanced capacity to withstand stressors imposed by arsenic, cyanide, alkylating agents, and reactive oxygen species. Our findings reveal a previously underappreciated contribution of inter-animal genetic exchange to the evolution of genomic, physiological, and ecological novelty.

items.title: Evolution of the male reproductive system in Penaeoidea (Dendrobranchiata): Integrating morphological and molecular data.
items.abstract: Penaeoidea shrimps exhibit substantial diversity in reproductive morphology, but the evolutionary history of the male reproductive system (MRS) and its congruence with molecular phylogenies remain poorly understood. This study characterized MRS morphology across Penaeoidea and used these morphological data, together with a molecular phylogeny of the species analyzed herein, to reconstruct the ancestral states of MRS traits and investigate their evolutionary patterns and taxonomic implications. The MRS of 11 species was examined using histological methods, and phylogenetic analysis was conducted. In Benthesicymidae and Aristeidae, as well as in Solenoceridae and Penaeini, the median vas deferens (MVD) bears accessory and spermatic ducts, representing a synapomorphic trait and the putative plesiomorphic condition for Penaeoidea. In contrast, Trachypenaeini, Parapenaeini, and Sicyoniidae share a single duct in the MVD. Within Penaeini, the accessory gland is simple in Farfantepenaeus species but highly complex, with multiple glandular chambers, in Litopenaeus schmitti, supporting the separation of these lineages and arguing against treating Penaeus as a single genus. Benthesicymidae, Aristeidae, Solenoceridae, and Sicyoniidae lack accessory glands, representing a homoplastic condition, whereas Trachypenaeini and Parapenaeini exhibit a simplified accessory gland. The plesiomorphic spermatophore condition appears to be morphologically complex. Phylogenetic analyses recovered Penaeidae as paraphyletic, and substantial differences in MRS morphology among tribes support the hypothesis that these lineages may warrant elevation to family rank.

items.title: Microbiome-derived proline dipeptides underpin improved nitrogen utilization efficiency in dairy cattle.
items.abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa-Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa-Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism.

items.title: Estimating the resilience of non-stationary systems.
items.abstract: A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them - such as global vegetation - are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

items.title: Transcriptomic biomarkers reveal jasmonic and salicylic acid states under field herbivory in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Plants coordinate defence against pathogens and herbivores through the crosstalk between salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA) signalling pathways. However, little is known about how plants integrate the phytohormone concentration profiles to shape defence states in complex field environments. Here we show that systematically varying combinatorial SA and JA concentrations in Arabidopsis thaliana reveals 43 distinct combination-specific transcriptional signatures beyond SA-JA antagonism. Leveraging these data, we develop and validate machine-learning-based transcriptomic biomarkers that independently measure the SA and JA response states from gene-expression data. Applying these biomarkers to field-grown A. thaliana shows that SA/JA response states are associated with the abundance and co-occurrence patterns of herbivores on individual plants. Our study provides a strategy for decoding hormonal responses to biotic environments from field transcriptomes, bridging the gap between molecular signalling and ecological dynamics.

items.title: Plant sexual reproduction in a warming world.
items.abstract: Sexual reproduction is the most heat-sensitive phase of the plant life cycle; however, studies of reproductive failure under heat stress have primarily focused on individual organs. Here, we propose a conceptual framework in which heat stress causes a system-level breakdown of male and female gametophyte development, shared metabolic and proteostatic support networks, and pollen-pistil interaction. This combined collapse within a narrow temperature window cannot be predicted from individual organs or gametophytes. Heat also remodels epigenetic makeup, generating stress memory, though its transmission across generations remains unresolved. We highlight that techniques such as single-cell omics, AI-driven phenotyping, and genome editing can provide valuable mechanistic insights to support the development of predictive, actionable breeding strategies for heat-resilient crops.

items.title: Embracing ignorance: tackling biodiversity knowledge shortfalls.
items.abstract: Global biodiversity information suffers from gaps, biases, and uncertainty over time and space, afflicting all taxonomic groups. Incomplete or biased data introduce uncertainty into models of biodiversity trends, potentially generating faulty inferences with knock-on effects for conservation. We revisit how the limitations of biodiversity knowledge are conceptualised, expanding the current classification to encompass eleven major shortfalls spanning taxonomic, ecological, evolutionary, and biocultural aspects, and examine the impediments that limit progress in reducing them. Information gaps have been moulded by our capacity and willingness to collect data, which are constrained by a series of financial, taxonomic, and technological impediments that vary across regions and taxa. Addressing these challenges is crucial for understanding biodiversity patterns and processes and developing effective conservation actions.

items.title: Recent environmental change shapes biotic homogenisation of Orthoptera and Mantodea communities in semi-dry grasslands.
items.abstract: Semi-dry grasslands are among the most species-rich ecosystems in Europe. However, many grassland remnants are undergoing gradual habitat degradation due to climate change, atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and the relaxation or abandonment of traditional management. While declines of specialised insects have repeatedly been reported, the extent to which these drivers promote long-term community reorganisation and biotic homogenisation remains poorly understood. Using a nationwide resurvey of 221 semi-dry grassland patches across Germany, spanning two to three decades, we investigated long-term changes in Orthoptera and Mantodea communities. We quantified changes in species richness, community composition, and beta diversity, and related these patterns to major global change drivers. Despite an increase in total species richness, these communities became increasingly homogenised, as indicated by declining beta diversity. Community reorganisation was characterised by pronounced winner-loser dynamics, with highly mobile generalists and thermophilous species expanding, whereas threatened species, low-mobility habitat specialists, and species associated with High Nature Value farmland declined. Winner species richness increased particularly in warm and dry regions, under elevated atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and outside protected areas. By contrast, low-mobility habitat specialists and threatened species persisted most successfully in structurally heterogeneous habitats. High shrub cover was negatively associated with both winners and losers, indicating an overall deterioration of habitat suitability. Our findings demonstrate that environmental change does not necessarily reduce species richness but can profoundly reorganise communities through selective filtering of species. Maintaining habitat heterogeneity with appropriate management strategies is therefore crucial for buffering biodiversity loss under ongoing global change.

items.title: Spatial and temporal reorganization of Polychaeta assemblages and trophic structure across the main habitats of the Mar Menor lagoon, Spain.
items.abstract: Coastal lagoons are heterogeneous and highly dynamic ecosystems that are particularly sensitive to anthropogenic pressures. This study analyses how polychaete assemblages in the Mar Menor lagoon (Spain) reorganized their taxonomic and trophic structure across main habitats between 1980s and 2017-2018 periods. We tested whether species composition, assemblage structure and trophic-group structure differed among habitats, and habitat-specific temporal changes. Polychaeta data from soft and hard bottom habitats and their biocenoses were analysed using PERMANOVA, PCO and SIMPER analyses. Species richness decreased from 1980s (77 species) to 2017 (54 species) and 2018 (67 species), whereas mean density increased significantly. Dissimilarities among periods were very high, indicating strong species composition turnover. For its part, trophic diversity declined up to the most recent periods, with predator richness decreasing and detritivore richness increase. Spatially, soft bottom habitats were mainly dominated by detritivore species of Capitellidae and Spionidae families, whereas hard bottoms assemblages were characterized by the non-indigenous species Timarete caribous and Hydroides elegans. Temporal changes were strongly habitat-dependent: whereas Caulerpa prolifera dominated biocenosis, unvegetated muddy bottoms and infralittoral rocky bottoms showed marked shifts towards detritivore and filter-feeder dominance; shallower soft bottoms dominated by Cymodocea nodosa, sandy bottoms and docks exhibited comparatively limited temporal variation in taxonomic and trophic structure. These findings demonstrate that polychaete assemblages experienced great reorganization either in taxonomic and trophic structure, and highlight the need to integrate taxonomic composition, diversity and trophic structure when monitoring ecological changes in coastal lagoons.

items.title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii: Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol.
items.abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol's antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5'-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: E-Service quality and customer satisfaction in online shopping: Implications for sustainable digital commerce.
items.abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has intensified competition among online retailers, making e-service quality increasingly important for building customer trust, satisfaction, and sustainable customer-platform relationships. This study examines the relationships among e-service quality, customer trust, customer satisfaction, and customer loyalty using a second-order Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) framework. The five SERVQUAL dimensions such as empathy, responsiveness, reliability, assurance, and tangibles were modeled as first-order constructs reflecting the higher-order construct of service quality. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 402 respondents with prior online-shopping experience. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and SEM were employed to assess the measurement and structural models. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and overall model fit. The structural results showed that service quality significantly and positively influenced customer trust and customer satisfaction, while customer trust significantly enhanced satisfaction. Trust also partially mediated the relationship between service quality and satisfaction, indicating that e-service quality improves satisfaction both directly and through increased customer confidence. The SERVQUAL dimensions contributed positively to overall service quality, with responsiveness and assurance showing particularly strong contributions, while empathy exhibited a comparatively moderate contribution. In contrast, customer loyalty had no significant direct effect on trust or satisfaction, and its indirect effect on satisfaction through trust was also nonsignificant. These findings demonstrate that reliable, responsive, secure, and well-designed digital services are important for strengthening trust and satisfaction in competitive e-commerce environments. By identifying trust as a key mechanism linking multidimensional e-service quality with customer satisfaction, the study contributes to SERVQUAL and digital-commerce literature and provides implications for the economic and relational sustainability of e-commerce platforms through more resilient and durable customer relationships.

items.title: The underappreciated role for phase variation and quasi-clonality in microbial populations.
items.abstract: Phase variation is a well-established phenomenon in some bacteria, where it generates heritable phenotypic variants within a population. These states, while reversible, are stable across generations, giving rise to quasi-clonal populations even when starting from a single bacterium. Underlying mechanisms include variation in short homopolymeric or heteropolymeric sequence repeats, DNA inversions mediated by site-specific recombination, reversible insertions and deletions, and switching between alternative methylation states. Although phase variation occurs in diverse bacteria, its contribution to phenotypic heterogeneity remains overlooked and use of the term is often absent in describing this phenomenon.

items.title: Fuzzy-clustering-based multi-scale intrusion detection for the industrial internet of things.
items.abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) faces severe intrusion-detection challenges under multi-protocol, multi-device, and massive heterogeneous traffic, especially extreme class imbalance and poor minority-class detection. To address this, we propose a fuzzy-clustering-based multi-scale intrusion detection model (FPBW-IDS). At the data level, we introduce boundary-prioritized FCM-SMOTE: fuzzy memberships distinguish core vs. border samples, interpolation is prioritized in high-membership regions, and sampling weights are adjusted by membership, thereby significantly enhancing minority-class representation and suppressing noise diffusion while keeping the majority class fixed at a multiplier of 1.0. At the feature-learning level, we build three parallel branches across the spatial, temporal, and frequency domains: parallel Pyramid Depthwise Separable Convolutions (PDSC) to capture spatial (cross-feature) dependencies, BiGRU to model temporal dependencies, and wavelet transforms to extract multi-scale spectral statistics; their outputs are fused with learned weighting to form a complementary tri-domain representation. Experiments on the CICIDS2017 dataset show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance under both unsampled and sampled settings: Accuracy 99.39%, Precision 98.22%, Recall 93.69%, F1 95.56% in the comprehensive comparison; and Accuracy 98.97%, Recall 99.09%, F1 96.69% in a recall-oriented setting, markedly reducing missed detections while maintaining stable training/validation curves and a small generalization gap. These results show the effectiveness and reliability of clustering-guided oversampling combined with tri-domain multi-scale representation for IIoT intrusion detection.

items.title: Whose morning, whose evening? Temporal asymmetries in intermedia agenda-setting between X and online news in Türkiye.
items.abstract: This study examines whether temporal ordering between X and online news varies across first-level issue and second-level attribute agendas in Türkiye's polarized media environment. The analysis draws on 448,664 X posts and 10,357 articles from 19 mainstream online news outlets collected during the 31-day period preceding and including the 31 March 2024 Istanbul local election. Using 12-hour AM/PM windows, we conducted 122 cross-lagged panel analyses-62 same-day AM → PM and 60 overnight PM→next-day AM panels across the two agenda levels-comparing issue- and attribute-indicator frequency profiles. First-level issue agendas were strongly synchronized, with correlations often approaching or exceeding r = .90, whereas second-level attribute relationships were weaker and less consistent. At the first level, morning online news issue salience more often preceded later X issue salience within same-day transitions, whereas evening X issue salience more often preceded the following morning's online news issue salience across overnight transitions. Most first-level cross-lagged correlations exceeded their Rozelle-Campbell (RCb) baselines, while second-level coefficients did so less consistently. These findings indicate that agenda leadership in a hybrid media system is temporally contingent and level-specific rather than static. The observed patterns represent temporally ordered associations and should not be interpreted as evidence of direct causal influence.

items.title: Source apportionment and non-carcinogenic health risk assessment of selected heavy metals in the Turag river area of Gazipur District, Bangladesh.
items.abstract: Introduction Rapid industrialization in Bangladesh, especially in Gazipur District, has raised concern over heavy metal contamination of soil and water and the associated health risks to nearby residents. This study compared the concentration, spatial distribution, probable sources, and non-carcinogenic health risk of five heavy metals (Hg, Ni, Mn, Zn, and Co) in soil and water in the Turag River areas in Gazipur District. Methods Soil and water samples were collected from 18 sites in the Turag River (including both industrial and non-industrial zones) and analyzed for five heavy metal concentrations (Hg, Ni, Mn, Zn, and Co) using inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Statistical analyses included principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), and Pearson correlation analysis, while non-carcinogenic human health risks were evaluated using the USEPA-based chronic daily intake (CDI), hazard quotient (HQ), and hazard index (HI) models for both adults and children. Results Mean soil metal concentrations followed the order Mn > Zn > Ni > Co > Hg in both zones, with markedly higher and more spatially concentrated Ni and Zn levels in the industrial zone near the Turag River areas. Spatial mapping, PCA, HCA, and correlation analyses consistently suggested a common anthropogenic influence on soil and water contamination in the industrial zone, with the strongest spatial concentrations observed near its northern boundary, compared with patterns consistent with multiple diffuse influences in the non-industrial zone. The modeled soil CDI values were generally higher for children than adults. Soil-based screening estimates indicated potential non-carcinogenic concern for children, including an Ni HQ of 1.66 in the industrial zone and cumulative hazard index values above the screening benchmark of 1 for children in both the industrial (HI = 2.32) and non-industrial (HI = 1.31) zones, while all modeled HQ and HI values for water remained below the screening benchmark of 1. Conclusion These soil-based screening estimates suggest potential non-carcinogenic concern for children, particularly regarding Ni in the industrial zone, but are based on the < 0.5 mm fraction of soil collected at 15-20 cm depth and may not represent actual exposure to ground-surface soil or airborne particles. The study highlighted the need for targeted control of potential industrial sources and child-focused environmental health monitoring in industrializing peri-urban districts of Bangladesh.

items.title: Weathering continuum in an aged taiga peatland oil spill.
items.abstract: Accidental oil spills in cold-region peatlands can result in long-term contamination, as low temperatures and waterlogged conditions may influence the rates and relative contributions of oil weathering processes. However, the progression and characteristics of oil weathering at aged oil spill sites in peatlands remain insufficiently characterized. To characterize the features and intensity of weathering processes, peat soil samples from an aged oil spill site in the taiga zone of Western Siberia were investigated using GC/MS. An approach combining mass chromatogram fingerprinting, n-alkane distribution and cross-plots of individual and integral parameters such as average number of C atoms, the decrease in the relative intensity of resolved peaks compared to the unresolved complex mixture, the (n-C 17 + n-C 18 )/(Pr + Ph) ratio, and changes in alkylbenzenes ratio was applied. This approach allowed to assess the degree, timing, and dominant mechanisms of oil weathering in soils, highlighting the necessity of a comprehensive analysis including integral parameters. Presence of different stages of weathering within a single spill site was revealed, from evaporation-dominated to advanced biodegradation, with indications of multiple biodegradation-related trends. Variations among samples, including deviations from general trends, indicate a strong influence of local environmental conditions on the evolution of oil contamination in cold-region soils. These findings contribute to a better understanding of oil transformation under cold-climate conditions and provide a framework for assessing the degree and characteristics of oil weathering and interpreting the weathering history of oil spills, which may support their assessment, management, and remediation in cold-region peatland environments.

items.title: Tribute to Prof Keith Boardman, AO, FRS, FATSE, FAA on his 100<sup>th</sup> birthday (August 16<sup>th</sup> 2026).
items.abstract: Keith Boardman carried out brilliant research when he led a group as Chief Research Scientist in the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Division of Plant Industry (Canberra) from 1960 to 1977. This research was highly successful. Working with Dr. Jan Anderson (a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) and a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science and Technology (FAA), Boardman was able to isolate the first convincing separation of Photosystem I and Photosystem II particles (Boardman and Anderson 1964). In a short period of less than twenty years, Keith Boardman, with the aid of Jan Anderson, brought photosynthesis into the modern era. Keith then had a productive career as an administrator with the CSIRO (becoming Chairman and Chief Executive) and advisor on science to several government bodies. Keith Boardman was honoured by election as a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science and Technology (FAA, 1972), a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS, 1978), a Fellow of the Australian Academy and Engineering (FATSE, 1986) and an Officer of the Order of Australia (AO, 1993).

items.title: Invasion analysis for structured populations: analytical principles and numerical workflows
items.abstract: All real populations show some form of structure—differences among individuals, such as life stage or physiological condition, that shape a species' ability to persist. Yet it remains challenging to incorporate population structure into models of species interactions. We provide a general framework for studying competition in structured populations by quantifying species' invasion growth rates. The crux of our approach is separation of timescales: the initial dynamics of a structured population depend on how exactly it is introduced, but these transient differences do not affect long-term invasion success. Depending on the research question, the relevant long-term growth rate when rare may equivalently be derived using analytical separation of timescales, matrix population theory, or numerical simulations. Using case studies spanning developmental stage, environmental state, and infection status, we illustrate how our methodology derives simple, ecologically meaningful invasion conditions for a variety of systems. Finally, we extend the approach to fluctuating resident dynamics, showing how to use simulations or a general mathematical framework known as Floquet theory to correctly quantify invasion growth. By unifying the quantitative methods of population biology and community ecology, our framework will allow ecologists to study species persistence and coexistence across a greater variety of demographically complex systems.

items.title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
items.abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.

items.title: Seven myths about causal inference in ecology: clarifications and common ground
items.abstract: Identifying and quantifying causal relationships from data is a central goal in ecology and conservation. To achieve this goal, ecologists are increasingly applying frameworks and methods from the broader, multidisciplinary causal inference literature. These applications have generated both enthusiasm and skepticism. Here, we address seven common sources of skepticism that we see as myths. Much of this skepticism treats causal inference as a competing research paradigm. However, it is better understood as a set of ideas and practices that can sharpen ecological reasoning and strengthen empirical evidence. The value of causal inference lies in clarifying the assumptions required to interpret statistical associations causally and in encouraging researchers to state these assumptions explicitly, justifying them using prior knowledge and biological reasoning. In this sense, causal inference does not replace what ecologists already do well. Rather, it helps reveal, refine, and communicate the logic already underlying empirical research with causal aims. Across the seven concerns that we examine, a common message emerges: debates about causal inference should focus less on labels and techniques and more on whether the assumptions behind a causal claim are credible, clearly stated, and fit for purpose when making causal claims in ecology.

items.title: Ecology, phylogeny, and host traits shape avian malaria infections and interaction networks in high Andean Polylepis forests
items.abstract: Parasites play important roles in ecological and evolutionary processes, yet host–parasite dynamics in high-elevation Neotropical ecosystems remain poorly understood. Specifically, we asked whether haemosporidian assemblages at extreme elevations are dominated by Leucocytozoon, whether infection patterns are phylogenetically and ecologically structured across avian hosts, and whether infections produce detectable physiological costs at the community level. We sampled 214 individuals representing 37 bird species across three Polylepis forest sites (~3700–4000 m a.s.l.) in northern Ecuador, and screened blood samples for Plasmodium, Haemoproteus, and Leucocytozoon. Overall infection prevalence was 39.7%, with Leucocytozoon accounting for 88.2% of infections. We identified 63 parasite lineages, including 40 previously undescribed lineages. Infection probability varied among host species, increased with body mass, and showed phylogenetic structure, with closely related host species tending to show similar infection probability. Host-specific analyses revealed non-random phylogenetic structure of parasite assemblages in several bird species. Quantitative host–parasite interaction networks showed low connectance, moderate specialization, and significant departures from null expectations, suggesting that only a limited subset of potential host–parasite associations is realized. Despite high prevalence and frequent coinfections, infection status was not associated with body condition, hemoglobin concentration, or hematocrit. Together, these results indicate that haemosporidian communities in high Andean Polylepis forests are highly diverse and exhibit pronounced non-random and phylogenetic structure in their host–parasite associations. The presence of numerous novel lineages further suggests that parasite diversity in tropical high-elevation ecosystems remains substantially underestimated.

items.title: Water Quality Variability and Its Implications for Mosquito Breeding: A Comparative Study from Northern Nigeria
items.abstract: Abstract Background Mosquito breeding habitat characteristics critically influence the abundance, survival, and distribution of malaria vectors. Aquatic habitat physicochemical properties influence larval development and may contribute to ecological adaptation and insecticide resistance. This study evaluated the physicochemical characteristics of mosquito breeding habitats across selected locations in Kano, Bauchi, and Kogi States, Nigeria. Methods A comparative cross-sectional study was conducted using water samples collected from nine mosquito breeding habitats, with three sampling sites selected from each state. Water temperature was measured in situ , while pH, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, total dissolved solids (TDS), salinity, turbidity, total hardness, ammonia, nitrate, and phosphate concentrations were determined using standard analytical procedures. All measurements were performed in triplicate. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), with statistical significance set at P P ) in several physicochemical parameters among the sampling locations, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in habitat quality. Conclusions The findings demonstrate that mosquito breeding habitats in northern Nigeria differ significantly in their physicochemical characteristics, reflecting varying environmental and anthropogenic influences. These variations may affect habitat suitability for mosquito development and have important implications for malaria vector ecology and integrated vector management. Vector surveillance programmes should include continuous monitoring of local water quality to strengthen evidence-based malaria control strategies.

items.title: Natural history update of the orange-clawed hermit crab Calcinus tibicen (Herbst, 1791) (Anomura: Diogenidae) in the Southwestern Atlantic
items.abstract: Abstract The Calcinus tibicen (Herbst, 1791) is one of the most widespread species of hermit crab in the Western Atlantic. However, important gaps remain in our knowledge of its ecology, distribution, and natural history in the South Atlantic. In this study, we present updated information on the geographic distribution and natural history of C. tibicen , including new records of its habitats, shell occupancy, and symbiotic associations. Data on its distribution, habitat use, and shell occupancy were obtained from field collections along the Brazilian coast. Additional occurrence records were compiled from literature reviews and public databases. In total, we recorded 1,306 occurrences, including 497 new records (417 in the North Atlantic and 80 in the South Atlantic). The species inhabits diverse microhabitats and is associated with several marine organisms, including anemones, corals, barnacles, mussels, sponges, zoanthids, and macroalgae. Specimens from Brazilian ecoregions primarily occupied gastropod shells, and epibionts were frequently recorded on these shells. Additionally, we present the first documented cases of C. tibicen associations with anemones and chitons. These findings expand our knowledge of this species' natural history and ecological interactions in the South Atlantic.

items.title: Platform critical toponymy: A reflexive extension of Bourdieu’s Theory of Practice for 21st-Century Critical Toponymy
items.abstract: Abstract Toponyms are not passive labels. They are arenas where spatial inscription, social memory, and distributive struggle converge. Although existing critical toponymy offers profound insights, it is being unsettled by a new historical condition: the platformization of place naming. This article proposes platform critical toponymy, a new paradigm of critical toponymy grounded in a reflexive extension of Bourdieu's theory of practice. By introducing three recursive mechanisms—platformization, datafication, and algorithmic governance—it reconstructs the field-capital-habitus triad to analyze how digital platform infrastructures reorganize the conditions under which toponyms are assigned, remembered, contested, and governed, and to advance data sovereignty, algorithmic accountability, and the democratization of naming rights. This paper (a) traces how critical toponymy expanded from colonial naming and identity recovery to heritage commodification and digital inscription, exposing the field's persistent urban normativity and Global North bias; (b) reconceives the field as a multi-scalar ecology in which state standardization, platform ranking, corporate branding, and local inscription overlap rather than simply oppose one another; (c) treats naming capital as a convertible and auditable asset composed of institutional, economic, cultural, social, and platform-symbolic forms, and clarifies the conditions under which such conversion is legitimized, contested, or blocked; and (d) reconceptualizes habitus as an evolving, politically and technologically mediated disposition shaped by official, commercial, community, platform-mediated, and academic rationalities. The paradigm is tested through four cross-contextually comparable cases. The article concludes by proposing that future research take data sovereignty, algorithmic accountability, participatory mapping, and the democratization of naming rights as its core concerns.

items.title: Differential metabolite production underlies disruption of the cystic fibrosis airway microbiota by pathogens.
items.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) results in accumulation of mucus in the airways that promotes pathogen colonization, leading to respiratory exacerbations, lung failure, and death. The CF airway harbors a complex microbiota, including pathogens and oropharyngeal bacteria. Here, we reanalyzed 5,260 16S rRNA gene microbiota data sets to infer associations between members of the CF microbiota. We determined that pathogens are more likely to proliferate and dominate when present, while oropharyngeal bacteria are generally present at lower abundances. We found that higher diversity and increasing numbers of pairwise associations between bacteria were positively correlated with lung function. In contrast, dominance of the microbiota by pathogens was associated with loss of lung function. We determined that pathogens are largely negatively associated with each other and oropharyngeal bacteria, suggesting they are antagonistic toward other bacteria. As a first test of this hypothesis, we cultured 1,597 isolates from 96 people with CF and performed 12,542 coculture assays against eight representative pathogens and oropharyngeal bacteria, finding 23% of interactions resulted in inhibition. Among our isolates, Pseudomonas were the most inhibitory, but we observed variable activity between different isolates. We further found Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, even those from the same donor and time point, exhibited significant differences in their metabolome and bioactivity profiles that correlated with acquisition of mutations. Together, our results suggest that pathogens may disrupt the CF microbiota and proliferate in part through bioactive metabolite production. Furthermore, these data highlight that characterizing multiple isolates is necessary to capture the full landscape of chemically mediated interactions within microbiomes.IMPORTANCEThe cystic fibrosis (CF) airway harbors a complex microbiota, including oropharyngeal bacteria and opportunistic pathogens that establish chronic infections. We found that microbiota diversity is correlated with health and that a pathogen-dominated microbiota is associated with low lung function. We then inferred potential microbial interactions by determining abundance associations between CF genera, which suggested that pathogens antagonize other bacteria. To test this prediction, we cultured bacteria from people with CF and performed thousands of coculture assays, finding that approximately one-quarter of interactions resulted in growth inhibition. Pseudomonas broadly inhibited other members of the CF airway microbiota. However, we observed marked variability in bioactivity and metabolite profiles of Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, even from the same donor at the same time. Our results suggest that pathogens disrupt the CF microbiota, possibly through bioactive metabolite production, and that characterizing multiple isolates is necessary to capture the complete picture of interactions in these communities.

items.title: Industrialization restructures the domestic dog gut microbiome while preserving host specificity.
items.abstract: Industrialization has reshaped human gut microbiomes, but its effects on other human-associated mammals remain poorly understood. Domestic dogs provide an informative comparative system because they have shared human environments and food systems for millennia yet retain distinct host biology. However, most canine microbiome studies have focused on industrialized companion, colony, or controlled-feeding dogs, limiting our understanding of the ecological range of the domestic dog gut microbiome. We analyzed fecal 16S rRNA gene profiles from 261 dogs sampled across Nepal, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles; 257 dogs remained after excluding those with reported recent antibiotic exposure. Lifestyle was the strongest measured correlate of canine gut bacterial composition, and this association persisted in restricted analyses of mature, non-shelter dogs sampled from temperate regions. Industrialized dogs differed from non-industrialized dogs through directional genus-level shifts, prevalence-defined VANISH-like and BloSSUM-like bacterial guilds, coabundance structure, and shifts in predicted functional potential. Non-industrialized dogs were not microbiologically uniform: pastoralist dogs showed non-industrialized gut bacterial community profiles but diverged from a simple forager-to-industrialized continuum. Cross-species comparisons with humans sampled across matched lifestyle categories showed parallel lifestyle-associated restructuring in both hosts, but host species remained the dominant axis of variation, and genus-level responses were largely host specific. These findings expand the ecological baseline for canine gut bacterial communities and identify industrialization-associated lifestyle change as a major axis of gut bacterial community restructuring in a long-term human-associated mammal. More broadly, they show that shared lifestyle transitions can impose parallel ecological pressures across host species without overriding host-specific community assembly. Importance Domestic dogs are one of the closest animal companions of humans, yet we know surprisingly little about how their gut microbiomes vary outside industrialized pet populations. This study shows that industrialization-associated lifestyle change is not only relevant to human microbiomes but also a broader ecological force that reshapes gut microbial communities in animals living alongside us. By comparing dogs across diverse human lifestyles, we show that shared environments can impose parallel pressures on the gut bacterial communities of humans and dogs, while each host maintains a distinct microbial identity. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities are shaped by the interaction between host biology and changing ecological conditions. Expanding microbiome research beyond industrialized settings is therefore essential for understanding what microbial diversity has been retained, altered, or lost during recent lifestyle transitions.

items.title: Enhanced control ability against cyanobacteria through combinations of multiple algicidal bacterial strains.
items.abstract: Algicidal bacteria are promising microorganisms for controlling harmful algal blooms (HABs) because of their ability to inhibit algal growth or lyse algal cells in aquatic systems. However, our understanding of how to enhance their performance within complex microbial communities remains limited. In this study, we evaluated the algicidal activity of previously isolated bacterial strains in a constructed cyanobacterial consortium dominated by Microcystis aeruginosa and containing indigenous lake microorganisms. Our results revealed that while individual strains generally showed limited inhibitory effects, certain strain combinations exhibited pronounced algicidal activity. Notably, co-inoculation of strain Chromobacterium sp. MERYL1-35 and strain Paucibacter sp. MERXLGS1 achieved the highest algicidal efficiency among the tested treatments. Growth assays and quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated that these two strains establish a distinct antagonistic interspecies interaction, where Chromobacterium exerts strong inhibitory effects on Paucibacter , accompanied by significant expression alterations in certain bacterial virulence and interaction-associated proteins. We propose that this collective enhancement in population survivability and antagonistic potential of Chromobacterium substantially contributes to the enhanced algicidal activity in the dual-strain system. These findings provide new insights into the ability-enhancing strategy of algicidal bacteria and their complex interactions with target cyanobacteria.IMPORTANCEEco-friendly and sustainable control methods of harmful algal blooms (HABs) have been urgently needed in recent years. In this study, we demonstrated that the removal efficiency of cyanobacteria by algicidal bacteria can be substantially enhanced through designed co-inoculation strategies. We found that the enhanced algicidal activity of the combined Chromobacterium and Paucibacter dual-strain inoculations is mediated by a unique antagonistic interaction, which differs from other consortia that more likely arise from cooperative strain interactions. These findings advance our understanding of the complex microbial interplay between algicidal bacteria and phytoplankton and may provide new insights into the development of biological control strategies targeting HABs.

items.title: Heritable differences in sexual signaling and morphology between urban and forest túngara frogs.
items.abstract: Urbanization drastically changes our planet, and persistence in urban areas requires species to adapt. Sexual signaling has been argued to be a driver of population divergence between urban and non-urban populations, but it is often unclear whether population divergence is adaptive and caused by plastic and/or genetic processes. Calling behavior of urban and forest túngara frogs (Engystomops pustulosus) provides a well-known example of urban adaptation. However, we lack insight into the underlying genetic divergence between populations and heritability of calling behavior. Our aim was to examine the relative contributions of plastic and genetic components to urban-forest differences in sexual signaling and associated morphological traits. We reared frogs of urban and forest descent in a common garden using a paternal half-sib breeding design and used quantitative genetic approaches informed by whole-genome sequencing to estimate heritability. We show heritable urban-forest differences in call rate and amplitude (depending on the social environment), and in body size and condition. Moreover, behavioral as well as morphological traits had low to moderate heritability estimates. Our study provides insights into the underlying mechanisms of urban versus forest phenotypic divergence and suggests that sexual signaling and associated morphological traits in túngara frogs have the potential to adaptively evolve.

items.title: Food plants play a significant role in influencing the ontogeny of sexual size dimorphism in the fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda.
items.abstract: The ontogenetic timing of sexual size dimorphism (SSD) emergence in insects, as well as the influence of larval dietary quality on dimorphic growth patterns, remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of host plant species - corn versus sugarcane - on life history traits and developmental growth trajectories in Spodoptera frugiperda (J.E. Smith) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), using a large sample size. Larvae reared on corn exhibited significantly shorter larval development durations, greater pupal masses, higher growth rates, reduced SSD, and less weight loss compared to those reared on sugarcane. The onset of SSD in individuals fed on corn was first detected 1 day prior to pupation, during the fifth instar, whereas in those fed on sugarcane, SSD became evident approximately 10 days earlier, during the third instar. This difference in the timing of SSD emergence is attributable to the prolonged developmental period observed in males. Female larvae achieved higher growth rates than males, primarily due to their extended larval development duration. Additionally, male larvae reared on corn showed a significant positive correlation between larval mass and development time, while those reared on sugarcane exhibited a slight negative correlation. These findings collectively enhance our understanding of the ontogeny of SSD and highlight the role of nutritional environment in shaping sex-specific developmental trajectories.

items.title: Are vacant lots within urban blocks a risk factor for Aedes aegypti higher occurrence and density on neighbouring properties?
items.abstract: The present study aimed to evaluate the potential relationship between the presence of vacant lots and the occurrence of Aedes aegypti (Diptera: Culicidae) mosquitoes in adjacent occupied properties. For that, we used entomological traps and georeferencing tools. The use of entomological traps, for example, Adultrap and ovitrap, is among the main strategies for the identification and monitoring of Ae. aegypti populations and its hotspots, often combined with geographic monitoring systems. A total of 225 ovitraps and 225 Adultraps, corresponding to 25 traps of each type per sentinel geographic unit (UGS), were inspected during each weekly sampling round, across nine defined areas, known as UGSs, in the Brazilian triple-border municipality of Foz do Iguaçu during a dengue epidemic period. The results were used to calculate the Adultrap Positivity Index (API) and Adult Density Index (ADI), as well as the Ovitrap Positivity Index (OPI) and the Egg Density Index (EDI). Vacant lots were identified through satellite images, and the results were calculated using Generalized Linear Mixed Model. Trap readings were aggregated across 143 urban blocks. Our statistical analysis detected no statistically significant association between block-level vacant-lot coverage and any of the evaluated entomological indices. For API, a 10-percentage-point increase in vacant-lot coverage corresponded to an estimated 5.7% reduction in positive Adultrap readings (expected-count ratio = 0.943; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.880-1.011; p = 0.101), although the CI was compatible with effects ranging from a 12.0% reduction to a 1.1% increase.

items.title: Beyond adversity: Dispositional mindfulness as a potential link between positive childhood experiences and lower hair cortisol concentration in adulthood.
items.abstract: Background Advers childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with altered stress regulation, yet less is known about how positive childhood experiences (PCEs) contribute to adaptive physiological functioning. PCEs may represent developmental resources that promote adaptive psychological and biological functioning. This study examined whether PCEs were associated with cumulative cortisol exposure, indexed by hair cortisol concentration (HCC), through dispositional mindfulness and resilience, and whether these associations varied according to cumulative childhood adversity. Methods A community sample of 210 adults (M age = 28.95, SD = 10.20, range = 19-77; 74.8% female) completed an online assessment battery. A subsample of 120 participants provided hair samples for cortisol assessment. Participants completed measures of Protective and Compensatory experiences (PACE significance), ACEs, dispositional mindfulness (MAAS), resilience (RS-14), and current stress (LSC-R). Hair cortisol concentration (HCC) from 3 cm proximal segment was assessed as an indicator of cumulative hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity. Results PACE sig. showed indirect association with lower HCC through greater dispositional mindfulness, whereas resilience did not. Moderation analyses suggested that the positive PACE sig.-MAAS association was stronger at higher levels of ACE exposure. Positive and adverse childhood experiences frequently co-occurred among participants with higher cumulative adversity. Conclusions These findings extend existing evidence on the psychological benefits associated with PCEs by providing preliminary support for dispositional mindfulness as a potential link between PCEs and lower cumulative cortisol exposure in adulthood. Considering positive developmental experiences alongside adversity may improve understanding of individual differences in psychological functioning and long-term HPA-axis activity.

items.title: Lost in Translation? A Scoping Review on the Reporting of Team-Based Learning Adaptations.
items.abstract: Introduction Team-based learning (TBL) is a popular instructional method within medical education. Much research has compared the efficacy of TBL to other learning approaches. However, little is known about how and why TBL is contextualised and enacted in practice. To address this gap, we asked: How often, in what ways, and for what reasons has TBL been adapted in medical education? Methods A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR framework. Searches of seven databases were conducted in 2024 and 2026. Articles were included if they were English-language empirical studies examining the application of TBL within medical education. Data was extracted regarding whether TBL had followed Michaelsen's original sequence of (broadly) Pre-class Preparation, Readiness Assessment (individual and team) and Application Exercises, or had been adapted. If adapted, we examined which elements of TBL had been contextualized along with the rationale for these changes. Results Across the 354 articles reviewed, more than half (n = 183) reported contextualized TBL. The number of articles reporting adaptations increased over time, across all contexts. Which elements of TBL had been adapted and in what ways varied widely but the most frequently changed or omitted component was the Application Exercise (49%), followed by Pre-class Preparation (34%, 62/183). Explicit rationales for adaptations were relatively rare (70/183 studies) but aligned with three broad categories: moving TBL online during the COVID-19 pandemic, saving time/workload, and educational efficacy. Discussion TBL contextualization was commonplace. While this itself is not problematic, there was little explicit articulation of how and why medical educators have adapted TBL for their own contexts. More explicit and better reporting of the rationale for TBL contextualization should allow scholars to identify and explore context-specific factors such as institutional pressures, cultural influences, educator preferences etc. that shape how TBL is enacted and how this may alter its efficacy and utility.

items.title: The Italian version of the benevolent childhood experiences scale: psychometric properties and incremental validity in predicting resilience beyond adverse childhood experiences.
items.abstract: Background Positive childhood experiences are increasingly recognized as developmental resources that may promote psychological adaptation beyond the absence of adversity. This study examined the psychometric properties of the Italian version of the Benevolent Childhood Experiences Scale (BCEs) and its incremental contribution to resilience beyond adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Methods A community sample of 644 Italian adults (68.94% women; M_age = 28.22, SD = 9.78) completed the BCEs, ACE-Q, and Brief Resilience Scale. Item endorsement rates, internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance across gender, correlations, and hierarchical regression analyses were conducted. Results Item endorsement was high, and a one-factor confirmatory factor analysis using WLSMV showed overall acceptable model fit. Internal consistency was moderate (KR-20 = 0.63; ω = 0.66), and gender invariance was partially supported. BCEs were negatively associated with ACEs and positively associated with resilience. In hierarchical regression analyses, BCEs made a small but statistically significant incremental contribution to the prediction of resilience beyond age, gender, and ACEs (ΔR² = 0.017). Conclusions Findings provide initial support for the Italian BCEs as a brief measure of benevolent childhood experiences and suggest a modest incremental contribution of BCEs to perceived resilience beyond adverse childhood experiences.

items.title: Distribution of combined p-values for baseline variables in a consecutive sample of randomized controlled trials.
items.abstract: Background Combined p-values derived from summary statistics of baseline variables in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are expected to follow a uniform distribution. Extreme values indicate similarity or dissimilarity across randomized groups. To date, investigations have been limited to a small number of clinical fields; here, we assess the distribution of combined p-values in a consecutive sample of RCTs. Methods Based on a PubMed search between February 1 and 18, 2022, 568 RCTs were included. Baseline variables were analysed using Carlisle's method, yielding one combined p-value per RCT. A threshold of combined p-values of p ≤ 0.05 or p ≥ 0.95 was applied. Differences in combined p-value distributions between subgroups were assessed using the two-sample Anderson-Darling (AD) test. Results 26.2% (149/568) of the included RCTs had combined p-values of p ≤ 0.05 or p ≥ 0.95, compared with the 10% expected by chance. Of these, 104 RCTs (18.3%) were found in the upper extreme tail of p ≥ 0.95 and 45 RCTs (7.9%) in the lower extreme tail of p ≤ 0.05. Smaller RCTs (N ≤ 100) had more extreme combined p-values than larger RCTs (N > 100) (AD test p = 0.001). RCTs with > 7 baseline variables had more extreme combined p-values than those with ≤ 7 variables (AD test p = 0.004). A sensitivity analysis showed that 20.6% of RCTs still had extreme combined p-values after controlling for reporting errors related to SE and SD. Another sensitivity analysis showed that some extreme results could be explained by assuming high correlations between baseline variables within an RCT. Conclusion A substantially higher proportion of RCTs in a consecutive sample exhibited extreme similarities or dissimilarities in baseline characteristics across groups than expected by chance (26.2% vs 10%), indicating problems with randomisation. Further investigation into the causes and implications of implausible baseline distributions in RCTs is warranted. Registered 2023-03-20 at https://www.researchweb.org/fourol/project/280487.

items.title: Increasing Support for Humanitarian Aid to Palestinian Civilians During the Israel-Gaza War Through Ideologically Tailored Social-Media Campaigns.
items.abstract: Promoting support for humanitarian aid to an adversarial outgroup is difficult during active war. We introduce a digital field-experimental approach that embeds psychologically grounded interventions in people's actual social-media environments. During the Israel-Gaza war, 6,105 adult Jewish Israeli Facebook users were assigned to a no-study-campaign control condition, a humanitarian-moral campaign emphasizing humanitarian obligation, or an instrumental-security campaign presenting aid as advancing Israeli security. Days after the campaigns ended, 4,784 participants completed the follow-up survey. Support for humanitarian aid declined in the control condition but increased under both campaigns, suggesting that psychological social-media interventions can buffer or reverse erosion of humanitarian attitudes during acute conflict. Political ideology moderated relative effectiveness: the instrumental-security campaign was especially effective among conservatives, whereas liberals responded positively to both. These findings provide partial support for ideological message matching and offer a scalable, ecologically valid framework for testing intergroup interventions in real-world settings.

items.title: Targeting Noradrenergic Regulation of the Astrocyte-Neuron Lactate Shuttle in Recognition Memory.
items.abstract: Noradrenergic signaling modulates memory formation. In astrocytes, noradrenaline (NA) activates β 2 -adrenergic receptors (β 2 -AR), promoting glycogenolysis and lactate production. Astrocyte-derived lactate contributes to synaptic plasticity through the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (ANLS). Here, we investigated the contribution of lactate-dependent processes to noradrenergic modulation of object recognition memory (ORM) using the novel object recognition (NOR) task and examined whether β 2 -AR mediate NA-induced changes in intracellular lactate levels in cultured astrocytes. Female Swiss mice were trained in the NOR task and treated with atomoxetine (ATO), a NA reuptake inhibitor, alone or combined with α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid (4CIN), a non-subtype-selective MCT inhibitor. Additional groups received the selective β 2 -AR antagonist ICI-118,551 (ICI) alone or combined with L-lactate. In parallel, primary rat astrocyte cultures expressing a FRET-based lactate sensor were used to assess intracellular lactate levels following NA application, MCT inhibition, or β 2 -AR blockade with butaxamine (BUT). ATO enhanced ORM, an effect prevented by co-administration of 4CIN. β 2 -AR blockade with ICI disrupted ORM, whereas L-lactate administration restored memory performance to control levels. In cultured astrocytes, NA increased intracellular lactate levels, consistent with β 2 -AR mediated stimulation of lactate production, whereas 4CIN increased intracellular lactate accumulation, likely due to reduced MCT-dependent lactate export. BUT prevented the NA-induced lactate increase, supporting the involvement of β 2 -AR signaling in this response. These findings support a functional relationship between noradrenergic β 2 -adrenergic signaling, MCT activity, and ORM, while the cellular findings indicate that β 2 -AR signaling contributes to NA-induced changes in intracellular lactate levels in cultured astrocytes.

items.title: CzeLex: A megastudy dataset of concreteness, imageability, age of acquisition, valence, and gender ratings for 9601 Czech words.
items.abstract: Understanding how semantics are processed at the lexical level has been a key aim for the cognitive sciences, with large-scale semantic rating studies in different languages playing a crucial role in facilitating the advancement and development of theories of lexical processing, as well as providing valuable methodological resources that can be used in empirical investigations. In this paper, we present the CzeLex database, a megastudy of 9601 Czech words that have been normed along five psycholinguistic dimensions from a large sample of 4405 Czech-speaking participants. We provide individual rating data at the item and participant levels, as well as aggregated data from both mean ratings and latent means derived using cumulative-link mixed modeling, along with a comprehensive analysis comparing aggregation methods. We demonstrate that the dataset has good reliability and that specific dimensions predict lexical processing measures in a lexical decision task, regardless of the aggregation method used. These norms are the largest available subjective rating resource for Czech and further contribute to the growing body of languages with openly available data on these dimensions. We hope that the dataset will be a valuable resource for researchers working on Czech, in addition to opening up new opportunities for cross-linguistic semantic investigations. All data, code, and analyses are available at https://osf.io/tqxfm .

items.title: Effective trialing of digital interventions in daily life - the mental health perspective.
items.abstract: Digital mental health interventions show promise but have yet to meet expectations. We discuss gaps between promising results of pilot studies and null findings in randomized controlled trials, focusing on two major approaches: just-in-time relapse prevention and just-in-time adaptive interventions. We propose that relapse prevention will profit from long-term studies capturing emerging episodes, and we suggest a novel framework for adaptive interventions including causality testing to proceed towards effective trialing.

items.title: Exploring the link between burning mouth syndrome and psychological factors: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a chronic disorder marked by burning sensations and pain in the lips, oral mucosa, and tongue, with recent studies indicating a higher prevalence of psychological symptoms and mental disorders among affected patients. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the association between BMS and psychological factors by systematically searching databases including PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ProQuest, Wiley, and Cochrane for studies published up to February 2026, assessing methodological quality and bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and applying a random effects model for meta-analysis. A total of 52 studies were included, with 16 addressing dichotomous outcomes and 36 examining continuous outcomes; results showed that individuals with BMS had 3.19 times higher odds of experiencing psychological disorders compared to controls (odds ratio 3.19; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.51-4.05, P < 0.001), and a strong positive association was found between BMS and psychological factors (standardized mean difference 0.80; 95% CI 0.67-0.93). These findings underscore the significant relationship between BMS and psychological factors, highlighting the necessity of psychological assessment and intervention as part of a multidisciplinary approach to BMS management.

items.title: Challenges in developing effective psychological wellbeing strategies among clinical diagnostic radiographers: A qualitative study.
items.abstract: Introduction The roots of healthcare delivery are premised on the core values of care and compassion. Research, however, indicates that the emotional costs of witnessing patients' pain and distress can adversely impact caregivers' ability to demonstrate compassion and empathy. Radiographers' roles are considered by many to be primarily technical and are often overlooked as a profession when considering practitioners psychological wellbeing. Building on the findings of recent research which evaluated the clinical factors impacting radiographers' psychological wellbeing in the UK, this research sought to evaluate the challenges radiographers face in developing effective wellbeing strategies. Methods A qualitative approach was used to generate data collection through in-depth one-to-one semi-structured interviews with twenty-three radiography practitioners working in the UK. Recruitment was undertaken via the research team's professional connections, the UKIO Congress Research Hub (2024) and the Society of Radiographers Live. Results The reflexive thematic analysis generated three themes focussed on the challenges and strategies radiographers use in safeguarding their psychological wellbeing in practice; 'organisational culture of carrying on', 'moral injury' and 'fear of judgement and consequences'. Conclusion The three identified themes highlight the complex difficulties and challenges radiographers face in safeguarding their psychological wellbeing. Although guilt and stigma associated with mental health are not unique to radiography, factors such as role perception, the need to keep going and feelings of professional isolation must be addressed if radiographers are to be supported in sustaining their mental health. Implications for practice Without addressing the institutionalised social constructs associated with mental health at an organisational level and the perceived inability of those experiencing difficulties to carry out their roles, stigma, discrimination and moral injury will persist. By challenging these constructs through education and openness, staff wellbeing, morale will be enhanced together with the delivery of care and compassion towards service users.

items.title: Current knowledge, key gaps, and opportunities for future research on high-impact, modifiable lifestyle behaviors to promote healthy aging in adults with cystic fibrosis in the era of modulator therapy.
items.abstract: Aging in cystic fibrosis (CF), once a hopeful possibility, is now a celebrated reality for many and attributable to expert multidisciplinary care, persistent research efforts, and fervent advocacy. The median age of survival of people with CF (PWCF) increased dramatically with the advent of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapies, particularly elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in 2019. However, as PWCF live longer, healthy aging is susceptible to the compound impact of residual CFTR dysfunction, chronic inflammation, emerging comorbidities, complexities of chronic disease management, and psychosocial burdens. We define healthy aging as maintaining physical and mental health in adults so they can remain autonomous and independent as long as possible, while also adapting lifestyle habits to support well-being and improve overall quality of life. Lifestyle factors, such as stress, nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and treatment adherence, are known to impact health outcomes in the general population. Identifying, testing, and implementing behavioral interventions addressing these factors has the potential to augment medical advances in CF care. Although the aging population of PWCF is increasingly heterogeneous and shaped by unique individual ecosystems, lifestyle behaviors impact all patients and crosscut this diversity. As CF science continues to advance toward curative therapies, parallel CF-specific research advances on modifiable lifestyle behaviors may support healthier aging and improve health outcomes. This paper outlines the current state of knowledge, identifies critical gaps, and highlights key opportunities for future research targeting modifiable lifestyle behaviors to promote healthy aging, preserve functional independence, and improve quality of life in the growing population of adults with CF.

items.title: Social Determinants of Sleep Health in Survivors of Childhood Cancer: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Survivors of childhood cancer frequently experience poor sleep quality, which affects behavioural, emotional, cognitive and physical health. Sleep health is multidimensional, encompassing regularity, satisfaction, alertness, timing, efficiency and duration, yet the influence of social, environmental and interpersonal factors on these dimensions remains poorly understood. This review examines sleep health dimensions among childhood cancer survivors and their associations with social determinants of health. A systematic review was completed in November 2025 using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO databases. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts, assessing links between social determinants and sleep outcomes. The risk of bias was evaluated using the ROBINS-E tool. Of 485 publications screened, 14 met the inclusion criteria. Most studies assessed sleep disturbances (n = 10), with fewer examining sleep duration (n = 5), alertness (n = 3) and sleep efficiency (n = 2). Social determinants, including race/ethnicity (n = 5), education (n = 6) and employment (n = 4), were associated with specific sleep dimensions; however, comprehensive analyses across the full spectrum of sleep remain limited. Social determinants influence several sleep dimensions among childhood cancer survivors, yet research rarely considers the multidimensional nature of sleep health. We propose a socio-ecological, multidimensional model to guide the development of targeted interventions and reduce sleep health disparities in this population.
